Refuse any statin due to age

Clinical assessment and risk discussion

Calculate the Pooled Cohort risk

A.q: A 27-year-old man has clusters of small yellowish-white papules (eruptive xanthomas) on his elbows after a weekend of heavy drinking. His triglyceride is 900 mg/dL and his low-density lipoprotein is normal. Which lipoproteins are most likely extremely elevated?
opts: Low-density lipoprotein and lipoprotein(a)
His low-density lipoprotein is normal, and these particles are tied to tendon xanthomas and atherosclerosis rather than eruptive papules.
Chylomicrons or very-low-density lipoprotein
Correct. Eruptive xanthomas are usually seen with extremely high chylomicrons or very-low-density lipoprotein, and alcohol inhibits hepatic fatty-acid oxidation, raising triglyceride.
Intermediate-density lipoprotein alone
Intermediate-density lipoprotein is the remnant after triglyceride delivery, not the particle behind eruptive xanthomas.
High-density lipoprotein and apolipoprotein A-I
High-density lipoprotein and its structural apolipoprotein A-I are protective and do not produce xanthomas.

A.io: Aortic regurgitation
A.q: Which cause of aortic regurgitation is a disease of the aortic root rather than the valve?
opts: Marfan syndrome
Correct. Marfan syndrome is an aortic root disease, alongside aortic dissection, cystic medial degeneration, familial aneurysm, aortitis and hypertension. The root dilates and pulls the cusps apart.
Rheumatic fever
Rheumatic fever damages the valve itself and is listed among the valvular causes of aortic regurgitation, not the root causes such as Marfan syndrome.
A bicuspid aortic valve
A congenital bicuspid valve is a valvular cause of aortic regurgitation. The root causes include Marfan syndrome, dissection and aortitis.
Infective endocarditis
Endocarditis destroys the valve cusps and is a valvular cause of aortic regurgitation; it can also cause the acute form. Marfan syndrome is a root cause.

opts: Evolocumab before trying a statin
Correct. The steps must be followed: high-intensity statins first, then ezetimibe and nicotinic acid, and the injectable only for patients refractory to drug therapy.
A high-intensity statin
A high-intensity statin is the common first regimen in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and is entirely appropriate.
A low saturated-fat, low-cholesterol diet
A diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol is part of his treatment, alongside the statin, so it is appropriate.
Addressing smoking and blood pressure
Aggressive reduction of vascular risk factors such as smoking, hypertension and diabetes is recommended, so this is appropriate.

opts: 50% or higher
Correct. Normal ejection fraction is 50% or more, and it is the dividing line for treatment: 50% or higher is preserved ejection fraction, 49% or less falls into a reduced group.
80% or higher
That sets normal far too high. Normal left ventricular ejection fraction is 50% or higher.
70% or higher
That sets normal too high and would label many healthy hearts abnormal. Normal is 50% or higher.
30% or higher
That sets normal far too low; 30% is well within reduced ejection fraction. Normal is 50% or higher.

A.q: A 62-year-old man arrives with blood pressure 232/128, confusion and blurred vision. Over the first hour, how far should his mean arterial pressure be reduced?
opts: By at least half, to remove the immediate danger
Overly rapid reduction is specifically harmful; the first-hour limit is about a fifth to a quarter of the mean arterial pressure.
By no more than about twenty to twenty-five percent

Correct, targeting around 160/100 to 110 over two to six hours and gradual normalization over a day or two. Autoregulation has adapted to the higher pressure, so dropping it to a chronic goal acutely can cause ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.
No reduction until imaging is complete
Stabilization and controlled reduction begin promptly alongside the focused assessment.
To below 130/80 within the first hour
Reducing to the chronic goal within an hour risks precisely the ischemic injury the controlled approach exists to avoid.

A.io: Acute myocardial infraction
A.q: A 60-year-old man with an occluded coronary artery is being rushed to the catheterization laboratory. His wife asks how quickly heart muscle is permanently damaged. Which time frame is most accurate?
opts: About 40 to 60 minutes
Correct. The heart is only 0.3% of body weight but consumes 7% of total oxygen demand, and irreversible injury occurs in about 40 to 60 minutes of ischemia. That is why rapid reperfusion matters.
About 24 to 48 hours
A day or two describes later healing, not the onset of permanent damage. Irreversible myocardial injury occurs within about 40 to 60 minutes of ischemia.
About 5 to 10 minutes
Ischemic muscle does not die within the first few minutes. Irreversible myocardial injury occurs after about 40 to 60 minutes, which is the window reperfusion races against.
About 6 to 8 hours
Waiting hours is far too long: irreversible myocardial injury begins after about 40 to 60 minutes of ischemia, so the damage accumulates well before six hours.

A.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
A.q: A 67-year-old woman has a holosystolic murmur, and the examiner is unsure whether it is tricuspid or mitral in origin. Which bedside maneuver best separates the two?
opts: Standing up quickly
Standing softens mitral regurgitation, but the maneuver that separates it from tricuspid regurgitation is inspiration, which increases the right-sided murmur.
Sustained handgrip
Handgrip raises resistance to ejection and makes mitral regurgitation louder, but it is not the maneuver named to separate the two. Inspiration increases only the tricuspid murmur.
Deep inspiration
Correct. Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so the tricuspid regurgitation murmur grows louder (the Carvallo sign) while mitral regurgitation does not. That distinguishes them.
Full expiration
Expiration increases left-sided murmurs, so it does not single out the tricuspid lesion. Inspiration makes tricuspid regurgitation louder and distinguishes it.

A.io: Mitral regurgitation
A.q: A 60-year-old man has palpitations and fatigue. There is a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla and is loudest in the left lateral decubitus position (lying on the left side). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mitral valve prolapse
Mitral valve prolapse gives a mid-systolic click at the apex and is usually asymptomatic. A holosystolic blowing murmur to the axilla is established mitral regurgitation.
Mitral regurgitation
Correct. Blowing means regurgitation and holosystolic narrows it to the mitral or tricuspid valve; the apex, the radiation to the axilla and the left lateral position mark mitral regurgitation.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic too, but it sits at the left mid or lower sternal border near the epigastrium and grows louder with inspiration. It does not radiate to the axilla.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the second right intercostal space radiating to the carotids. This murmur is blowing and holosystolic.

A.q: What is the treatment of choice in homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia?
opts: Fibrate monotherapy with diet
Triglyceride is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia, so a fibrate targets the wrong lipid.
Lifestyle and dietary change alone
Lifestyle cannot correct a receptor defect with total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 mg/dL.
Low-density lipoprotein apheresis
Correct. Apheresis, like dialysis, is the elective removal of low-density particles from the circulation; most patients also need more than one drug, starting with high-intensity statins.
Moderate-intensity statin alone
Moderate intensity is far too weak; high-intensity statins are the usual drug regimen alongside apheresis.

A.q: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has no cardiac symptoms. Her echocardiogram is normal. Which drug class is recommended first to lower her risk of heart failure?
opts: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
The antagonist belongs to symptomatic heart failure, strongly in reduced ejection fraction. Stage A with diabetes calls for a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Beta blocker as the first agent
A beta blocker is a stage B therapy, added once structural disease exists. In stage A with diabetes the first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Loop diuretic such as bumetanide
A loop diuretic treats congestion, which she does not have. Stage A with diabetes calls for a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. Risk factors with a normal heart and no symptoms are stage A, at risk for heart failure, and the one strong drug recommendation there is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes, not a beta blocker.

A.io: Non-ST segment elevation
A.q: A 64-year-old woman with an hour of chest pressure at rest has ST depression in two consecutive leads and a standard troponin I of 0.3 ng/mL. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Stable angina
Stable angina is exertional pain relieved by rest, with no troponin rise. Rest pain with ST depression and an abnormal troponin I is a non-ST-elevation infarction.
An ST-elevation myocardial infarction
An ST-elevation infarction needs ST elevation in two or more leads. She has ST depression with an abnormal standard troponin I (0.3 ng/mL), a non-ST-elevation infarction.
Unstable angina
Unstable angina has normal troponin levels. A standard troponin I of 0.3 ng/mL is above the 0.04 ng/mL cut-off, and the elevated troponin is what separates infarction from unstable angina.
A non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction

Correct. ST depression greater than 1 mm and/or T-wave inversion in two or more consecutive leads with an elevated troponin is a non-ST-elevation infarction. A standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal, and 0.3 ng/mL is well above it.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman with prior heart attacks collapsed without any prodrome while climbing stairs and woke within 20 seconds. Which referral should accompany her cardiac testing?
opts: Physical therapy referral
Physical therapy is not part of the listed cardiogenic work-up, which pairs cardiac tests with cardiology.
Cardiology consultation
Correct. Arrhythmic, structural and vascular cardiogenic syncope each pair their tests with cardiology consultation.
Neurology consultation
Neurology suits autonomic failure or seizure; an abrupt collapse with cardiac history points to cardiology.
Dietitian referral
A dietitian has no listed role in cardiogenic syncope, whose work-up pairs cardiac tests with cardiology consultation.

opts: Refer to a hypertension specialist
Correct. Referral is reserved for truly difficult cases after the full sequence has been worked through rather than being an early substitute for it.
Stop spironolactone and restart from a single agent
The approach builds on the regimen already in place rather than discarding it and beginning again.
Add a second mineralocorticoid antagonist
Duplicating the mineralocorticoid antagonist class is not among the described escalation steps.
Accept the current pressure as his individual goal

A.q: A 52-year-old woman has recurrent anginal chest pain during periods of work stress and anxiety. Her electrocardiogram shows ST changes during symptoms, and coronary angiography shows normal coronary arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Unstable angina
Unstable angina is a change in stable angina from atherosclerotic plaque and is an acute coronary syndrome. Normal coronary arteries in a stressed woman point to microvascular angina.
Stable angina
Stable angina comes from atherosclerotic narrowing that coronary angiography, the gold standard for coronary artery disease, would show. Her coronary arteries are normal.
Microvascular angina

Correct. Microvascular angina (formerly cardiac syndrome X) is angina with ST changes, possibly with elevated biomarkers, but normal coronary arteries on the angiogram; it is more frequent in women and often associated with stress or anxiety.
Vasospastic angina

Vasospastic angina strikes at rest between midnight and early morning, mostly in smokers under 50, with transient ST elevation. Her stress-related angina in a woman with normal arteries fits microvascular angina.

A.q: Which description defines syncope?
opts: Dizziness and tunnel vision without collapse
Warning symptoms such as dizziness, lightheadedness and tunnel vision without losing consciousness define near-syncope, also called presyncope.
Prolonged unconsciousness needing support
Syncope is transient and self-limited, and recovery is spontaneous. Prolonged unconsciousness needing support falls outside the definition.
Collapse with confusion lasting an hour
Prolonged confusion afterward points away from syncope, whose recovery is spontaneous and complete, and toward causes such as seizure.
Brief loss of consciousness, then full recovery
Correct. Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness with inability to maintain postural tone, followed by spontaneous recovery.

A.io: Define each class of the New York Heart Association (NYHA) symptomatic and functional classification of heart failure.
A.q: A 71-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is comfortable at rest but becomes breathless after only a few steps across a room. Which New York Heart Association class describes him?
opts: Class III
Correct. Symptoms with only slight exertion, such as a few steps across a room, and none at rest are class III. Class II is symptoms with ordinary exertion and class IV is symptoms at rest.
Class IV
Class IV is symptoms at rest, and he is comfortable at rest. Slight exertion provoking symptoms is class III.
Class II
Class II is symptoms with ordinary exertion. Breathlessness after only slight effort, like a few steps across a room, is class III.
Class I
Class I is the absence of any heart failure symptoms. Breathlessness with only slight exertion is class III.

A.io: Acute coronary syndrome
A.q: A 59-year-old man had 30 minutes of chest pressure at rest. His electrocardiogram shows nonspecific T-wave changes, and his first troponin I is not abnormal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Discharge him home now
A single troponin I that is not abnormal does not end the workup after rest pain. Troponin is used to rule an infarction out, and that takes a repeat level.
Order a calcium score
A coronary calcium score stratifies future risk and is not used to diagnose an acute coronary syndrome. The next step after rest pain is a repeat troponin I.
Give a thrombolytic agent
Thrombolytics are for an ST-elevation infarction when percutaneous intervention is two or more hours away. Nonspecific T-wave changes do not qualify; repeat the troponin I.
Repeat the troponin I
Correct. Troponin is drawn serially: when one is drawn, a second follows, because the change over time is what matters. A rising troponin I would turn this presentation into an infarction.

Pressors are not outpatient drugs; home options for neurogenic syncope are midodrine or droxidopa with slow position changes.
Pressors are hospital-only drugs

Only if she avoids salt

Only after a tilt-table test

opts: It filters the bad cholesterol out
Correct. Apheresis is like dialysis: the elective removal of low-density particles from the circulation, and it is the treatment of choice for the homozygous disorder.
It lowers his triglyceride level
His triglyceride is normal; the machine removes low-density lipoprotein particles.
It replaces his missing liver cells

It cures the disorder in weeks

A.q: A 34-year-old woman has progressive leg edema and jugular venous distension (distended neck veins). At the apex there is a low-pitched diastolic rumble with an opening snap. Which is the most likely cause of her right-sided heart failure?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy leads the diastolic chain with a fourth heart sound. An apical diastolic rumble with a snap is mitral stenosis.
Mitral valve stenosis

Correct. A rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap is mitral stenosis, one of the three causes of right-sided failure with chronic left-sided failure and pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation gives a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration. An apical diastolic rumble with a snap is mitral stenosis.
Aortic valve stenosis
Aortic stenosis is the most common valvular cause of heart failure overall but does not give an apical diastolic rumble with a snap. This is mitral stenosis.

A.q: An 81-year-old woman has progressive breathlessness and ankle edema over three months. Her N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide is 720. What does this level suggest for her age?
opts: Heart failure is likely
Correct. Older than 75, an N-terminal fragment above 450 makes heart failure likely. In a younger patient the threshold would be 125.
Heart failure is ruled out
No rule-out applies at 720. Older than 75, a level above 450 makes heart failure likely.
Only a younger cut-off applies
The age-specific threshold exists precisely for patients older than 75: above 450 heart failure is likely.
The level is normal for her age
The age-adjusted threshold over 75 is 450, and 720 exceeds it. Heart failure is likely.

A.q: A 68-year-old smoker with peripheral arterial disease has blood pressure of 168/94 despite three agents. An abdominal bruit is audible, ultrasound shows a right kidney 2 cm smaller than the left, and he has had two episodes of sudden pulmonary edema. What is the most likely underlying cause?
opts: Renovascular disease

Correct. The cluster is characteristic: resistant pressure, an abdominal bruit, asymmetric kidneys and recurrent flash pulmonary edema. In an older patient with established vascular disease the mechanism is atherosclerotic stenosis, often bilateral and progressive.
Chronic kidney disease from diabetes
Diabetic kidney disease reduces both kidneys' function together rather than producing a 2 cm size discrepancy with a bruit.
Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism also presents with resistant hypertension, but with unexplained hypokalemia rather than asymmetric kidneys and an abdominal bruit.
Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea contributes to resistant hypertension, but through nocturnal sympathetic activation, without bruits or asymmetric kidneys.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman with reduced ejection fraction is started on spironolactone alongside her loop diuretic. Which counseling point is most accurate?
opts: It replaces the need for her beta blocker
The antagonist adds to the beta blocker rather than replacing it; both are core classes. It spares potassium, so levels are checked.
It is only a short course for congestion
Spironolactone is a strong, ongoing recommendation in reduced ejection fraction, not a short diuretic course. It spares potassium, so levels are checked.
It wastes potassium like her loop diuretic
Loops and thiazide-like diuretics waste potassium; spironolactone spares it. That is why her potassium is monitored.
It spares potassium, so levels are checked
Correct. Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, a potassium-sparing diuretic, which is why her potassium and renal function will be followed alongside the potassium-wasting loop.

A.q: A 3-year-old boy has his pressure recorded at a well visit, and a new staff member flags it as low by comparing it with an adult's normal range. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Measure it again in adult units
The units are not the issue; the reference range is, because norms change with age.
Start a vasopressor for hypotension
Vasopressors are for the emergency department and intensive care, and a reading has not yet been shown to be low for his age.
Order an echocardiogram at once
Echocardiography evaluates structural heart disease; the first step is judging the reading against age-specific norms.
Compare it with norms for his age
Correct. Blood pressure norms are affected by age, so a child's reading is judged against the normal range for his age rather than an adult's.

A.q: A 25-year-old woman fainted once after standing for an hour in the heat at a graduation, with warmth and nausea first and rapid recovery. Her examination and readings are normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Begin midodrine daily
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is not first-line for a vasovagal faint.
Refer for echocardiography
Echocardiography is for structural cardiogenic syncope; a triggered faint with a prodrome points to a reflex cause.
Start fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, which her normal readings do not suggest.
Advise avoiding the trigger
Correct. Vasovagal syncope is treated by trigger avoidance, here prolonged standing in the heat, with safety precautions when unavoidable.

A.q: A 71-year-old woman had her diuretic dose increased 1 week ago for high readings. She now feels lightheaded whenever she stands and nearly fainted at church. Supine she is 132/78 with a heart rate of 70; standing she is 108/68 with a heart rate of 96. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope is triggered by fear, pain, heat or prolonged standing, with a transient reflex rather than a medication-linked postural fall.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Correct. Medication and volume loss are typical non-neurogenic causes, and the heart rate rise from 70 to 96 shows the autonomic reflex is intact.
Chronic cardiogenic hypotension
Chronic cardiogenic hypotension comes from reduced ejection fraction heart failure or cardiomyopathy, which nothing here suggests.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
The neurogenic form shows a minimal heart rate rise because the autonomic system has failed; her rise is significant.

A.q: Which apolipoprotein is critical in triglyceride clearance?
opts: Apolipoprotein(a)
Apolipoprotein(a) forms lipoprotein(a), a causal atherosclerosis risk factor; it does not clear triglyceride.
Apolipoprotein A-I
Apolipoprotein A-I is the structural protein of high-density lipoprotein, found on all of its particles, rather than a triglyceride-clearance protein.
Apolipoprotein B-48
Apolipoprotein B-48 is the intestinal structural protein of chylomicrons; the clearance role belongs to apolipoprotein E.
Apolipoprotein E
Correct. Apolipoprotein E is important in triglyceride metabolism and critical in triglyceride clearance, which is why its mutation lets chylomicron and very-low-density remnants accumulate.

A.q: What imaging is required when dissection is suspected, and what does a normal chest radiograph mean?
opts: Immediate cross-sectional vascular imaging
Correct. The radiograph may show a widened mediastinum, but it cannot rule the diagnosis out, so a normal film must not be allowed to end the workup.
Imaging can wait until blood pressure is controlled
The imaging is immediate and surgical involvement urgent, since the diagnosis determines both the pressure target and the operation.
A chest radiograph alone is sufficient to exclude it
A normal chest radiograph specifically does not exclude dissection, which is why cross-sectional angiography is required.
Echocardiography is the definitive study
Immediate cross-sectional vascular imaging is what is required; echocardiography establishes coarctation rather than excluding dissection.

A.q: A 59-year-old man remains at 158/96 on three agents at maximally tolerated doses. What is the commonest explanation to exclude first?
opts: Progressive renal artery stenosis
Renovascular disease is one secondary cause to consider, but it is not the commonest reason control appears resistant.
An incorrectly sized cuff
Measurement error belongs on the list, but nonadherence is specifically named as commonest.
Medication nonadherence
Correct, and it heads a list that also includes measurement error, white coat effect, high sodium or alcohol intake, interfering drugs, and undiagnosed sleep apnea or secondary hypertension.
Undiagnosed primary aldosteronism
Secondary hypertension is on the list to rule out, but nonadherence is the commonest single explanation for apparent resistance.

A.q: A 58-year-old man's pressure is 100/64, which is normal for many adults but far below his usual 150/90, and he now feels lightheaded. How should this reading be interpreted?
opts: As normal, since it is above 90
No single fixed number defines hypotension; relative hypotension must be considered against the patient's usual pressure.
As proof of autonomic failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not by one resting reading.
As relative hypotension for him
Correct. Hypotension is a fall below normal, and normal is judged against the patient's age, comorbidities and own baseline, so a relative fall can be significant.
As a measurement artifact
A reading consistent with his symptoms should not be dismissed; each reading is a snapshot to interpret, not to discard.

A.q: Which drug combinations are preferred as initial therapy?
opts: An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker
This combination is specifically prohibited: dual renin-angiotensin blockade raises hyperkalemia and kidney injury risk without additional benefit.
A beta blocker with a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
This pairing risks severe bradycardia and heart block because both slow nodal conduction.
Two thiazide-type diuretics together
Combining agents of the same class adds adverse effects without the complementary mechanism that the preferred pairings provide.
A renin-angiotensin blocker with a calcium blocker or diuretic

Correct, because the classes act by complementary mechanisms. A single-pill combination is preferred where two agents are started, since it improves adherence. That means an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker paired with a dihydropyridine or a thiazide-type diuretic.

A.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
A.io: Acute coronary syndrome
A.q: A 54-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with 30 minutes of chest pressure. Which pair of studies does every patient with chest pain receive?
opts: Treadmill stress test and D-dimer
A D-dimer is only a maybe in the chest pain workup, and a stress test is not done on arrival with active pain. Every patient gets a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.
Coronary angiography and echocardiogram
Coronary angiography is the gold standard for coronary disease but not the universal first study. Every chest pain patient starts with a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.
Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph
Correct. All chest pain patients get a chest radiograph and a stat electrocardiogram. Blood work (complete blood count, metabolic panel, coagulation studies, troponin) follows.
Calcium score and a lipid panel
A calcium score is for risk stratification, not acute chest pain, and lipids can come later. The universal first pair is a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
A.q: A 24-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has palpitations and lightheadedness on standing that ease when she lies down. Within 8 minutes of standing her heart rate rises from 72 to 108 while her pressure stays steady. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension combines a pressure fall with a minimal heart rate rise, the opposite of her pattern.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear or heat with bradycardia, not a sustained tachycardia on standing.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

Correct. A rise of more than 30 beats per minute within 10 minutes of standing, improving when lying down, in a young woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome fits the syndrome, sometimes expanded as positional.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension requires a pressure fall that meets criteria; her pressure stays steady.

A.io: Acute coronary syndrome
A.q: Where does the pain of acute coronary syndrome most commonly refer?
opts: Straight to the back
Pain going straight through to the back is the pancreatic pattern. Acute coronary syndrome most commonly refers to the jaw, tooth or arm.
Right lower quadrant
The right lower quadrant is not a coronary referral site. Acute coronary syndrome refers mostly to the jaw, tooth or arm, sometimes the epigastrium.
Right scapular region
Right scapular pain is the gallbladder pattern. Acute coronary syndrome pain most commonly refers to the jaw, tooth or arm.
Jaw, tooth or arm
Correct. Acute coronary syndrome pain refers most commonly to the jaw, tooth or arm, but it can go to the back, the scapular region, or the epigastrium and left upper quadrant.

A.io: Mitral stenosis
A.q: A 48-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has an echocardiogram showing a markedly enlarged left atrium. Which complication is she at greatest risk of developing?
opts: Concentric hypertrophy
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy is the pressure response to aortic stenosis. Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium instead, and that leads to atrial fibrillation.
Left ventricular dilation
Eccentric left ventricular dilation is the volume response of aortic and mitral regurgitation. Mitral stenosis loads the left atrium, predisposing to atrial fibrillation.
Atrial fibrillation

Correct. In mitral stenosis the left atrium enlarges under raised pressure, and left atrial enlargement predisposes to an abnormal rhythm such as atrial fibrillation, which is common in severe disease.
Aortic root dilation
Aortic root dilation is a cause of aortic regurgitation, found on echo. Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium, which predisposes to atrial fibrillation.

A.io: Tricuspid stenosis
A.q: A 53-year-old woman with severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is scheduled for valve replacement. Which valve type is preferred?
opts: Bioprosthetic valve

Correct. For severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis, bioprosthetic valve replacement is preferred; balloon valvotomy and repair are reserved for hepatic congestion or severe systemic venous congestion.
Annuloplasty ring
Annuloplasty treats tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation. When a stenotic tricuspid valve is replaced, bioprosthetic is preferred.
Mechanical valve
A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation. In tricuspid stenosis bioprosthetic replacement is the preferred valve.
Balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy is reserved for tricuspid stenosis with hepatic congestion that may lead to cirrhosis or severe venous congestion. The preferred replacement is bioprosthetic.

A.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
A.q: A 78-year-old man was treated in the intensive care unit with dobutamine for acute heart failure. His daughter asks whether he can continue it at home to keep his heart strong. What is the most appropriate response?
opts: Only if his blood pressure is high
Blood pressure does not make dobutamine a home drug. Inotropes are for intensive care use only.
Yes, as long-term home maintenance
Dobutamine is not a home maintenance therapy; inotropes are for intensive care use only.
Inotropes are for intensive care only

Correct. Inotropic therapy, including dobutamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine and milrinone, is for intensive care use only. Outpatient therapy is guideline-directed therapy for his ejection fraction group.
Yes, in place of his other medicines
Inotropes do not replace guideline-directed therapy and are for intensive care use only.

Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
A.q: A 32-year-old man arrives for his first adult screening visit, having eaten lunch an hour ago. Which lipid test can be done today without fasting?
opts: Triglyceride with high-density cholesterol
Triglyceride is the fasting-dependent value, so this pair cannot be drawn after a meal.
Total and high-density cholesterol
Correct. Total and high-density cholesterol need no fasting; their ratio is the most efficient and cost-effective way to predict coronary risk.
Triglyceride and total cholesterol
Triglyceride requires a 9- to 12-hour fast, so it cannot be done validly after lunch.
Calculated low-density lipoprotein
A calculated low-density value relies on fasting triglyceride and needs a 9- to 12-hour fast.

Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
A.q: A 74-year-old man reports fainting twice after standing. Before any test is ordered, which part of his evaluation is most important for identifying the source?
opts: A detailed history
Correct. History is the most important portion of accurately diagnosing the source of orthostatic syncope, or of referring to the right specialty for confirmation.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and cannot replace the history in orthostatic syncope.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope; the history comes first and decides whether it is needed.
A chest radiograph
A chest radiograph is not part of the orthostatic evaluation; the history is what identifies the likely source.

A.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
A.io: ST segment elevation
A.q: Why can nitroglycerin cause shock in a right ventricular infarct?
opts: It provokes coronary spasm
Nitroglycerin relieves coronary spasm rather than causing it. The problem in a right ventricular infarct is the fall in preload and output.
It triggers major bleeding
Bleeding is the danger of thrombolytics, not nitroglycerin. Nitroglycerin causes shock here by lowering the preload the right ventricle depends on.
Lost preload drops output
Correct. The infarcted right ventricle is preload dependent; decreasing preload reduces the Frank-Starling effect, the ventricle fails into right-sided heart failure, output falls and shock follows.
It blocks the atrioventricular node
Nitroglycerin does not block conduction. In a right ventricular infarct it drops the preload the failing right ventricle needs, and output falls.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
A.q: A 50-year-old woman on a statin has reached her low-density lipoprotein goal, but her triglyceride remains 260 mg/dL after lifestyle changes. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Add a fibrate or niacin
Correct. The primary aim is the low-density goal, and if triglyceride stays above 200 mg/dL once it is reached, additional triglyceride-lowering therapy (a fibrate or niacin) is indicated.
Continue with no change
Triglyceride above 200 after the low-density goal is reached is the trigger for more treatment.
Stop the statin and watch
The statin achieved the primary target and stays; the residual triglyceride is treated in addition.
Begin apheresis sessions
Apheresis is the treatment of choice for homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, not for residual triglyceride.

A.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
A.q: A 74-year-old woman presents with acute right hemiparesis and aphasia of two hours' duration. Her blood pressure is 196/104. How should her blood pressure be managed?
opts: Leave the blood pressure entirely untreated
A distinct protocol applies rather than no management at all, so the pressure is managed by different rules.
Reduce the mean arterial pressure by a quarter in an hour
That is the general hypertensive emergency approach, and acute stroke follows a distinct protocol instead.
Reduce the pressure to below 130/80 immediately
Applying a chronic prevention target acutely is exactly what the caution warns against.
Follow the acute stroke protocol, not chronic targets
Correct. Acute stroke is specifically excepted from the general emergency reduction approach, because driving the pressure to a chronic target can extend the ischemic injury.

A.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
A.q: A 24-year-old woman with hypertension has weak delayed femoral pulses and a leg pressure lower than her arm pressure. Which study establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Renal duplex ultrasound
Renal duplex investigates renovascular disease, which is suggested by an abdominal bruit and asymmetric kidneys rather than by femoral pulse delay.
Echocardiography
Correct, and the referral that follows is to a vascular surgeon or a structural cardiologist. The bedside findings raise the question; the echocardiogram answers it.
A morning aldosterone to renin ratio
That screens for primary aldosteronism, which does not produce an arm-to-leg pressure gradient.
Polysomnography
Sleep study investigates obstructive sleep apnea, suggested by snoring and witnessed apneas.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
A.q: A 52-year-old man with low high-density lipoprotein has improved his lifestyle, and his clinician is weighing a drug chosen specifically to raise high-density lipoprotein. Which drug raises it most?
opts: Colesevelam
Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant that lowers low-density lipoprotein 15% to 30% as an adjunct and is not used to raise high-density lipoprotein.
Niacin
Correct. Niacin raises high-density lipoprotein 15% to 35%, better than other medications, compared with fibrates 10% to 30%, statins 5% to 22% and ezetimibe 8%.
Pravastatin
Statins such as pravastatin raise high-density lipoprotein 5% to 22%, less than niacin.
Ezetimibe
Ezetimibe raises high-density lipoprotein only about 8% and is used mainly as a low-density adjunct.

A.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
A.q: A 62-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has pulmonic regurgitation. She has no symptoms of right heart failure. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty
Balloon valvuloplasty opens severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis, and valvuloplasty is itself the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation. Treat the underlying condition.
Transcatheter valve replacement
Transcatheter replacement is used for severe aortic stenosis. Pulmonic regurgitation is managed by treating what drives it, such as pulmonary hypertension.
Treat the underlying condition

Correct. Management of pulmonic regurgitation is to treat the underlying condition -- here the pulmonary hypertension, the high-pressure cause -- with referral when it is seen on echo or right heart failure develops.
Lifelong warfarin therapy
Warfarin is for mechanical valves. Pulmonic regurgitation is managed by treating the underlying condition, here pulmonary hypertension.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
A.q: For reflex hypotension, what is the treatment principle?
opts: Reduce or remove the medication
Reducing or removing a medication is the approach for iatrogenic hypotension, where a drug is the offending agent.
Treat the autonomic disease
Treating an underlying condition is the approach for orthostasis, such as autonomic failure or volume loss, rather than for reflex causes.
Start a vasopressor infusion
Vasopressor infusions are for the emergency department and intensive care only, not the management of reflex hypotension.
Reduce or remove the trigger
Correct. The principle is to remove the offending agent or trigger: reflex causes are managed by reducing or removing the trigger.

A.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
A.q: Which drug is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist for a mechanical valve?
opts: Warfarin

Correct. Warfarin is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist, the long-term anticoagulant for mechanical heart valves; if surgery requires heparin instead, warfarin is bridged until the ratio is therapeutic.
Heparin
Heparin is not a vitamin K antagonist; it is the bridging agent used around surgery. The most common vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent, not a vitamin K antagonist. The most commonly used vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.
Aspirin
Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent, and antiplatelets are ranked below vitamin K antagonists for mechanical valves. The vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.

A.io: Mitral valve prolapse
A.q: A 22-year-old healthy woman has no symptoms. On a routine examination a mid-systolic click is heard at the apex with no murmur. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis gives an opening snap and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex, usually decades after rheumatic fever. A lone mid-systolic click is prolapse.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic blowing murmur radiating to the axilla. A click with no murmur is prolapse, which may later progress to regurgitation.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is a harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the second right intercostal space, mostly in older adults. A mid-systolic click is prolapse.
Mitral valve prolapse
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse usually affects healthy women aged 15 to 30, is usually benign and asymptomatic, and gives a mid-systolic click at the apex as the leaflets flare into the left atrium.

A.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
A.q: A 50-year-old man starting home monitoring asks how to do it. What should he be told?
opts: One reading each morning for three days
That collects far less data than the standard schedule and is more vulnerable to a single odd value.
Readings only when he feels unwell
Most patients with mild to moderate hypertension have no reliable blood pressure-related symptoms, so symptom-triggered readings would miss the point.
Two readings morning and evening for seven days

Correct, and the accompanying instruction matters as much: do not overreact to the highest single reading, because acting on outliers generates anxiety and unnecessary changes in therapy. They are taken at least a minute apart and the average is reported.
Continuous monitoring over twenty-four hours at home
That describes ambulatory monitoring rather than the home schedule with a validated upper-arm device.

A.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
A.q: A 73-year-old woman with chronic heart failure has a B-type natriuretic peptide that has risen by 100 since her last visit. What does this change imply?
opts: No change in her relative risk of death
The level carries prognostic weight: each rise of 100 adds about 35% to the relative risk of death.
About 35% higher relative risk of death
Correct. Each increase of 100 carries about a 35% increase in the relative risk of death, so a rising level is a warning sign even when symptoms seem stable.
About 5% higher relative risk of death
That understates it. Each rise of 100 carries about a 35% increase in the relative risk of death.
About 90% higher relative risk of death
That overstates it. Each rise of 100 carries about a 35% increase in the relative risk of death.

A.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
A.q: Which finding is a sign of low perfusion rather than congestion in heart failure?
opts: Breathless lying flat
Orthopnea is a sign of congestion. Low perfusion shows as a narrow pulse pressure, cool extremities and low sodium.
Narrow pulse pressure

Correct. Low perfusion shows as a narrow pulse pressure, sleepiness or obtundation, low serum sodium, cool extremities, hypotension on an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and renal dysfunction.
An enlarged liver
Hepatomegaly is a sign of congestion. Low perfusion shows as a narrow pulse pressure, cool extremities and low sodium.
Distended neck veins
Jugular venous distension is a sign of congestion. Low perfusion shows as a narrow pulse pressure, cool extremities and low sodium.

A.io: ST segment elevation
A.q: A 62-year-old man has crushing chest pain. His electrocardiogram shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which artery is most likely occluded?
opts: Left marginal branch
The left marginal branch comes off the circumflex and supplies the lateral left ventricle, seen in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Inferior elevation in II, III and aVF points to the right coronary artery.
Diagonal branch artery
A diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery can cause lateral changes in I, aVL, V5 and V6. The inferior leads point to the right coronary artery.
Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery is the culprit for anterior and septal leads V1-V4. ST elevation in II, III and aVF is inferior, the right coronary artery.
Right coronary artery

Correct. Leads II, III and aVF are the inferior leads, and inferior ST elevation points to the right coronary artery (and/or the circumflex). The right coronary artery also supplies the atrioventricular node.

A.io: Pulmonic stenosis
A.q: A 12-year-old boy has a harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border that increases with inspiration. Which is the most appropriate test to evaluate the valve?
opts: Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph cannot show valve motion or flow across the valve. Pulmonic stenosis is diagnosed by echocardiogram, with an increased jet on Doppler.
Electrocardiogram only
An electrocardiogram may show right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy, but it cannot show the valve. An echocardiogram is needed.
Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is not the test used to diagnose pulmonic stenosis. An echocardiogram shows abnormal valve motion and the increased Doppler jet.
Echocardiogram
Correct. Pulmonic stenosis is diagnosed by echocardiogram, which shows abnormal valve motion and an increased jet velocity across the valve on Doppler.

A.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
A.q: A 52-year-old man reads 124/78 in clinic, but his home average over seven days is 142/90. Why does this matter?
opts: It carries real risk despite normal office readings
Correct. This is masked hypertension, and it is the reason out-of-office measurement is not merely a way of avoiding overtreatment: it also finds the patients whose risk the clinic reading conceals.
It indicates his home device is miscalibrated
A validated upper-arm device used to the standard schedule is the reference, not the office reading.
It is a benign pattern requiring no follow-up
It carries clinically important cardiovascular risk, which is precisely why identifying it matters.
It means he has white coat hypertension
White coat hypertension is the opposite pattern, with high office and normal home readings.

A.io: Aortic stenosis
A.q: A 72-year-old woman reports six months of breathlessness when she walks her dog and one episode of fainting while gardening. She has never had cardiac imaging. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Electrocardiogram alone
An electrocardiogram may show left ventricular hypertrophy in severe disease, but with low sensitivity and questionable specificity. It cannot exclude the lesion; echocardiography is needed.
Transesophageal echocardiogram
Transesophageal imaging is useful for congenital aortic stenosis. In an older adult with likely degenerative disease, the transthoracic echocardiogram is the study to order.
Transthoracic echocardiogram

Correct. Any patient with symptoms suggestive of aortic stenosis (exertional chest pressure, shortness of breath or syncope) should get an echocardiogram. Transthoracic imaging shows thickened, calcified leaflets with reduced opening.
Left heart catheterization
Left heart catheterization gives the definitive findings, but it is not where the workup starts. Suggestive symptoms are first answered with a transthoracic echocardiogram.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
A.q: A 44-year-old man with a sedentary job has a triglyceride of 280 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein of 165 mg/dL and non-high-density cholesterol of 205 mg/dL. He has no xanthomas. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Severe hypertriglyceridemia
The severe form needs triglyceride above 500 mg/dL, usually without raised low-density lipoprotein.
Mixed dyslipidemia
Correct. Triglyceride above 150 with low-density lipoprotein above 130 or non-high-density above 160 defines mixed dyslipidemia, the most common type in clinical practice.
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Chylomicronemia has fasting triglyceride usually above 1000 with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The homozygous form presents in childhood with total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 and normal triglyceride.

A.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
A.io: Acute myocardial infraction
A.q: A 59-year-old man is ready for discharge after an ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His heart rate is 78/min with no bradycardia. Which drug class improves survival rates across the board after infarction?
opts: Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitor
Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitors have fallen out of favor and are not a survival therapy after discharge. The class that improves survival rates across the board is the beta blocker.
Calcium channel blocker

Calcium channel blockers do not improve prognosis overall after infarction; only diltiazem and verapamil reduce mortality, and only with preserved left ventricular function. Beta blockers improve survival across the board.
Beta blocker
Correct. Beta blockers improve survival rates across the board after myocardial infarction, so they belong in post-infarction management unless bradycardia or another contraindication is present.
Sublingual nitroglycerin
Sublingual nitroglycerin relieves anginal pain as needed but carries no survival claim. The post-infarction class that improves survival across the board is the beta blocker.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
A.q: A 40-year-old woman's mother had a myocardial infarction at 70 and her brother had one at 50. She asks which relative's heart attack raises her own coronary risk. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Neither relative's
Her brother qualifies: a male first-degree relative with a myocardial infarction before 55 is a nonmodifiable genetic risk factor. Only her mother, at 70, falls outside the cut-off.
Only her brother's

Correct. Family history counts when a male first-degree relative had sudden death or myocardial infarction before 55, or a female first-degree relative before 65. Her brother at 50 qualifies; her mother at 70 does not.
Both relatives'
Only one qualifies. The cut-offs are under 55 for a male first-degree relative and under 65 for a female one, so her brother at 50 counts but her mother at 70 does not.
Only her mother's
A female first-degree relative counts only if the event came before 65. Her mother was 70, so she does not qualify; her brother, a male relative under 55, does.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
A.q: A 69-year-old man has breathlessness and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). His chest radiograph shows blunted costophrenic angles, cephalization (prominent upper-lobe vessels) and an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Which study best measures his ejection fraction?
opts: A repeat chest radiograph
A radiograph shows effusion, vessels and heart size but no ejection fraction. The multigated acquisition scan measures it most accurately.
Multigated acquisition scan

Correct. The radiograph supports heart failure with effusion, cephalization and an increased cardiothoracic ratio, but cannot measure function. The multigated acquisition scan is the most accurate for ejection fraction.
Right heart catheterization
Catheterization grades hemodynamic severity. The multigated acquisition scan is the most accurate for ejection fraction.
Twelve-lead electrocardiogram
The electrocardiogram shows ischemia, hypertrophy or strain but not ejection fraction. The multigated acquisition scan is the most accurate.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 38-year-old man has an average home blood pressure of 126/78. He has no diabetes, no kidney disease and no cardiovascular history. What should he be advised?
opts: No intervention is needed until he reaches stage 1
Lifestyle treatment is recommended for every category, including readings below the threshold for medication.
Recheck in five years with no advice in the interim
That defers an intervention recommended at every blood pressure category, including this one.
Lifestyle treatment

Correct. An elevated reading that does not yet warrant medication still warrants an intervention, and lifestyle measures continue alongside drugs later rather than being replaced by them. It is recommended at every blood pressure category.
Start a thiazide-type diuretic now
Medication is not indicated at this reading, and lifestyle measures apply first and throughout.

B.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores

B.q: A 63-year-old man with exertional chest pressure has a nuclear stress test that is abnormal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Coronary calcium score
A calcium score adds risk stratification, not anatomy, and does not follow an abnormal stress test. The next step is cardiac catheterization.
Repeat the stress test
Repeating an abnormal nuclear study only delays the answer. An abnormal nuclear stress test goes on to cardiac catheterization.
Cardiac catheterization
Correct. An abnormal nuclear stress test leads to cardiac catheterization, where coronary angiography, the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease, defines the lesions.
Discharge with no follow-up
An abnormal nuclear stress test is not a result to walk away from. It is followed by cardiac catheterization to look at the coronary arteries.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
B.q: Before starting a statin for triglyceride of 500 mg/dL or more, which conditions should be ruled out?
opts: Cushing syndrome and liver failure
These are secondary causes of raised low-density lipoprotein, not the rule-outs for triglyceride of 500 or more.
Smoking and obesity only
Diabetes, smoking and obesity are the rule-outs for low high-density lipoprotein.
Alcoholism and pregnancy
Correct. With triglyceride of 500 mg/dL or more rule out diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, alcoholism, pregnancy and hypothyroidism before starting a statin.
Nephrotic syndrome and anorexia nervosa
These belong to the list for elevated low-density lipoprotein, alongside hypothyroidism and primary biliary cirrhosis.

B.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
B.q: A 60-year-old woman without diabetes has a 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 11% and an uncertain statin decision. She has never smoked and has no family history of premature disease. Her coronary artery calcium score is zero. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Order a skin biopsy
Skin biopsy confirms homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and plays no part in this decision.
Add ezetimibe now
Ezetimibe is an add-on to a maximal statin in very high-risk disease, not a primary-prevention starter.
Start a high-intensity statin
High intensity is for clinical disease, very high low-density lipoprotein or high 10-year risk, not a zero calcium score.
Withhold or delay the statin
Correct. A calcium score of zero lowers risk, so statin therapy may be withheld or delayed, except in cigarette smokers, diabetes or a strong family history of premature disease.

B.q: A 45-year-old man has an isolated high-density lipoprotein of 34 mg/dL with normal low-density lipoprotein and triglyceride. Before treatment is planned, which conditions should be excluded?
opts: Pregnancy and kidney disease
Pregnancy and chronic kidney disease are rule-outs for triglyceride of 500 or more, not for low high-density lipoprotein.
Nephrotic syndrome and anorexia
Nephrotic syndrome and anorexia nervosa are rule-outs when low-density lipoprotein is elevated.
Diabetes, smoking and obesity
Correct. With low high-density lipoprotein, rule out diabetes mellitus, cigarette smoking and obesity, then address them as the main levers.
Pancreatitis and gallstones
Neither is a rule-out before a statin; pancreatitis is a complication of very high triglyceride.

B.q: Which categories of disease are listed behind neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: Dehydration, blood loss and poor intake
These describe who develops non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, where the problem is volume and the autonomic response remains intact.
Coughing, sneezing and urination
These bodily functions are triggers of situational reflex syncope, which is a reflex event rather than autonomic failure.
Infarction, heart failure and valve disease
These are structural cardiogenic causes of syncope, evaluated with echocardiography and cardiology consultation rather than orthostatic vitals.
Diabetic, genetic and autoimmune disorders
Correct. Each can damage the autonomic nervous system, and long-standing diabetes with peripheral neuropathy is the classic route to diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

B.q: Why is overly rapid blood pressure reduction harmful in a hypertensive emergency?
opts: It causes rebound hypertension within hours
Rebound on abrupt withdrawal is a limitation of central alpha-2 agonists rather than the reason for controlled reduction here.
Autoregulation has adapted to the higher pressure

Correct. The organs have reset the range over which they protect their own perfusion, so returning the pressure to normal too quickly leaves them underperfused at a value that would be safe in anyone else. Reducing too fast can cause ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.
It has no harm; rapid reduction is preferred
Rapid reduction is specifically described as capable of causing ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.
It precipitates hyperkalemia
Potassium disturbance relates to renin-angiotensin blockade and mineralocorticoid antagonists rather than to the rate of pressure reduction.

B.q: A 27-year-old woman reports several brief faints over 6 months with a warm, nauseated prodrome, but she cannot recall what was happening before most of them. Her examination is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Order a tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is the listed test for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and a negative result tells little.
Keep a log of each episode
Correct. A log of pattern and frequency supports a history-based diagnosis of reflex syncope and helps identify the triggers to avoid.
Arrange an echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope, which her prodrome and normal examination do not suggest.
Start fludrocortisone now
Fludrocortisone is best with the tachycardia syndrome; reflex syncope is managed by identifying and avoiding triggers.

B.q: A 14-year-old girl with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia remains severely elevated despite a high-intensity statin, ezetimibe and regular apheresis. Which adjunct is approved at her age?
opts: Colesevelam
Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant for extra low-density lowering, not the adjunct approved for homozygous disease from age 12.
Gemfibrozil
Gemfibrozil is a fibrate for triglyceride, which is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia.
Fish oil
Fish oil is associated with lower coronary death in general, but it is not an adjunct for the homozygous disorder.
Evinacumab
Correct. Evinacumab, an intravenous monoclonal antibody that lowers low-density lipoprotein and triglyceride, is adjunct therapy for patients 12 years and older with the homozygous disorder.

B.q: A 61-year-old woman has had left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction for five years. Over two months she has developed leg edema, jugular venous distension (distended neck veins), an enlarged liver, nausea and poor appetite. Which is the most likely explanation for her new findings?
opts: Primary liver disease with ascites
The enlarged liver here is congestion from right ventricular failure, which also explains her distended neck veins and edema.
Worsening systolic failure of the left only
Left-sided worsening would add orthopnea and crackles. Edema, neck veins and portal congestion mean the right ventricle has now failed.
High-output failure from increased demand
High-output failure comes from anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula. Her picture is right-sided failure following chronic left-sided disease.
Right-sided failure from her left-sided failure

Correct. Chronic left-sided failure is the most common cause of right-sided failure. Systemic overload gives edema and distended neck veins; portal overload gives nausea, poor appetite and hepatomegaly.

B.q: A 60-year-old man with a prior heart attack asks whether eating fish will help his heart. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Eat fish only once a month
Once a month falls short of the at least 2 servings a week that are recommended.
Fish raises his coronary risk
Fatty fish or fish-oil supplements are associated with lower coronary risk and coronary death, not higher.
Fish can replace his statin
Fish is an addition to therapy; the statin remains the backbone of secondary prevention.
Eat fish at least twice a week
Correct. Fatty fish or fish-oil supplements are associated with lower risk of coronary disease and coronary death, and at least 2 servings of fish per week are recommended.

B.q: A 76-year-old man is seen in the emergency department after fainting while voiding at night. His examination is normal. Which test excludes hypoglycemia as the cause?
opts: A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and says nothing about blood sugar.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural heart disease, not the glucose level at the time of a faint.
Orthostatic vital signs
Orthostatic readings test for a postural pressure fall; hypoglycemia is excluded by measuring glucose.
A blood glucose level
Correct. A normal blood glucose rules out hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, as blood counts and a metabolic panel address infection and metabolic causes.

B.io: Acute coronary syndrome
B.q: A 34-year-old man has chest tightness the morning after a long-distance run that left his leg muscles sore. The team wants a blood marker specific to heart muscle. Which marker should be measured?
opts: Troponin C
Troponin C is one of the three troponin types but is not the heart-specific one. Troponin I is specific to the heart, which matters after skeletal muscle strain.
Smooth-muscle troponin
Smooth muscle cells contain no troponin at all; troponins belong to cardiac and skeletal muscle. The heart-specific marker is troponin I.
Any troponin type
Troponins occur in both cardiac and skeletal muscle, so the type matters after a long run. Troponin I is the heart-specific troponin.
Troponin I

Correct. Troponins are proteins of cardiac and skeletal muscle, and there are three types (I, T and C), but troponin I is the one specific to the heart, so skeletal muscle injury from his run does not confound it.

B.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
B.q: A 28-year-old man had a surgical valvuloplasty as a child to relieve right ventricular outflow obstruction. He now has a brief, high-pitched decrescendo early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space that radiates toward the mid right sternal border with full inspiration. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid. This murmur is a brief early diastolic decrescendo.
Pulmonic regurgitation

Correct. A brief, high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space with inspiratory radiation (the Graham Steell murmur) is pulmonic regurgitation, and surgery on the right ventricular outflow tract is its most common cause.
Aortic regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation is a blowing diastolic murmur at the third intercostal space radiating to the apex, a left-sided murmur louder on expiration, with bounding pulses.
Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis is at the left upper sternal border too, but it is a harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur. This murmur is early diastolic, which is regurgitation.
