B.q: A 59-year-old woman develops a persistent dry cough six weeks after starting lisinopril. Her blood pressure is at goal. What is the appropriate response?
opts: Stop all antihypertensive therapy
A tolerability problem with one agent is managed by substitution rather than by abandoning treatment.
Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker
Correct. The cough is bradykinin-mediated and occurs in up to about one in five. Angiotensin receptor blockers do not raise bradykinin, so the effect is lost while the therapeutic action is kept.
Add an antitussive and continue the lisinopril
Switching class removes the mechanism rather than masking the symptom, and an equally effective alternative exists.
Add losartan to the lisinopril
Dual renin-angiotensin blockade is specifically prohibited because of hyperkalemia and kidney injury risk.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
B.q: A 46-year-old woman with microvascular angina asks which factor tends to go along with her episodes. Her coronary arteries were normal on angiography. What should she be told?
opts: Cocaine or amphetamine use
Cocaine and amphetamine are drugs that precipitate vasospastic angina, not the association described for microvascular angina, which is stress or anxiety.
The hours after midnight
Episodes between midnight and early morning describe vasospastic angina. Microvascular angina is often associated with stress or anxiety and is more frequent in women.
Stress or anxiety

Correct. Microvascular angina is more frequent in women and is often associated with stress or anxiety. Proposed mechanisms include endothelial dysfunction, insulin resistance and estrogen deficiency.
Triptan migraine therapy
Triptans can precipitate vasospastic angina and are avoided in it. The factor described for microvascular angina is stress or anxiety.

B.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
B.q: A 79-year-old woman with cardiomyopathy has had pressures around 92/58 for many months. She has intermittent lightheadedness that comes and goes. How is her hypotension best classified?
opts: Acute reflex hypotension
Reflex hypotension is triggered and transient, not a pressure that runs low for months.
Long-lasting acute infectious hypotension
Infection from bacteremia to septic shock causes long-lasting acute hypotension, not months of waxing symptoms.
Acute toxic hypotension
Toxic or medication-mediated overdose causes acute hypotension of sudden onset with a specific trigger.
Chronic cardiogenic hypotension
Correct. Cardiogenic causes such as cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction heart failure produce chronic hypotension, which waxes and wanes and is intermittently symptomatic.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 22-year-old woman faints while having blood drawn. Just before, she felt warm, nauseated and sweaty, and she recovered fully within a minute of lying down. Her examination and standing readings afterward are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope is triggered by a bodily function or physical action such as urination, not by fear or pain.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Correct. Fear and pain are vasovagal triggers, a prodrome of warmth, nausea and sweating precedes it, and it is most common in young women; recovery is rapid and complete.
Cardiogenic arrhythmic syncope
Arrhythmic syncope tends to strike abruptly without a warm, nauseated prodrome, often after palpitations.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension produces a reproducible fall on standing with a minimal heart rate rise; her standing readings are normal.

B.io: Aortic stenosis
B.q: A 64-year-old man has an echocardiogram for palpitations that incidentally shows mild aortic stenosis. He has no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Start a nitrate for prevention
Nitrates drop preload and are avoided in aortic stenosis, and medical treatment does not change its course. The step is a cardiology consult to plan follow-up.
Transcatheter valve replacement
Replacement is for severe aortic stenosis with symptomatic systolic dysfunction or a bicuspid valve. Mild asymptomatic disease is referred to cardiology for evaluation and follow-up.
Cardiology consultation

Correct. All patients with evidence of aortic stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult to evaluate them and set the frequency of follow-up, even when the finding is mild and incidental.
No follow-up is needed
Aortic stenosis progresses; 10 to 20% reach significant stenosis within 10 to 15 years. Evidence of it on echocardiogram calls for a cardiology consult to set follow-up.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 73-year-old man has vomited for 2 days and fainted on standing. Supine he is 136/78 with a heart rate of 66; after 3 minutes standing he is 104/64 with a heart rate of 94. What does this heart rate response indicate?
opts: Failure of the autonomic system
Autonomic failure blunts the heart rate rise; a rise of 28 beats shows the reflex is working.
A reflex surge in vagal tone
A vagal surge slows the heart, as in vasovagal syncope, rather than producing a brisk rise on standing.
An intact autonomic response
Correct. A heart rate rise from 66 to 94 as pressure falls shows an intact baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic response, which favors non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
A primary ventricular arrhythmia
A ventricular arrhythmia is suspected from abrupt collapse and palpitations; a proportional rise on standing is a reflex, not an arrhythmia.

B.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
B.q: A 58-year-old woman with a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration is examined further. Which additional finding is most expected?
opts: Delayed, weak carotid pulse
A delayed, weakened carotid with a forceful apex is the clue to severe aortic stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure.
A collapsing radial pulse
A collapsing, water hammer pulse is the Corrigan pulse of aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation gives an elevated jugular venous pressure with neck pulsations.
Head bobbing with each beat
Head bobbing is the de Musset sign of aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation gives elevated jugular pulsations and a venous thrill.
Elevated jugular pulsations
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure with visible neck pulsations, and there may be a venous thrill (a palpable vibration) over the right jugular vein.

B.io: Stable
B.q: A 58-year-old man with exertional chest pain says he "had a heart cath" last week. The report shows dye was injected and the coronary arteries were imaged, revealing a stenosis, but nothing was done to the vessel. Which term names what was performed?
opts: Percutaneous coronary intervention
Percutaneous coronary intervention is the placement of a stent to keep the artery open. No stent or balloon was used here; the vessel was only imaged with dye.
Coronary artery bypass graft
A coronary artery bypass graft anastomoses a mammary or radial artery, or a vein, to the coronary artery beyond the obstruction. It is open surgery, not dye imaging through a catheter.
Coronary angiography

Correct. Coronary angiography is the injection of dye to identify a lesion or blockage, and it is the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease. Nothing was done to the vessel, so no intervention took place.
Plain old balloon angioplasty
Plain old balloon angioplasty opens a narrowed artery with a balloon and no stent. This report describes imaging only, with nothing done to the stenosis.

B.io: Mitral regurgitation
B.q: A 64-year-old man, three days after an acute myocardial infarction, has sudden breathlessness, crackles in both lungs and a new holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Which is the most likely cause?
opts: Papillary muscle rupture

Correct. An acute myocardial infarction with papillary muscle rupture is an acute cause of mitral regurgitation, and acute mitral regurgitation presents with left-sided heart failure symptoms such as dyspnea and rales.
Myxomatous degeneration
Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse, a chronic cause of mitral regurgitation. The sudden murmur three days after an infarction points to papillary muscle rupture.
Tricuspid annular dilation
Tricuspid annular dilation causes tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension, heard at the lower sternal border. An apical murmur after infarction is papillary muscle rupture.
Rheumatic heart disease
Rheumatic heart disease is a cause of mitral regurgitation, but it does not arrive suddenly three days after an infarction. Papillary muscle rupture does.

B.io: Mitral stenosis
B.q: What causes hoarseness (Ortner syndrome) in mitral stenosis?
opts: Left atrium pressing the right recurrent laryngeal nerve
The nerve involved is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which loops near the enlarged left atrium. The right nerve is not in its path.
Left atrium pressing the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
Correct. An enlarged left atrium impinges on the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and causes hoarseness, Ortner syndrome. Pressing on the esophagus, it causes dysphagia instead.
Right atrium pressing the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
The right atrium sits away from the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. It is the enlarged left atrium of mitral stenosis that causes Ortner hoarseness.
Pulmonary artery pressing the right vagus nerve trunk
Hoarseness in mitral stenosis is attributed to the enlarged left atrium pressing on the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, not to the pulmonary artery.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 58-year-old woman has a blood pressure of 224/126 with no headache, no visual change, no chest pain, a normal neurological examination and a normal creatinine. How should this be classified?
opts: Severe asymptomatic hypertension

Correct. An emergency is defined by acute hypertension-mediated ORGAN INJURY, not by crossing a numeric threshold. A very high pressure with no acute organ involvement is not an emergency, and that distinction decides how fast the pressure is brought down. It is not a hypertensive emergency.
A hypertensive emergency, because the systolic exceeds 220
No absolute numeric cutoff defines an emergency; acute hypertension-mediated organ injury is what does.
Resistant hypertension
Resistance means pressure above goal despite three complementary drugs at maximally tolerated doses, which is not what is described.
Hypertensive encephalopathy
Encephalopathy would require confusion, seizures or a neurological deficit, and her examination is normal.

B.q: A 49-year-old newly diagnosed hypertensive patient has fundoscopy showing generalized arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nicking, with no hemorrhages or exudates. What does this tell you?
opts: These findings indicate a hypertensive emergency
Optic disc edema marks acute hypertensive injury; chronic arteriolar changes do not.
These changes reflect current blood pressure only
Focal narrowing, hemorrhages and exudates are the findings tied to current pressure; these two relate to current and previous.
They reflect current and previous pressure
Correct. Generalized narrowing and nicking record the accumulated burden, whereas focal narrowing, hemorrhages and exudates relate to CURRENT pressure only.
These findings carry no prognostic weight
Hypertensive retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk independently of the blood pressure level.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: What does management of combined right and left heart failure include?
opts: Symptom management, comfort care and transplant
Correct. Combined failure is managed with symptom control, comfort care and heart transplant, the same end-of-spectrum options that appear for right-sided failure alongside palliative care.
Inotropes continued at home as maintenance
Inotropic therapy such as dobutamine or milrinone is reserved for the intensive care unit. Combined failure is managed with symptom control, comfort care and transplant.
Observation until symptoms become persistent
Waiting is not the plan. Combined failure is managed actively with symptom control, comfort care and consideration of transplant.
Calcium channel blockers for symptom control
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. Combined failure is managed with symptom control, comfort care and transplant.

B.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
B.q: A 66-year-old man has just recovered from replacement of his aortic valve with a mechanical valve. Which long-term antithrombotic therapy is recommended?
opts: Heparin as permanent outpatient therapy
Heparin is used to bridge when surgery interrupts warfarin until the ratio is therapeutic. The long-term therapy for a mechanical valve is a vitamin K antagonist.
No therapy after the recovery period
Stopping after the postoperative period applies to biological valves. A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist.
Aspirin alone as antiplatelet therapy
Vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over antiplatelet agents for a mechanical valve. Aspirin alone does not meet the need for lifelong anticoagulation.
Warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist

Correct. In patients with mechanical heart valves, vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended for long-term management over no vitamin K antagonist and over antiplatelet agents. Warfarin is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist.

B.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
B.q: A 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a normal echocardiogram asks whether she should take metoprolol, as her father did, to prevent heart failure. Which reply is most accurate?
opts: No drug helps until symptoms appear
Stage A with diabetes carries a strong drug recommendation before any symptoms: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
A loop diuretic is the preventive drug
Loop diuretics relieve congestion and do not prevent heart failure. In stage A with diabetes the first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Metoprolol is the first drug for prevention
A beta blocker is not the first drug in stage A. For an at-risk patient with diabetes the recommended first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Dapagliflozin comes first, not a beta blocker

Correct. As an at-risk patient with diabetes and a normal heart she is stage A, where the first recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin. A beta blocker enters at stage B.

B.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
B.io: Acute myocardial infraction
B.q: Pericarditis after a myocardial infarction is known as which syndrome?
opts: Cardiac syndrome X
Cardiac syndrome X is the former name of microvascular angina: angina with normal coronary arteries on angiography. Post-infarction pericarditis is Dressler syndrome.
Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder of the aorta, not a complication of infarction. Pericarditis after a myocardial infarction is Dressler syndrome.
Dressler syndrome
Correct. Pericarditis after infarction is Dressler syndrome, one of the mechanical complications alongside heart failure, rupture, ventricular aneurysm, thromboembolism and cardiogenic shock.
Brugada syndrome
Brugada syndrome is an inherited electrical disorder, not a post-infarction complication. Pericarditis after a myocardial infarction is called Dressler syndrome.

B.io: ST segment elevation
B.q: A 65-year-old man has 30 minutes of crushing chest pressure. His electrocardiogram shows a new left bundle branch block; a tracing last month was normal. How should this be managed?
opts: As an ST-elevation infarct
Correct. A new left bundle branch block with ischemic symptoms is treated as an ST-elevation myocardial infarction equivalent: aspirin and activation of the catheterization team without waiting.
As a benign conduction delay
An old, known bundle branch block may be incidental, but a new one with 30 minutes of chest pressure is an ST-elevation infarction equivalent and treated as such.
As stable angina
Stable angina is exertional pain relieved by rest with a stable tracing. A new left bundle branch block with ongoing pressure is treated as an ST-elevation infarction.
As unstable angina
Unstable angina shows nonspecific changes such as inverted T waves. A new left bundle branch block is an ST-elevation infarction equivalent and is managed as one.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: A 71-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy has an ejection fraction of 25%, is class II on optimal guideline-directed therapy, and has metastatic cancer with an expected survival of a few months. Which is most appropriate regarding an implantable defibrillator?
opts: Implant it before discharge
His fraction and class qualify, but the life expectancy criterion of at least one year does not. The device is not indicated.
It is not indicated for him

Correct. The device is indicated only with a life expectancy of at least one year, together with ejection fraction 35% or less, class II or III and optimal therapy. His expected survival of months fails that criterion.
Implant it after a cardiac arrest
The criteria do not wait for an arrest, and his life expectancy of months fails them. The device is not indicated.
Implant it once he is class IV
Class IV falls outside the class II to III criterion, and his life expectancy still fails. The device is not indicated.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: A 76-year-old man with heart failure has cool extremities, a narrow pulse pressure and increasing confusion. His urine output has fallen and creatinine has doubled. Which complication has developed?
opts: Nephrotic syndrome from proteinuria
Nephrotic syndrome is a primary kidney disorder. His low perfusion signs explain acute kidney injury with falling urine output.
Acute kidney injury from low perfusion
Correct. Cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure and obtundation are signs of low perfusion, and renal dysfunction with acute kidney injury and falling urine output is part of the same picture.
Urinary retention from prostatic disease
Nothing points to an obstructed outlet, and the perfusion signs explain the kidneys. This is acute kidney injury from low perfusion.
Hypertensive kidney damage from years
Chronic hypertensive damage does not appear over days with cool extremities. This is acute kidney injury from low perfusion.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 59-year-old hypertensive man is breathless with bibasal crackles and raised jugular venous pressure. Is chest radiography appropriate?
opts: Yes, because findings suggest pulmonary edema
Correct. Radiography is appropriate when dyspnea or findings suggest pulmonary edema, when cardiomegaly is suspected, or when a widened mediastinum is a concern.
No, because chest radiography is never indicated in hypertension
It is not indicated ROUTINELY for uncomplicated hypertension, which is different from never being indicated.
No, because a normal film would exclude dissection
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude dissection, so that is not a reason either way.
Yes, as a routine part of every hypertensive workup
Routine chest radiography is specifically not indicated for uncomplicated hypertension.

B.io: Mitral valve prolapse
B.q: A 31-year-old woman with known mitral valve prolapse is followed over several years. Which complication can the prolapse progress to?
opts: Mitral regurgitation
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse may develop the signs and symptoms of mitral regurgitation; prolapse is also listed among the chronic causes of mitral regurgitation.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is a narrowing that comes mostly from rheumatic heart disease. Prolapse lets the leaflets flare backward, so it progresses to regurgitation.
Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is mainly rheumatic worldwide and congenital in the United States. Mitral valve prolapse may progress to mitral regurgitation.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is degenerative in older adults or from a bicuspid valve. Mitral valve prolapse progresses to mitral regurgitation.

B.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
B.io: ST segment elevation
B.q: A 68-year-old woman with right ventricular infarction (ST elevation in V4R) is given sublingual nitroglycerin in triage, and her blood pressure falls to 70/40 mmHg. What explains the fall?
opts: Thrombolytic bleeding
Thrombolytics carry a risk of intracerebral hemorrhage, but she received nitroglycerin, not a thrombolytic. The fall comes from lost preload to the right ventricle.
Lost preload

Correct. Nitroglycerin reduces preload, which removes the Frank-Starling effect the injured right ventricle depends on. Output drops further, the right ventricle fails and the patient goes into shock.
Myocardial rupture
Myocardial rupture is a mechanical complication of infarction, not the immediate effect of a nitrate. Here nitroglycerin removed the preload the right ventricle needs.
Ventricular aneurysm
A ventricular aneurysm develops later as a complication of infarction. An abrupt fall after nitroglycerin in right ventricular infarction is from lost preload.

B.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
B.q: A 57-year-old man had an ejection fraction of 25% two years ago. On guideline-directed therapy his repeat echocardiogram now shows 46%. How is his heart failure now classified?
opts: Improved ejection fraction
Correct. A fraction that was 40% or less and has recovered above 40% is improved ejection fraction. The number alone would read mildly reduced, but his history is what defines the group.
Preserved ejection fraction
Preserved ejection fraction is 50% or more, which he has not reached. Recovery above 40% from a reduced value is improved ejection fraction.
Mildly reduced ejection fraction
46% alone would be mildly reduced, but his earlier 25% changes the label. Recovery from the reduced range above 40% is improved ejection fraction.
Resolved heart failure
Heart failure is not relabeled as resolved when the fraction recovers. Recovery above 40% from 25% is improved ejection fraction.

B.io: Pulmonic stenosis
B.q: What is the usual cause of pulmonic stenosis?
opts: Degenerative calcification
Degenerative calcification is the aortic stenosis process of patients over 70. Pulmonic stenosis is almost always congenital.
Congenital disease
Correct. Pulmonic stenosis, obstruction of right ventricular outflow to the lungs, is almost always congenital. Carcinoid disease is another cause, and it is commonly part of tetralogy of Fallot.
Rheumatic fever
Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis and, worldwide, of tricuspid stenosis. Pulmonic stenosis is almost always congenital.
Intravenous drug use
Intravenous drug use leads to tricuspid valve endocarditis and primary tricuspid regurgitation. Pulmonic stenosis is almost always congenital.

B.io: Unstable
B.q: A 63-year-old man has had chest pressure at rest for two days. His electrocardiogram shows inverted T waves, and two standard troponin I levels are 0.01 ng/mL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Unstable angina
Correct. Pain at rest with nonspecific electrocardiogram changes, usually inverted T waves, and a normal troponin I is unstable angina. A standard troponin I at or below 0.04 ng/mL is not abnormal.
ST-elevation infarction
An ST-elevation myocardial infarction shows ST elevation above 1 mm in two or more leads with elevated troponin I. His tracing shows only inverted T waves and his troponin I is not abnormal.
Infarction without ST elevation
A non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction needs an elevated troponin I, meaning standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL. His two values of 0.01 ng/mL are not abnormal, so this is unstable angina.
Stable angina
Stable angina is brought on by exertion and relieved by rest and nitroglycerin. Pain that now occurs at rest has become unstable angina, an acute coronary syndrome.

B.io: Aortic regurgitation
B.q: A 60-year-old man with aortic insufficiency has an echocardiogram showing a regurgitant fraction of 62%. Which severity does this indicate?
opts: Severe regurgitation
Correct. Aortic regurgitation is severe when 50% or more of the blood that passed the valve comes back. A fraction of 30 to 49% is moderate and below 30% is mild.
Ungradeable by echocardiogram
Regurgitant fraction is exactly how echocardiography grades aortic regurgitation; catheterization is definitive but not necessary. A fraction of 62% is severe.
Mild regurgitation
Mild aortic regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction below 30%. A fraction of 62% is well into the severe range of 50% or more.
Moderate regurgitation
Moderate aortic regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction of 30 to 49%. At 62%, more than half the output is returning, which is severe.

B.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
B.q: A 62-year-old man had a heart attack two years ago and takes no lipid-lowering drug. His low-density lipoprotein is 140 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate statin therapy?
opts: High-intensity statin

Correct. Clinical atherosclerotic disease at 75 or younger calls for a high-intensity statin to lower low-density lipoprotein by 50% or more; moderate intensity only if high intensity is not tolerated.
Moderate-intensity statin
Moderate intensity is the fallback when high intensity is not tolerated, not the first choice after a heart attack.
Low-intensity statin
Low intensity lowers low-density lipoprotein under 30%, which is inadequate for secondary prevention.
Risk calculation first
The 10-year risk calculation is for primary prevention; established disease already qualifies for a high-intensity statin.

B.q: A 45-year-old man has two days of breathlessness after a viral illness. His N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide is 90. How should the result be read?
opts: Acute heart failure is ruled out
Correct. An N-terminal fragment below 300 rules out acute heart failure with a negative predictive value above 90%, and 90 is also below the under-75 heart failure threshold of 125.
Heart failure is likely
Younger than 75, heart failure becomes likely above 125. A level of 90 rules out acute failure.
The result is indeterminate
At 90 the result is clearly below the rule-out level of 300. Acute heart failure is ruled out.
Acute heart failure is likely
Nothing near this level suggests acute failure. Below 300 the N-terminal fragment rules it out.

B.io: Tricuspid stenosis
B.q: A 49-year-old woman with severe tricuspid stenosis develops worsening hepatic congestion, and her team fears progression to cirrhosis. Which intervention is reserved for this situation?
opts: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement treats severe aortic stenosis. In tricuspid stenosis with threatening hepatic congestion, balloon valvotomy or repair is reserved.
Afterload reduction therapy only
Afterload reduction treats chronic aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid stenosis threatening cirrhosis calls for balloon valvotomy or valve repair.
Balloon valvotomy or valve repair
Correct. Balloon valvotomy and valve repair are reserved for tricuspid stenosis with hepatic congestion that may lead to cirrhosis, or with severe systemic venous congestion.
Mitral valve clip placement
A mitral valve clip treats severe mitral regurgitation. Hepatic congestion from tricuspid stenosis is the indication for balloon valvotomy or repair.

B.q: A 50-year-old woman has a waist circumference of 38 inches, triglyceride of 190 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein of 45 mg/dL, blood pressure of 134/88 and fasting glucose of 104 mg/dL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mixed dyslipidemia
Mixed dyslipidemia needs low-density lipoprotein above 130 or non-high-density above 160 with triglyceride above 150; her findings are the metabolic cluster.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 with palmar xanthomas.
Metabolic syndrome
Correct. Any three of five criteria establish it; she meets four: waist above 35 inches, triglyceride above 150, high-density lipoprotein below 50 in a woman and blood pressure above 130/85.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia
The severe form requires triglyceride above 500 mg/dL; hers is 190, which is only borderline high.

B.q: A 65-year-old man with new heart failure also describes pressure-like chest pain for the past day. His electrocardiogram shows new T-wave inversions. Which additional laboratory test is indicated?
opts: Thyroid hormone level
Thyroid testing looks for a high-output cause. Chest pain with ischemic changes calls for troponin.
Repeat natriuretic peptide
The natriuretic peptide supports heart failure but does not address infarction. Troponin does.
Cardiac troponin
Correct. Troponin is ordered when there is concern for an acute infarction or for heart failure secondary to ischemic cardiomyopathy, and chest pain with new inversions raises exactly that concern.
Hepatic function panel
Liver tests do not address ischemia. Chest pain with new inversions calls for troponin.

B.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
B.q: Why is a beta blocker the wrong first choice for an at-risk patient with diabetes and a normal heart?
opts: Diabetes makes any drug unnecessary
Diabetes is exactly what triggers treatment in stage A: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
A loop diuretic must be started first
A stage A patient has no congestion to treat. The first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Beta blockers are banned in all heart failure
Beta blockers are core therapy in reduced ejection fraction and a stage B recommendation. They are simply not the first choice in stage A.
The first drug is a sodium-glucose inhibitor
Correct. In stage A the only strongly recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes. The beta blocker is a stage B therapy once structural disease exists.

B.q: A 42-year-old woman has low-density lipoprotein of 290 mg/dL with a normal triglyceride. She has firm nodules along both Achilles tendons (tendon xanthomas), and her father had a heart attack at 48. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia

Correct. Low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 mg/dL, normal triglyceride, Achilles tendon xanthomas (present in about 75%) and premature coronary disease in a first-degree relative fit one mutant allele.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The homozygous form presents in childhood with total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 mg/dL and atherosclerosis before puberty.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia
Severe hypertriglyceridemia means triglyceride above 500 mg/dL, usually without raised low-density lipoprotein, the reverse of her panel.
Mixed dyslipidemia
Mixed dyslipidemia raises triglyceride above 150 as well as low-density lipoprotein; her triglyceride is normal.

Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: Which diastolic change on standing meets the orthostatic criterion?
opts: A fall of more than 10 mmHg within 3 minutes
Correct. A diastolic fall of more than 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing meets the orthostatic criterion alongside the systolic thresholds.
A fall of more than 10 mmHg within 10 minutes
The window for orthostatic pressure criteria is 3 minutes; the 10-minute window belongs to the tachycardia syndrome's heart rate criteria.
A fall of more than 20 mmHg within 3 minutes
More than 20 mmHg within 3 minutes is the systolic threshold with a normal baseline, not the diastolic one.
A fall of more than 30 mmHg within 3 minutes
More than 30 mmHg is the systolic threshold used when baseline pressure is elevated with supine hypertension, not the diastolic criterion.

B.q: A 47-year-old woman with familial dysbetalipoproteinemia asks what the disorder means for her long-term health. Which complication is it associated with?
opts: Sudden death in childhood
Sudden childhood death belongs to homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, which presents before puberty.
Accelerated atherosclerosis
Correct. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia is associated with accelerated atherosclerosis, the long-term danger of its remnant-driven rise in triglyceride and cholesterol.
Recurrent acute pancreatitis
Pancreatitis is the risk of triglyceride above 500 mg/dL, as in chylomicronemia; her levels run 250 to 500.
Loss of vision
Her disorder shows in the skin as palmar and tuberoeruptive xanthomas; its long-term danger is accelerated atherosclerosis, not the eyes.

B.q: A 55-year-old man with hypertensive retinopathy achieves good blood pressure control. What can be expected of his retinal findings?
opts: The changes are permanent once established
Control of hypertension can produce regression of retinopathy, so the finding is not a fixed one.
The changes have no relationship to blood pressure
Retinal changes are a direct consequence of the pressure, and they predict long-term stroke risk.
The changes will progress regardless of control
Progression is not inevitable, and regression of the retinopathy with good control is described.
Control can lead to regression of the retinopathy
Correct, so the finding is both a prognostic marker and something that can improve with treatment. Retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk independently of the pressure level.

B.q: What is the screening test, and what result is positive?
opts: Plasma free metanephrines
Metanephrines are the initial test for pheochromocytoma, which produces catecholamine excess rather than mineralocorticoid excess.
A morning aldosterone to renin ratio above roughly 20:1

Correct. Both halves matter: the ratio can be raised simply because renin is very low, so an aldosterone concentration above about 15 to 20 nanograms per deciliter is required alongside it. The aldosterone concentration itself must also be adequate for the ratio to count.
A renal duplex ultrasound
Duplex ultrasound screens for renal artery stenosis rather than for autonomous aldosterone production.
A twenty-four hour urinary cortisol measurement
That is used to investigate Cushing syndrome rather than aldosteronism, which is screened with the aldosterone to renin ratio.

B.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
B.q: A 68-year-old woman with coronary disease felt her heart race and then collapsed without warning in a store. She has recovered and is stable in the office. Which test should be obtained first?
opts: Orthostatic vital signs
Orthostatic readings look for a postural fall; her abrupt collapse with palpitations points to the heart rhythm.
An episode log
An episode log supports the history in reflex syncope; palpitations before an abrupt collapse call for a rhythm tracing.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is listed for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not for a suspected arrhythmia.
An electrocardiogram
Correct. A suspected arrhythmia is investigated first with an electrocardiogram, then monitoring, a stress test and cardiology consultation.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
B.q: Which dietary measure is used when triglycerides exceed 500 mg/dL?
opts: A high-fat ketogenic diet
A high-fat pattern runs against the very low-fat diet advised when triglyceride exceeds 500.
A very low-fat diet
Correct. Above 500 mg/dL management is a very low-fat diet (under 15% of calories from fat), weight management, physical activity, and a fibrate, niacin or both.
Added daily alcohol
Alcohol inhibits hepatic fatty-acid oxidation and raises triglyceride; it should be limited, not added.
A high-carbohydrate diet
Excess carbohydrate increases hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion, which worsens hypertriglyceridemia.

B.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
B.q: An 80-year-old man in the intensive care unit with acute heart failure has cool extremities and hypotension, and inotropic support is being considered. Which agents are used for this?
opts: Dobutamine or milrinone
Correct. Inotropic therapy for intensive care use includes the sympathomimetics dobutamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine and the phosphodiesterase inhibitor milrinone.
Spironolactone or eplerenone
These are mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for chronic reduced ejection fraction. Inotropic support uses dobutamine or milrinone.
Diltiazem or verapamil
These are calcium channel blockers, which are avoided in heart failure. Inotropic support uses dobutamine or milrinone.
Losartan or irbesartan
These are angiotensin receptor blockers for chronic therapy. Inotropic support in intensive care uses dobutamine or milrinone.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 21-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome after her heart rate rose by 38 within 10 minutes of standing. Which is the most appropriate first treatment?
opts: Restrict salt and fluid
Restriction runs opposite to the treatment, which increases water and salt intake.
Increase water and salt intake
Correct. Increasing water and salt intake is the first listed treatment, with fludrocortisone as the drug best suited to the syndrome.
Begin vasopressin
Vasopressin is a pressor reserved for the emergency department and intensive care, not an outpatient syndrome.
Start midodrine
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope, a postural pressure fall from autonomic failure, not this syndrome.

B.q: A 58-year-old hypertensive man has abrupt severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back, maximal at onset. His right arm pressure is 176/92 and his left is 138/78. A chest radiograph is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Delay imaging until the blood pressure is controlled
Imaging is immediate, because the diagnosis determines both the pressure target and the operation.
Reassure him, since the chest radiograph is normal
The radiograph may show a widened mediastinum but cannot rule the diagnosis out.
Obtain immediate cross-sectional vascular imaging

Correct. A normal chest radiograph does NOT exclude dissection, so a normal film must not end the workup. The pain that is maximal at onset and the asymmetric arm pressures both point to it, and surgical involvement is urgent.
Obtain an echocardiogram to establish the diagnosis
Echocardiography establishes coarctation; immediate cross-sectional vascular imaging is what is required here.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 79-year-old man with Parkinson disease faints when he gets up at night. His readings show a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Cut fluids to avoid night trips
Reducing fluid lowers volume and worsens postural falls; it is not listed advice for orthostatic syncope.
Stop all activity for a month
Inactivity is not a listed treatment; the advice targets how he changes position, alongside treating the cause.
Sit first, then stand up slowly
Correct. Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, and understanding why helps him follow the advice.
Leap up to trigger his reflexes
Abrupt standing is what provokes the fall; with autonomic failure the reflex cannot compensate, so slow change is the advice.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
B.q: A 24-year-old man has chest pain at rest with transient ST-segment elevation during the episode that resolves, and his coronary arteries show no high-grade stenosis. He smokes cigarettes and uses a recreational drug on weekends. Which substance should he be counseled to avoid because it can precipitate this condition?
opts: Nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin relieves vasospastic episodes, and response to it is part of the diagnosis. The substance to avoid is cocaine, a known precipitant of spasm.
Cocaine
Correct. Drugs that may precipitate vasospastic angina include cocaine, ephedrine, marijuana, alcohol, amphetamine and triptans. It is relatively uncommon and often strikes those under 50.
Amlodipine
Amlodipine is a first-line calcium channel blocker that prevents vasospastic episodes. Cocaine, along with amphetamine and ephedrine, precipitates them.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, the first-line therapy for vasospastic angina, not a trigger. Cocaine is among the drugs that precipitate spasm.

B.io: Acute myocardial infraction
B.q: Which artery supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle?
opts: Right marginal branch
The right marginal branch supplies the right ventricle's margin. The posteromedial papillary muscle takes its blood from the posterior interventricular branch.
Diagonal branch
The diagonal (lateral) branch supplies the left ventricular free wall. The posteromedial papillary muscle is supplied by the posterior interventricular branch.
Anterior interventricular branch
The anterior interventricular branch supplies the anterolateral papillary muscle, together with the circumflex. The posteromedial muscle depends on the posterior interventricular branch.
Posterior interventricular branch

Correct. The posteromedial papillary muscle is supplied by the posterior interventricular branch alone. The anterolateral papillary muscle has two sources: the anterior interventricular and circumflex branches.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 66-year-old with confirmed renal artery stenosis has recurrent flash pulmonary edema and progressive renal decline despite optimal medical therapy. What is the appropriate step?
opts: Early referral for revascularization assessment

Correct. Recurrent flash pulmonary edema, progressive renal decline despite optimal therapy, and truly refractory control are the three features that trigger early referral, rather than the mere presence of narrowing on imaging.
Refer any patient in whom screening finds renal artery narrowing
Narrowing found on screening does not by itself warrant intervention; the clinical features listed do.
Continue medical therapy; revascularization is never indicated
Those three specific features are exactly the situations in which referral is indicated.
Add a second dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Adding a second agent of the same class does not address the anatomic problem and is not among the described steps.

C.io: Aortic regurgitation
C.q: A 66-year-old man with chronic aortic regurgitation has no symptoms, but his echocardiogram now shows a reduced ejection fraction. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Percutaneous balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy treats severe symptomatic mitral stenosis. For aortic regurgitation with a reduced ejection fraction the step is evaluation for valve surgery.
Evaluation as a surgical candidate

Correct. Chronic aortic regurgitation with a mildly reduced or reduced ejection fraction, with or without symptoms, makes the patient a surgical candidate. Left untreated, survival is only about 2 to 3 years.
Continue afterload reduction alone
Afterload reduction is the medical management for aortic regurgitation with preserved ejection fraction. Once the ejection fraction falls, he is a surgical candidate even without symptoms.
Wait until symptoms develop
Waiting is not appropriate: chronic aortic regurgitation with a reduced ejection fraction makes him a surgical candidate whether or not he has symptoms.

C.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
C.io: ST segment elevation
C.q: A 63-year-old man has ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF and in the right-sided lead V4R, consistent with right ventricular infarction. His blood pressure is 104/66 mmHg. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: A heparin drip
A heparin drip is started once catheterization is confirmed in an ST-elevation infarction. In right ventricular infarction the drug to avoid is nitroglycerin.
Nitroglycerin

Correct. In a right ventricular infarct, do not give nitroglycerin: it lowers preload, the failing right ventricle loses its Frank-Starling support, output falls further and the patient can go into shock.
Chewable aspirin
Chewable aspirin is given in every ST-elevation infarction, including one involving the right ventricle. The drug to avoid here is nitroglycerin, which drops preload.
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel, a P2Y12 receptor antagonist, is given once catheterization is confirmed. Right ventricular involvement rules out nitroglycerin, not antiplatelet therapy.

C.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
C.io: Acute myocardial infraction
C.q: A 63-year-old man is recovering from an ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Several weeks later he develops pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial friction rub. Which complication of the infarction does this represent?
opts: Ventricular aneurysm
A ventricular aneurysm is a mechanical complication of the infarcted wall itself. It does not produce pleuritic pain with a pericardial friction rub; that is pericarditis (Dressler syndrome).
Myocardial rupture
Myocardial rupture is a catastrophic mechanical complication with sudden collapse. Pleuritic pain and a friction rub weeks later describe pericarditis (Dressler syndrome).
Thromboembolism
Thromboembolism causes stroke or limb ischemia from a clot leaving the heart. Pleuritic chest pain with a pericardial friction rub is pericarditis (Dressler syndrome).
Pericarditis

Correct. Pericarditis (Dressler syndrome) is listed among the mechanical complications of myocardial infarction. Pleuritic pain with a friction rub weeks after the infarct points to the pericardium rather than the ventricle.

C.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
C.q: Asymptomatic left ventricular hypertrophy places a patient in which heart failure stage?
opts: Stage A
Stage A requires normal heart function with risk factors only. Hypertrophy is structural disease, which moves the patient to stage B.
Stage C
Stage C requires past or current symptoms. Hypertrophy without symptoms is stage B.
Stage B

Correct. Stage B is asymptomatic structural heart disease, and left ventricular hypertrophy counts as structural disease, like ischemic cardiomyopathy and systolic or diastolic dysfunction. Stage A requires a structurally normal heart.
Stage D
Stage D is advanced heart failure. Asymptomatic hypertrophy is stage B, pre-heart failure.

C.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
C.q: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has asymptomatic left ventricular hypertrophy on echocardiogram. She already takes an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Which drug class should be added for her diabetes-related risk?
opts: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
The antagonist belongs to symptomatic heart failure. In stage B with diabetes the added class is the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. In stage B with diabetes the added class is the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor
Correct. She is stage B, and stage B carries a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for patients with diabetes as well as the converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.
Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
The neprilysin combination belongs to symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in functional class II or III. Stage B with diabetes adds a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: Spironolactone and eplerenone belong to which group?
opts: Thiazide-like diuretics
The thiazide-like diuretics are hydrochlorothiazide and metolazone. Spironolactone and eplerenone are potassium-sparing mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
Potassium-wasting loop diuretics
The loop diuretics are furosemide and bumetanide, which waste potassium. Spironolactone and eplerenone are potassium-sparing mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
Sodium-glucose inhibitors
The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. Spironolactone and eplerenone are mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
Potassium-sparing receptor antagonists
Correct. Spironolactone and eplerenone are mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, the potassium-sparing diuretics, and a strong recommendation in reduced ejection fraction.

C.q: A 16-year-old boy with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia has progressive atherosclerosis despite maximal drug therapy and apheresis. Which referral may help by supplying the receptors he lacks?
opts: Kidney transplantation
The kidney does not clear low-density lipoprotein through receptors; the liver is the organ that supplies them.
Liver transplantation
Correct. Liver transplantation may prove helpful in the homozygous disorder by providing low-density lipoprotein receptors that his own liver lacks or cannot use.
Carotid ultrasound only
Imaging would describe the disease, not treat it; transplantation addresses the missing receptors.
Bariatric surgery
Weight loss improves triglyceride and high-density lipoprotein, but cannot fix an inherited receptor defect.

C.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
C.q: A 58-year-old man with known dilated cardiomyopathy has worsening breathlessness. Blood pressure is 102/64, a third heart sound (an extra sound in early diastole just after the second heart sound) is present, and he has crackles. Which ejection fraction is the echocardiogram expected to show?
opts: About 45%
45% is mildly reduced, between the two chains. Dilated cardiomyopathy with a third sound and low pressure fits a clearly reduced value near 25%.
About 25%

Correct. Dilated cardiomyopathy is the systolic chain: poor contraction, a reduced ejection fraction of 40% or less, low-normal pressure, a third heart sound and pulmonary edema. A value near 25% fits.
About 60%
A preserved ejection fraction belongs to the diastolic chain of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Dilated cardiomyopathy with these signs gives a reduced value near 25%.
About 75%
A high value is the opposite of a failing squeeze. Dilated cardiomyopathy with a third sound fits a reduced ejection fraction near 25%.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: A 44-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance and palpitations for two months, and now ankle edema and breathlessness. Heart rate is 124 and B-type natriuretic peptide is elevated. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: High-output failure from hyperthyroidism

Correct. Hyperthyroidism raises peripheral demand, and the heart answers with a faster rate and stronger contraction until the heart failure syndrome appears: fatigue, dyspnea, edema and palpitations.
Diastolic failure from hypertension
She has no long hypertension or fourth sound. The weight loss, tremor and heat intolerance point to high-output failure from hyperthyroidism.
Systolic failure from ischemic disease
Nothing suggests infarction or ischemia, and the thyroid picture explains increased demand. This is high-output failure from hyperthyroidism.
Right-sided failure from mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis gives a diastolic rumble with an opening snap, not a hyperthyroid picture. This is high-output failure from hyperthyroidism.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: What produces the pressure drop in non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: A vagal surge with sudden bradycardia
A vagal surge with bradycardia and vasodilation is the vasovagal reflex chain, which is transient and triggered rather than postural.
A rapid ventricular rhythm on standing
A rapid ventricular rhythm is an arrhythmic cardiogenic cause, often with abrupt collapse and palpitations, not an orthostatic mechanism.
Low output or weak vasoconstriction
Correct. Reduced cardiac output and/or impaired vasoconstriction without a primary autonomic disorder leaves the brain poorly perfused on standing.
Failed norepinephrine release from nerves
Inadequate norepinephrine release from sympathetic neurons is the neurogenic mechanism, marked by only a minimal heart rate rise.

C.io: Acute coronary syndrome
C.q: A 52-year-old woman with two hours of chest pressure has a high-sensitivity troponin I of 16 ng/L. How should this value be interpreted?
opts: Abnormal only in a man
It is the reverse. A man's high-sensitivity troponin I becomes abnormal at 20 ng/L, a woman's at 12 ng/L, so 16 ng/L is abnormal in her and would not be in a man.
Too low to report
Only the lowest values are below the reportable range. A high-sensitivity troponin I of 16 ng/L is above the women's 99th percentile of 12 ng/L, so it is abnormal.
Abnormal for a woman
Correct. The 99th-percentile (abnormal) high-sensitivity troponin I value is 12 ng/L for women and 20 ng/L for men. At 16 ng/L, her high-sensitivity troponin I is abnormal.
Normal for any adult
High-sensitivity troponin I cut-offs are sex-specific: 12 ng/L for women and 20 ng/L for men. A woman's high-sensitivity troponin I of 16 ng/L is abnormal.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 20-year-old woman has a classic history of palpitations and lightheadedness on standing that improve lying down, but her tilt-table test is negative. How should the negative result be interpreted?
opts: It does not exclude the syndrome
Correct. With a sensitivity of about 40%, many patients with the syndrome test negative, so a negative result tells almost nothing; a positive result, with specificity above 80%, carries more weight.
It points to autonomic failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a pressure fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not by a negative tilt-table test.
It rules the syndrome out
Ruling out requires high sensitivity. At about 40%, a negative tilt-table test leaves the diagnosis open.
It points to a cardiac cause
A negative tilt-table test says nothing about the heart; cardiac causes are pursued with an electrocardiogram or echocardiography.

C.io: Mitral regurgitation
C.q: A 69-year-old woman has severe mitral regurgitation. Which electrocardiogram finding is most expected?
opts: An expected normal tracing
Severe mitral regurgitation dilates the left atrium under volume and pressure load, so left atrial enlargement is the expected finding, not a normal tracing.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy is the pulmonic stenosis electrocardiogram. Severe mitral regurgitation shows left atrial enlargement.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy is the tricuspid stenosis pattern. Mitral regurgitation enlarges the left atrium.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. Severe mitral regurgitation shows left atrial enlargement and left ventricular hypertrophy on the electrocardiogram, though with low sensitivity and questionable specificity.

C.q: A 48-year-old Black man develops lip and tongue swelling three months after starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. What should be known about this?
opts: A beta blocker is the appropriate substitution
The usual substitution is an angiotensin receptor blocker, and beta blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.
It is two to four times more common in this group

Correct. It is a bradykinin-mediated class effect of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition. Angiotensin receptor blockers can usually be used instead, though angioedema with them remains possible. An angiotensin receptor blocker is usually substituted.
An angiotensin receptor blocker carries no risk whatsoever
Angioedema with an angiotensin receptor blocker remains possible, although substitution is usually appropriate.
It is a dose-related effect that resolves on dose reduction
It is a class effect rather than a dose phenomenon, and the agent is stopped rather than reduced.

C.q: A 52-year-old woman has a fasting low-density lipoprotein of 215 mg/dL on repeat testing. Her thyroid function, kidney function and urinalysis are normal, and she has no atherosclerotic disease. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: High-intensity statin
Correct. Low-density lipoprotein of 190 mg/dL or more is severe primary hypercholesterolemia: begin a high-intensity statin without calculating 10-year risk.
Coronary artery calcium scoring
Calcium scoring is reserved for uncertain intermediate-risk decisions, not severe hypercholesterolemia.
Lifestyle alone for six months
Lifestyle continues, but at this level a high-intensity statin is indicated now rather than after a delay.
Moderate-intensity statin after risk calculation
Risk calculation and moderate intensity belong to low-density lipoprotein of 70 to 189; at 190 or more no calculation is needed.

C.q: A 66-year-old woman on amlodipine reports swollen ankles that are worse by evening. Her jugular venous pressure is normal and her lungs are clear. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: Heart failure requiring a loop diuretic
A normal jugular venous pressure and clear lungs argue against fluid overload, and the edema here is vasodilatory.
Hypoalbuminemia from thiazide therapy
Thiazide concerns are hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hyperuricemia and volume depletion.
An adverse effect of renin-angiotensin blockade
Ankle edema is a dihydropyridine effect; renin-angiotensin blockers cause cough, hyperkalemia, a creatinine rise and angioedema.
Dependent ankle edema

Correct. It follows from arterial vasodilation rather than fluid overload, which is why a diuretic does not fix it. Flushing, headache and gingival enlargement belong to the same class. It is the commonest effect of a dihydropyridine.

Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: A 59-year-old woman started a moderate-intensity statin six weeks ago for primary prevention. She feels well. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Recheck lipids in two years
Two years is far too long to judge adherence and response; the first recheck belongs at 4 to 12 weeks.
Repeat the lipid panel now
Correct. Adherence and percentage response are assessed with a repeat lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting a statin, then every 3 to 12 months as needed; six weeks falls in that window.
Stop the statin, she feels well
Feeling well is expected; the statin prevents events rather than treating symptoms.
Double the intensity without labs
Changes are guided by the measured percentage response, so labs come before any adjustment.

C.q: A 71-year-old woman with resistant hypertension is started on lisinopril. Her creatinine rises markedly within a week. What does this suggest?
opts: Bilateral renal artery stenosis

Correct. Where perfusion depends on angiotensin-mediated efferent arteriolar tone, blocking it drops the filtration pressure sharply. This is one of the recognized clues to renovascular disease, and it is why the agent is contraindicated in bilateral stenosis. A hemodynamically significant unilateral stenosis does the same.
Acute interstitial nephritis from the medication
Interstitial nephritis is not the mechanism described for this pattern; the abrupt rise on renin-angiotensin blockade points to renal artery stenosis.
Progression of underlying diabetic nephropathy
Diabetic nephropathy declines over months to years rather than jumping within a week of starting a renin-angiotensin blocker.
Expected drug effect requiring no change in approach
A small early creatinine rise can be acceptable, but a MARKED rise specifically points toward renovascular disease rather than being dismissed.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: How does the heart rate behave in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: It falls sharply first
A sudden slowing belongs to the vasovagal reflex, where vagal outflow surges, rather than to autonomic failure on standing.
It rises significantly
A significant rise shows an intact baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic response, which favors the non-neurogenic form instead.
It rises only minimally
Correct. Failed autonomic signaling means the heart rate rises less than expected even as pressure falls, which is the tell that separates it from volume loss.
It exceeds 120 per minute
A rate above 120 per minute within 10 minutes of standing is a criterion for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome.

C.q: Which adverse effects and cautions attach to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors?
opts: Sedation, dry mouth and rebound hypertension on withdrawal
Those are limitations of the central alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine, whose abrupt withdrawal produces rebound hypertension, rather than of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition.
Dependent ankle edema, flushing and headache
These are effects of the dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers rather than of renin-angiotensin blockade.
Hyperuricemia precipitating gout
That is a thiazide effect, related to urate handling rather than to angiotensin blockade.
Dry cough, hyperkalemia, creatinine rise and angioedema

Correct. The cough is bradykinin-mediated, which is why switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker usually resolves it while keeping the same therapeutic effect. They are avoided in pregnancy, in prior angioedema and in bilateral renal artery stenosis.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: A 62-year-old woman is three days out from a myocardial infarction complicated by acute heart failure, with an ejection fraction of 30%. A colleague proposes an implantable defibrillator before discharge. Which step is premature at this point?
opts: Optimizing her guideline therapy
Optimizing therapy is part of the pathway now. What is premature is the implantable device.
Implanting a defibrillator now

Correct. After acute heart failure from infarction, the pathway is a wearable defibrillator, optimized therapy and cardiac rehabilitation, then a repeat echocardiogram; the implantable device follows only if there is no improvement.
Starting a wearable defibrillator
The wearable defibrillator is exactly the first step for her. What is premature is the implantable device.
Referring to cardiac rehabilitation
Cardiac rehabilitation is part of the pathway now. What is premature is the implantable device.

C.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
C.q: What is the most common cause of tricuspid regurgitation?
opts: Rheumatic scarring of the leaflets
Rheumatic scarring leads to stenosis of the mitral valve and, worldwide, the tricuspid valve. Tricuspid regurgitation most often follows annular dilation.
Carcinoid disease of the valve
Carcinoid disease is listed for pulmonic and tricuspid stenosis and pulmonic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation most often follows annular dilation.
Endocarditis from intravenous drug use
Endocarditis in intravenous drug users is the primary cause of tricuspid regurgitation, but not the most common. That is annular dilation with pulmonary hypertension.
Pulmonary hypertension dilating the annulus

Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation is most commonly due to dilation of the tricuspid annulus from right ventricular dilation in the setting of pulmonary hypertension. Primary disease is infective endocarditis in drug users.

C.io: ST segment elevation
C.q: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 points to which culprit artery?
opts: Posterior interventricular branch
The posterior interventricular branch runs in the inferior groove and supplies the inferior septum. The lateral leads point to the left circumflex artery.
Left circumflex artery
Correct. The lateral leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 point to the left circumflex artery or a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery.
Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery is the culprit for inferior changes in II, III and aVF. The lateral leads point to the left circumflex artery (or a diagonal branch).
Right marginal branch
The right marginal branch supplies the right ventricle from the right coronary artery. The lateral leads point to the left circumflex artery.

C.io: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal variant)
C.q: Vasospastic angina typically occurs under which circumstance?
opts: After a large meal
A meal is not the trigger. Vasospastic angina occurs at rest, caused by coronary spasm, and drugs such as cocaine, amphetamine or triptans may precipitate it.
With deep breathing
Pain that changes with breathing or position points away from cardiac ischemia. Vasospastic angina occurs at rest and responds to nitroglycerin.
At rest

Correct. Vasospastic angina occurs at rest, from coronary artery vasospasm in normal or diseased arteries, and responds to nitroglycerin. Most patients have their pain between midnight and early morning.
During exertion
Pain brought on by exertion and relieved by rest is stable angina. Vasospastic angina is the opposite pattern: it occurs at rest, often between midnight and early morning.

C.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
C.q: A 35-year-old woman standing at an outdoor event in the heat develops tunnel vision, lightheadedness and dizziness but is still conscious. If her pressure keeps falling, what is likely to follow?
opts: A prolonged coma
Syncope is transient and self-limited, so a prolonged coma is not the expected outcome of falling pressure here.
A brief faint
Correct. Her symptoms are near-syncope, which precedes syncope: a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness followed by spontaneous recovery.
A generalized seizure
Seizure is a separate, non-hypotensive cause of loss of consciousness and does not follow near-syncope from low pressure.
Supine hypertension
Supine hypertension is high pressure while lying flat, a comorbidity rather than a consequence of near-syncope.

C.q: A 57-year-old man with confirmed resistant hypertension has had his diuretic optimized and his other two agents titrated to maximally tolerated doses. His filtration rate and potassium are normal. Which fourth agent has the most evidence?
opts: A beta blocker
Beta blockade appears among the later escalation options chosen by physiology and comorbidity rather than as the evidence-supported fourth agent.
A second dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Adding a second agent of the same class is not among the described steps and duplicates a mechanism.
Spironolactone
Correct, provided the filtration rate and potassium allow. It is added after the foundational three are optimized rather than instead of doing so.
Hydralazine
Hydralazine is a later addition and requires combination therapy because of reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.

C.q: A 24-year-old man has severe epigastric pain radiating to his back. Clusters of small yellowish-white papules (eruptive xanthomas) cover his buttocks and the backs of his arms, and fundoscopy shows opalescent retinal vessels (lipemia retinalis). His fasting triglyceride is 2100 mg/dL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The heterozygous cholesterol disorder has low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 with normal triglyceride and tendon xanthomas, not pancreatitis.
Metabolic syndrome
Metabolic syndrome needs three of five criteria such as triglyceride above 150; it does not produce triglyceride above 2000 with lipemia retinalis.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 mg/dL with palmar xanthomas, far below 2100.
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome

Correct. Fasting triglyceride above 500 and usually above 1000 mg/dL, acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas and lipemia retinalis (sometimes with hepatosplenomegaly) define this syndrome, which can present in childhood or adulthood.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: What level of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol is classified as low?
opts: Below 150 mg/dL
150 mg/dL is the upper limit of normal triglyceride, not a high-density lipoprotein threshold; low high-density lipoprotein is below 40.
Below 60 mg/dL
60 mg/dL is the high threshold that counts as a negative risk factor; low begins below 40 mg/dL.
Below 40 mg/dL
Correct. High-density lipoprotein below 40 mg/dL is low and counts as a major coronary risk factor, while 60 mg/dL or more is high and removes one risk factor from the count.
Below 100 mg/dL
100 mg/dL is the optimal cutoff for low-density lipoprotein, not a high-density lipoprotein category.

Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: Which outcome is associated with consuming fatty fish or fish-oil supplements?
opts: More low-density lowering than statins
Statins are the most effective low-density drugs; fish oil is not a low-density lowering drug.
Lower risk of coronary death

Correct. Fatty fish or fish-oil supplements are associated with lower risk of coronary heart disease and coronary death, may lower thrombotic stroke risk, and at least 2 servings of fish a week are advised.
Higher high-density lipoprotein than niacin
Niacin raises high-density lipoprotein better than other medications; fish oil's benefit is lower coronary risk and coronary death.
Cure of familial hypercholesterolemia
No drug cures the receptor defect; the homozygous form needs apheresis and multiple drugs.

C.q: A 45-year-old man is newly diagnosed with hypertension. Which baseline studies are obtained?
opts: A chest radiograph and echocardiogram in every patient
Neither is routine: chest radiography is specifically not indicated for uncomplicated hypertension, and echocardiography is reserved for defined indications.
Plasma free metanephrines in every patient
Metanephrines are ordered when the history suggests pheochromocytoma rather than as a universal baseline study.
Creatinine alone, with nothing further
The panel is considerably broader, covering renal assessment, electrolytes, metabolic studies, thyroid screening and urinalysis.
Renal function, electrolytes, glucose, lipids and urinalysis

Correct, with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio alongside the creatinine. The panel does three jobs at once: screens for secondary causes, measures organ damage, and establishes a baseline before drugs that alter potassium and renal function are started. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and a full blood count complete it.

C.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
C.q: A 52-year-old woman has pulmonic regurgitation on echocardiogram and has developed leg edema and distended neck veins. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Cardiology referral
Correct. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when it is seen on echocardiogram or when there are right heart failure signs and symptoms, both of which she has.
Repeat echo in 5 years
Deferring for years ignores her right heart failure. Pulmonic regurgitation on echo or with right heart failure signs is referred now.
Start lifelong warfarin
Warfarin is for mechanical heart valves. Pulmonic regurgitation with right heart failure signs is referred to cardiology.
No follow-up needed
An incidental leak may be quiet, but she now has right heart failure signs. Pulmonic regurgitation seen on echo or with right heart failure is referred.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: A 70-year-old man admitted with acute heart failure has diuresed well. On the day of planned discharge his B-type natriuretic peptide is 360. What does this predischarge level suggest?
opts: Higher risk of 30-day readmission
Risk rises with higher levels. Below 430 predischarge, the readmission risk is lower.
The level carries no prognostic value
Predischarge levels do carry prognostic meaning: below 430 is linked to lower 30-day readmission.
Acute heart failure is still likely
Acute failure becomes likely above 900. A predischarge level of 360 is below 430 and linked to lower readmission.
Lower risk of 30-day readmission
Correct. A predischarge level below 430 carries a lower risk of readmission within 30 days, which supports discharge planning.
