C.q: Which examination findings support a suspicion of aortic dissection?
opts: Weak femoral pulses present since childhood
Long-standing weak femoral pulses with upper limb hypertension suggest coarctation rather than an acute dissection.
Normal and symmetric pulses, which exclude the diagnosis
Absence of pulse findings specifically does not exclude dissection, which is why imaging is driven by the clinical suspicion rather than the examination alone.
Pulse deficits, asymmetric arm pressures or a new deficit

Correct, but their absence proves nothing: absent pulse findings do not exclude the diagnosis, so a normal pulse examination must not close the question. An aortic regurgitation murmur belongs on the list too.
Bilateral leg edema
Peripheral edema is a clue to chronic kidney disease among the secondary causes rather than a finding in acute dissection.

C.io: Pulmonic stenosis
C.q: A 16-year-old boy has a harsh, high-pitched crescendo-decrescendo mid-systolic ejection murmur at the left second to fourth intercostal spaces at the sternal border. It grows louder with inspiration, and the second heart sound is split. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pulmonic stenosis

Correct. Harsh means stenosis and systolic narrows it to the aortic or pulmonic valve; the left upper sternal border, the inspiratory increase of a right-sided murmur and the split second sound mark pulmonic stenosis.
Pulmonic regurgitation
Pulmonic regurgitation sits at the second left intercostal space too, but it is a brief early diastolic decrescendo murmur. Harsh and systolic means stenosis.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation also grows louder with inspiration, but it is holosystolic at the left lower sternal border near the epigastrium, not a harsh ejection murmur.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is harsh and systolic but sits at the second right intercostal space, radiates to the carotids and is a left-sided murmur that is louder on expiration.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 75-year-old man with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from multiple system atrophy has supine hypertension (high blood pressure while lying flat). He remains symptomatic on standing despite slow position changes. Which treatment should be avoided?
opts: Slow position changes
Slow positional changes are first-line for every orthostatic patient and are continued whatever medication is chosen.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa is the better choice with supine hypertension, which makes it the drug to consider here rather than the one to avoid.
Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is avoided in heart failure because it retains salt and water; supine hypertension is not its listed contraindication.
Midodrine
Correct. Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope but is avoided with supine hypertension, severe heart disease and chronic kidney disease.

C.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
C.q: A 63-year-old man with mildly reduced ejection fraction (fraction 44%) has ankle edema and breathlessness. Which therapy carries the strongest recommendation?
opts: A mineralocorticoid antagonist
The antagonist is a weak recommendation in mildly reduced ejection fraction. A diuretic as needed carries the strongest one.
A neprilysin combination drug
The angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is weak in mildly reduced ejection fraction. A diuretic as needed carries the strongest recommendation.
A diuretic as needed

Correct. In mildly reduced ejection fraction, diuretics as needed carry the one strong recommendation. The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is moderate; the beta blocker, antagonist and renin-angiotensin drugs are weak.
An evidence-based beta blocker
In mildly reduced ejection fraction the beta blocker is a weak recommendation. The strongest is a diuretic as needed for his congestion.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
C.q: An 81-year-old woman has a pressure of 104/64 at a routine visit and feels well. She worries because it is lower than her usual readings. What should she be told about this reading?
opts: One reading is a snapshot in time
Correct. Each reading is only a snapshot in time and is judged against age, comorbidities and the possibility of relative hypotension, together with symptoms.
Pressure norms are fixed for all ages
Blood pressure norms are affected by age, which is exactly why a reading needs context rather than a single fixed cutoff.
It proves autonomic nerve failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not by one low resting reading.
Any reading this low needs pressors
Pressors are for the emergency department and intensive care; an asymptomatic outpatient reading does not call for them.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: A 45-year-old woman has new swelling of both legs, heavy protein in her urine and low-density lipoprotein of 220 mg/dL. Before a statin is started, which condition should be ruled out?
opts: Nephrotic syndrome
Correct. Elevated low-density lipoprotein calls for ruling out nephrotic syndrome, which drives excess very-low-density production and raises triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein.
Metabolic syndrome
Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed from waist, triglyceride, high-density lipoprotein, blood pressure and glucose, not proteinuria.
Familial chylomicronemia
Chylomicronemia is a triglyceride disorder with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas, not edema and proteinuria.
Heterozygous familial form
A genetic cause is sought only after secondary causes are ruled out, and her edema and proteinuria point to the kidney.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: A 36-year-old woman has just been told she has heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. She asks whether any single test can prove it. Which answer is accurate?
opts: A skin biopsy proves it in her case
Skin biopsy with receptor-activity measurement confirms the homozygous form, not the heterozygous one.
Fundoscopy settles the question
Fundoscopy looks for lipemia retinalis in chylomicronemia and plays no part in confirming her disorder.
No definitive test exists for her form
Correct. No definitive diagnostic test is available for the heterozygous form; the skin biopsy with receptor activity confirms only the homozygous disorder.
A calcium score of zero rules it out
Calcium scoring guides primary-prevention statin decisions and cannot exclude an inherited receptor defect.

C.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
C.q: A 70-year-old man fainted at home and has recovered. His electrocardiogram and glucose are normal. Which tests look for an infectious or metabolic contributor?
opts: A blood count and metabolic panel
Correct. Unremarkable blood counts and a metabolic panel lower suspicion of an infectious or metabolic source, as glucose and the electrocardiogram address hypoglycemia and dysrhythmia.
Orthostatic vitals only
Orthostatic readings test for a postural fall and cannot detect an infectious or metabolic source.
A tilt-table test and a log
A tilt-table test belongs to the tachycardia syndrome and a log to reflex syncope; neither screens for infection.
An echocardiogram and stress test
These evaluate structural and arrhythmic cardiac causes rather than infection or metabolic disturbance.

C.io: Aortic stenosis
C.q: A 74-year-old man with untreated severe aortic stenosis now has breathlessness on exertion, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and ankle swelling. Without valve replacement, which average survival is expected from this symptom?
opts: About 3 years
About 3 years belongs to exertional syncope. Heart failure or exertional dyspnea is the most common cardinal symptom and has the shortest survival, about 2 years.
About 5 years
About 5 years is the average survival once angina appears. Heart failure symptoms such as exertional dyspnea and orthopnea carry the worst prognosis, about 2 years.
About 10 years
A decade is far too long; once aortic stenosis becomes symptomatic, prognosis is severely worsened. With heart failure symptoms the average survival is about 2 years.
About 2 years
Correct. Of the cardinal symptoms, heart failure or exertional dyspnea is the most common and carries the worst prognosis, about 2 years. Angina carries about 5 years and syncope about 3 years.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 69-year-old man reports lightheadedness and dimming vision within a minute or two of standing, which settles when he sits. His examination at rest is normal. Which test should be performed first?
opts: Orthostatic vital signs
Correct. Pressure and heart rate taken supine and again within 3 minutes of standing show whether orthostatic criteria are met and which type the heart rate response suggests.
A stress test
A stress test belongs to the arrhythmia work-up of cardiogenic syncope, not the first test for a postural pattern of symptoms.
A tilt-table test
The tilt-table test is the listed test for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and its sensitivity of about 40% makes a negative result weak.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope; symptoms that follow standing call first for a postural pressure measurement.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 67-year-old woman with 20 years of type 2 diabetes has fainted twice shortly after getting out of bed. Her mucous membranes are moist, and vibration and light-touch sensation are reduced in both feet. Supine she is 140/80 with a heart rate of 70; after 3 minutes standing she is 110/66 with a heart rate of 74. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear, pain or heat with a transient reflex, not a reproducible postural fall on standing.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
The non-neurogenic form shows a significant heart rate rise from an intact autonomic reflex and usually volume depletion; she has neither.
Cardiogenic arrhythmic syncope
An arrhythmia typically causes abrupt collapse without warning and often palpitations; her faints follow standing, with a regular exam.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Correct. The systolic fall of 30 mmHg meets the criterion, the heart rate barely rises, and long-standing diabetes with neuropathy points to diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 58-year-old woman with fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation is found to have blood pressure of 146/96 with a predominantly diastolic elevation. Which mechanism fits?
opts: Autonomous aldosterone secretion
Aldosteronism produces resistant hypertension with hypokalemia rather than cold intolerance and constipation.
Catecholamine excess from an adrenal tumor
Pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal symptoms rather than the sustained hypothyroid picture described.
Hypothyroidism raising vascular resistance
Correct. Hypothyroidism raises systemic vascular resistance, which lifts the diastolic pressure, whereas hyperthyroidism raises cardiac output and lifts the systolic.
Hyperthyroidism raising cardiac output
That produces a predominantly SYSTOLIC elevation with tachycardia, and her symptoms point the other way.

C.io: Mitral stenosis
C.q: Left atrial enlargement in mitral stenosis predisposes to which rhythm?
opts: Complete heart block
Heart block is not the rhythm the stretched left atrium produces. Mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation and thromboembolism.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. Rising left atrial size and pressure predispose to atrial fibrillation, which is a risk factor for thromboembolism and is common in severe mitral stenosis.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia arises from the ventricles. The dilated left atrium of mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation.
Sinus bradycardia
A slow sinus rhythm is not the danger here. The enlarged left atrium of mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 64-year-old man with hypertension has heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction and a myocardial infarction six months ago. Which class is preferred for him?
opts: A beta blocker

Correct. Beta blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension, but reduced ejection fraction heart failure, recent infarction and ischemic disease are exactly the comorbidities that select them.
A non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Verapamil and diltiazem are avoided where the ejection fraction is already reduced, as it is here.
Hydralazine as monotherapy
Hydralazine requires combination therapy because of reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Clonidine
Central alpha-2 agonists are limited by sedation and rebound hypertension and have no preferred indication here.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: A 73-year-old woman has grade II diastolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 46%. She has fatigue and breathlessness with exertion but has never had pulmonary or peripheral edema and has never needed a diuretic. Does she meet a clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure?
opts: Yes, because she has symptoms
Symptoms make heart failure clinical, but calling it congestive requires congestion, meaning edema, which she has never had.
Yes, because her fraction is 46%
Her fraction places her in the mildly reduced group; it does not make the heart failure congestive. Congestion, meaning edema, is required.
Yes, because she is older than 65
Age does not define the diagnosis. A clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure requires congestion, meaning edema.
No, because congestion is required

Correct. A clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure requires congestion, meaning pulmonary or peripheral edema. She has symptoms and a mildly reduced ejection fraction, but without edema the congestive label does not apply.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
C.q: A 38-year-old woman who smokes a pack of cigarettes a day asks whether smoking really matters for her heart at her age. Which counseling point is accurate?
opts: It matters only with diabetes
Smoking is an independent modifiable risk factor; it does not need diabetes to count. It is a strong predictor especially in women younger than 45.
It is a strong predictor at her age
Correct. Smoking is a modifiable coronary risk factor and a strong predictor, especially in women younger than 45. Her age makes the counseling more urgent, not less.
It raises risk only in men
Smoking raises risk in both sexes and is a strong predictor especially in women younger than 45, so it matters for her now.
It matters only after menopause
Smoking is not a postmenopausal risk only. It is a strong predictor of coronary disease especially in women younger than 45, which is exactly her group.

C.io: Angina pectoris
C.q: A 60-year-old woman has episodes of jaw and tooth pain when she walks uphill that ease when she rests. Her dentist found no dental cause. Which is the most likely cause of her pain?
opts: Gallbladder disease
Gallbladder pain refers to the right scapular region and is not brought on by walking uphill. Exertional jaw and tooth pain is referred ischemic pain.
Pancreatitis
Pancreatic pain goes straight through to the back and is not exertional. Jaw and tooth pain with exertion that eases with rest is referred cardiac pain.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection refers pain to the left or interscapular region and is not a recurrent exertional pattern. Referral to the jaw and teeth fits ischemia.
Myocardial ischemia
Correct. Exertional pain relieved by rest is ischemic, and acute coronary syndrome refers pain most commonly to the jaw, tooth or arm. Toothache is even listed among the descriptors of angina.

C.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
C.io: Unstable
C.q: A 66-year-old man with chest pain has a nuclear stress test showing a perfusion defect that does not reverse at rest. What does this fixed defect indicate?
opts: Prior infarction
Correct. On a nuclear stress test, a reversible perfusion defect indicates ischemia, while a non-reversible (fixed) defect indicates infarction.
A normal study
A normal study shows no perfusion defect at all. A defect that does not reverse at rest indicates infarction.
Coronary vasospasm
Vasospasm is diagnosed by provoking spasm at angiography, not by a fixed nuclear defect. A non-reversible defect indicates infarction.
Reversible ischemia
Ischemia produces a reversible defect that fills in at rest. A defect that stays at rest is non-reversible and indicates infarction.

C.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
C.q: A 45-year-old woman without diabetes has low-density lipoprotein of 120 mg/dL and a 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 3%. She has no risk-enhancing factors. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Moderate-intensity statin
A moderate-intensity statin is started at intermediate risk when the discussion favors it; at 3% lifestyle is emphasized.
Emphasize lifestyle
Correct. Low risk (under 5%) calls for a risk discussion that emphasizes lifestyle to reduce risk factors, rather than a statin.
Ezetimibe alone
Ezetimibe is an adjunct to a maximal statin in higher-risk patients, not therapy for low-risk primary prevention.
High-intensity statin
High intensity is for clinical disease, severe hypercholesterolemia or high 10-year risk, not a 3% estimate.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 43-year-old woman's previously well-controlled blood pressure has risen over two months. She denies missing doses. What should the medication review specifically cover beyond her prescriptions?
opts: Only agents started within the past week
The review is not bounded that tightly; a substance taken for months can be responsible.
Only intravenous medications given in hospital
The categories named are over-the-counter, recreational, licorice and herbal supplements.
Only her antihypertensive agents
Reviewing the antihypertensives addresses adherence, but the question is what else may be raising the pressure.
Over-the-counter drugs, licorice and supplements

Correct, and patients frequently do not volunteer any of these because they do not regard them as medication. A sudden loss of previously stable control is itself a clue to a secondary cause. Recreational substances belong in the same review.

C.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
C.q: A 78-year-old man fell in the bathroom at 3 a.m. while urinating standing up, after two beers the evening before. He felt a swimmy head, nausea and sweating first and recovered quickly. His vital signs, neurologic examination and glucose are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension causes a sustained postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not a reflex tied to voiding.
Situational reflex syncope
Correct. Nocturnal voiding after abruptly rising triggers an exaggerated autonomic reflex, and alcohol and relative dehydration add to it; this is micturition syncope.
Hypoglycemic loss of consciousness
Hypoglycemia is a non-hypotensive cause of syncope, and his normal glucose rules it out.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows emotional stress, fear, pain, heat or prolonged standing rather than a bodily function such as urination.

C.io: Non-ST segment elevation
C.q: A 64-year-old man with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction is stabilized and taken to the catheterization laboratory. Dye shows a tight narrowing of the anterior interventricular artery, which is opened with a balloon and held open with a drug-eluting stent. Which term names the procedure that opened the artery?
opts: Percutaneous coronary intervention

Correct. Percutaneous coronary intervention is the placement of a drug-eluting or non-drug-eluting stent to keep the coronary artery open. Anything done to the vessel during the catheterization, beyond imaging it, is the intervention.
Coronary angiography
Coronary angiography is the injection of dye to identify the lesion or blockage. It showed the narrowing here, but it did not open the artery; the stent placement did.
Plain old balloon angioplasty
Plain old balloon angioplasty opens a narrowed artery without a stent. Once a stent is left in place to hold the artery open, the procedure is a percutaneous coronary intervention.
Left heart catheterization
Left heart catheterization is the introduction of a guidewire for access to the heart chambers and coronary arteries. It is the access, not the stent that opened the vessel.

C.io: Unstable
C.q: A 60-year-old woman has chest pressure that began at rest. Her electrocardiogram shows T-wave inversion in two consecutive leads. Which result would make this a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
opts: Pain that began at rest
Pain at rest defines unstable angina as well as infarction. What makes it a non-ST-elevation infarction is an elevated troponin I.
Relief with nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin usually, but not always, helps unstable angina and may help an infarction too. Relief does not separate them; an elevated troponin I does.
Troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL
Correct. Elevated cardiac markers (troponin or high-sensitivity troponin) are what separate a non-ST-elevation infarction from unstable angina. A standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal.
Inverted T waves persisting
Inverted T waves occur in both unstable angina and non-ST-elevation infarction. The electrocardiogram cannot separate them; an elevated troponin I does.

C.io: Mitral valve prolapse
C.q: A 19-year-old woman is found to have a mid-systolic click at the apex at a sports physical. She feels well. Which is the most appropriate initial test?
opts: Electrocardiogram
An electrocardiogram does not show valve anatomy. The diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse is made by echocardiogram.
Echocardiogram
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed by echocardiogram, which shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets greater than 5 mm bowing into the left atrium during systole.
Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph does not show the leaflets or their motion. A mid-systolic click is investigated with an echocardiogram showing redundant leaflets.
Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is invasive and not how prolapse is diagnosed. An echocardiogram shows the thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.

C.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
C.q: A 68-year-old woman has fatigue and breathlessness with exertion. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 45%, and her fraction has never been lower. Which heart failure group describes her?
opts: Reduced ejection fraction
Reduced ejection fraction is 40% or less. At 45% she falls in the mildly reduced band.
Improved ejection fraction
Improved ejection fraction needs an earlier value of 40% or less. Hers has never been lower, so she is mildly reduced.
Mildly reduced ejection fraction
Correct. 45% falls in the 41 to 49% band, and with no earlier value of 40% or less there is nothing to make it improved ejection fraction. Her treatment then resembles preserved ejection fraction.
Preserved ejection fraction
Preserved ejection fraction starts at 50%. At 45% she falls in the mildly reduced band.

C.io: Tricuspid stenosis
C.q: A 50-year-old woman has severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis with leg swelling and jugular venous distension. Before any procedure, which medical regimen is appropriate?
opts: Warfarin with a heparin bridge
Warfarin with heparin bridging is anticoagulation for mechanical valves. Tricuspid stenosis is managed with low salt, a diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist.
Nitrates, beta blocker, calcium blocker
Nitrates, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are the avoid list for aortic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis is managed with salt restriction, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist.
Low salt, diuretic, aldosterone antagonist
Correct. Severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is managed with a low-salt diet, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist, with bioprosthetic valve replacement preferred when the valve is replaced.
Afterload reduction with hydralazine
Afterload reduction is medical management for chronic aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid stenosis uses low salt, a diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist.

C.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
C.q: A 49-year-old man is discharged after receiving a mechanical aortic valve. Which medication must he be told he will take for life?
opts: Warfarin
Correct. A mechanical valve of titanium and carbon needs lifelong anticoagulation, and warfarin, the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist, is recommended for long-term management.
Nitroprusside
Nitroprusside is an intravenous vasodilator used briefly in intensive care for acute aortic regurgitation. A mechanical valve needs lifelong warfarin.
Heparin
Heparin is only a bridge when warfarin has to stop for surgery. The medication for life after a mechanical valve is warfarin.
Aspirin
Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent, and vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over antiplatelet agents for a mechanical valve. Warfarin is the lifelong drug.

C.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
C.q: A 48-year-old man without cardiovascular disease has hypertension and smokes. His clinician wants to estimate his 10-year risk of atherosclerotic disease to guide statin therapy. Which tool is appropriate?
opts: Pooled Cohort Equation

Correct. It estimates 10-year primary risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in patients 40 to 79 without pre-existing disease, using variables such as age, sex, cholesterol, systolic pressure, diabetes and smoking.
Metabolic syndrome criteria
The syndrome's five criteria define a diagnosis; they do not give a 10-year risk percentage.
Fundoscopic examination
Fundoscopy finds lipemia retinalis in chylomicronemia and has no role in 10-year risk estimation.
Skin biopsy for receptors
Skin biopsy confirms homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and does not estimate population risk.

D.io: Acute coronary syndrome
D.q: A 59-year-old woman with chest pressure has a first high-sensitivity troponin I of 8 ng/L and a second, drawn later, of 30 ng/L. How should the second result be interpreted?
opts: A lab error to ignore
A rise between draws is exactly what serial troponins look for. Her second high-sensitivity troponin I of 30 ng/L is abnormal for a woman and must be acted on.
A normal result for a woman
The women's high-sensitivity troponin I 99th percentile is 12 ng/L; 30 ng/L is well above it. The result is abnormal and rising.
A stable, reassuring result
A jump from 8 to 30 ng/L in high-sensitivity troponin I is not stable. A second value higher than the first is the change serial draws are meant to catch.
A rising, abnormal result

Correct. Serial troponins are drawn to watch the change. Her second high-sensitivity troponin I of 30 ng/L is above the women's 99th percentile of 12 ng/L and higher than the first, so another is ordered as cells continue to die.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 72-year-old woman has supine hypertension (high blood pressure while lying flat). Lying down she is 176/96; after 3 minutes standing she is 152/90, and she feels mildly lightheaded. Do these readings meet the orthostatic criterion?
opts: No; readings need 10 minutes
Ten minutes is the window for the heart rate criteria of the tachycardia syndrome; orthostatic pressure criteria use 3 minutes.
Yes; the fall exceeds 20 mmHg
More than 20 mmHg is the systolic threshold for a normal baseline. Supine hypertension raises the systolic threshold to more than 30 mmHg.
No; a fall over 30 mmHg is needed
Correct. With an elevated baseline or supine hypertension the systolic fall must exceed 30 mmHg; hers is 24 and the diastolic fall is only 6.
Yes; any fall with symptoms counts
The criteria are numeric thresholds within 3 minutes of standing; symptoms alone do not meet them.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: Which drug used for hypotension has only mild efficacy?
opts: Vasopressin
Vasopressin is a pressor reserved, with epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and phenylephrine, for the emergency department and intensive care.
Midodrine
Midodrine is described as best with neurogenic syncope, the first choice there unless supine hypertension, severe heart disease or kidney disease is present.
Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is described as best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and it is avoided in heart failure.
Droxidopa
Correct. Droxidopa has mild efficacy, is better with supine hypertension, and is usually used as an adjunct with midodrine or fludrocortisone.

D.io: Pulmonic stenosis
D.q: A 25-year-old woman has severe congenital pulmonic stenosis with exertional dyspnea and syncope. Which procedure is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty

Correct. Severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms is treated with pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty, with diuretics for right heart failure symptoms; severe congenital disease may require valve replacement.
Tricuspid annuloplasty
Annuloplasty treats tricuspid regurgitation caused by annular dilation. Severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis is treated with balloon valvuloplasty.
Mitral balloon valvotomy
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy of the mitral valve treats severe symptomatic mitral stenosis. Her obstruction is at the pulmonic valve.
Aortic valve replacement
Aortic valve replacement treats severe aortic stenosis. Severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis is opened with pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty.

D.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
D.q: An ejection fraction of 45% that has never been lower places heart failure in which group?
opts: Preserved ejection fraction
Preserved ejection fraction starts at 50%. A value of 45% is in the mildly reduced band of 41 to 49%.
Reduced ejection fraction
Reduced ejection fraction is 40% or less. A value of 45% is in the mildly reduced band.
Improved ejection fraction
Improved ejection fraction needs a prior value of 40% or less. With no lower prior value, 45% is mildly reduced ejection fraction.
Mildly reduced ejection fraction
Correct. 45% sits inside the 41 to 49% band, and because it has never been lower there is no prior reduced value that would make it improved ejection fraction.

D.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
D.io: Non-ST segment elevation
D.q: Which TIMI (Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction) score justifies an early invasive approach?
opts: 5 or higher
Waiting for 5 sets the bar too high. A TIMI score of 3 or higher already justifies intensive care or emergent revascularization.
3 or higher
Correct. A TIMI score of 3 or higher (3 to 7) calls for intensive care or emergent revascularization, the score an interventionalist uses to justify catheterization and stenting.
Only the maximum
The maximum is not required. Any TIMI score from 3 upward calls for intensive care or emergent revascularization.
1 or higher
A single point does not justify an invasive approach. The threshold is a TIMI score of 3 or higher, which calls for intensive care or emergent revascularization.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 30-year-old woman with vasovagal syncope must have regular blood draws for a chronic illness and has fainted at two of them. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Take safety precautions during draws
Correct. When a trigger cannot be avoided, safety precautions during the trigger are recommended, alongside trigger avoidance wherever possible.
Fast and restrict fluids beforehand
Poor intake and dehydration lower volume and make fainting more likely rather than less.
Take midodrine before each draw
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is not listed for preventing vasovagal episodes.
Stop the blood draws altogether
The draws are needed for her illness; when a trigger is unavoidable, the advice is safety precautions rather than stopping care.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
D.q: A 16-year-old girl has palpitations and dizziness on standing. Within 10 minutes of standing her heart rate rises from 70 to 114, and her pressure does not fall. Does this meet the heart rate criterion for her age?
opts: No; adolescents need a rise of 50
The adolescent threshold is 40 beats per minute, and her rise of 44 clearly exceeds it.
Yes; any rise over 20 per minute
A rise of 20 is too low for any age group; the adult threshold is more than 30 and the adolescent threshold 40.
Yes; the rise exceeds 40 per minute
Correct. In adolescents the threshold is an increase of 40 beats per minute; her rise of 44 within 10 minutes meets it.
No; the rise must occur in 3 minutes
The window for this syndrome is 10 minutes; 3 minutes is the window for orthostatic pressure criteria.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
D.q: From what age is age itself a coronary risk factor in women?
opts: 40 years
Forty is too early for either sex. Age is a coronary risk factor from 45 in men and 55 in women.
55 years
Correct. Age counts as a nonmodifiable coronary risk factor from 55 years in women and 45 in men; premenopausal women carry less risk than men, and the gap narrows with age.
45 years
Forty-five is the threshold for men. In women, age becomes a nonmodifiable coronary risk factor at 55 years.
65 years
Sixty-five is later than the threshold. Age counts as a risk factor from 55 years in women.

D.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
D.q: A 67-year-old woman with heart failure has cool, clammy extremities, a narrow pulse pressure and sleepiness, along with orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and leg edema. Which bedside hemodynamic profile fits?
opts: Cold and wet
Correct. Low-perfusion signs (cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure, obtundation) plus congestion signs (orthopnea, edema) place her in the cold and wet profile, hypoperfusion with congestion.
Cold and dry
Cold and dry is low perfusion without congestion. Her orthopnea and edema mean she is congested, so she is cold and wet.
Warm and dry
Warm and dry is the normal profile. She has both low perfusion and congestion, so she is cold and wet.
Warm and wet
Warm and wet is congestion with adequate perfusion. Her cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure and sleepiness mean perfusion is low, so she is cold and wet.

D.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
D.q: A 61-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction asks why his clinician raises one medicine at a time rather than starting everything at full strength. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Only one drug can be taken at once
Reduced ejection fraction uses several classes together. They are increased step by step as blood pressure and tolerance allow.
Medicines stop once symptoms go
Therapy aims to improve survival and slow progression as well as symptoms, so it continues. It is optimized as tolerated.
Therapy is optimized as tolerated
Correct. Guideline-directed therapy is prioritized for his comorbidities and optimized as hemodynamically stable, so each class is increased as blood pressure and tolerance allow.
Full doses are unsafe in any patient
The point is not a universal ban on full doses. Therapy is optimized as hemodynamically stable, increasing each class as tolerated.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 70-year-old man with orthostatic hypotension keeps standing up quickly despite being told not to, because he does not see why it matters. Which approach most improves his adherence?
opts: Repeat the same instruction
Repeating an instruction without the reason rarely changes behavior; understanding is what drives compliance.
Explain why the pressure falls
Correct. Understanding is the key to compliance: once a patient knows why the pressure falls on standing, slow position changes make sense and are followed.
Add a vasopressor at home
Vasopressors are for the emergency department and intensive care only and do not address adherence.
Stop discussing it with him
Dropping education abandons the most important tool; patient education is central to managing hypotension.

D.io: Angina pectoris
D.q: A 55-year-old man who received a heart transplant has exertional shortness of breath and fatigue but no chest pain. His daughter asks how he could have heart disease without pain. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Transplanted hearts can have silent ischemia

Correct. A transplanted heart is one of the settings for silent ischemia, along with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy: chest discomfort may be absent, and shortness of breath or fatigue may be the only signs.
His shortness of breath rules out the heart
Shortness of breath is one of the presenting symptoms of silent ischemia, alongside cough, nausea, diaphoresis, dizziness and fatigue. It points toward the heart, not away.
Transplanted hearts cannot become ischemic
A transplanted heart can become ischemic; it simply may not signal pain. A transplanted heart is listed among the causes of silent ischemia.
Chest pain appears only with a full infarct
Angina is chest discomfort from transient ischemia short of infarction, so pain does not wait for an infarct. In a transplanted heart the ischemia may be silent.

D.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
D.q: A 70-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 22%) is breathless even at rest. He does not yet take a renin-angiotensin drug. Which renin-angiotensin option fits his symptom class?
opts: An angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
The neprilysin combination is recommended for class II to III. At rest he is class IV, which the converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker covers.
No renin-angiotensin drug once class IV
Class IV does not remove renin-angiotensin therapy; the converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker is recommended through class IV.
A calcium channel blocker such as verapamil
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. In functional class IV the renin-angiotensin option is a converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker.
A converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker

Correct. Symptoms at rest are class IV. An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker covers class II to IV, while the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is recommended for class II to III.

D.q: A 44-year-old man with episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and pallor has raised plasma free metanephrines and an adrenal mass. He is scheduled for resection. What must be established before surgery?
opts: Neither, provided the tumor is resected promptly
Blockade is required before resection to prevent catecholamine surge during manipulation.
Alpha blockade first, then beta blockade
Correct, and the order is not negotiable: isolated beta blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
Either order, provided both are established before surgery
The sequence itself matters, which is why alpha blockade is specified first and beta blockade only afterwards.
Beta blockade first, then alpha blockade
This reversal is the dangerous one. Beta blockade without prior alpha blockade leaves vasoconstriction unopposed.

D.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
D.q: When should pulmonic regurgitation be referred?
opts: Only after a first episode of syncope
Syncope is not the trigger. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when seen on an echocardiogram or with right heart failure symptoms or signs.
On echo or with right heart failure
Correct. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when it is seen on an echocardiogram or when there are symptoms and signs of right heart failure.
Only when the cause is iatrogenic
The cause does not decide referral. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when seen on an echocardiogram or with right heart failure.
Never, since it is always benign
Significant pulmonic regurgitation overloads the right ventricle and causes right heart failure. It is referred when seen on echo or with those signs.

D.io: Mitral stenosis
D.q: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis is in sinus rhythm. Which electrocardiogram finding is most expected?
opts: Left atrial abnormality

Correct. Mitral stenosis raises left atrial size and pressure, so the electrocardiogram shows left atrial abnormality. Atrial fibrillation is common in severe disease, and right ventricular hypertrophy appears with pulmonary hypertension.
Right atrial enlargement only
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy is the tricuspid stenosis pattern. Mitral stenosis shows left atrial abnormality.
Right axis deviation alone
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy is the electrocardiogram of pulmonic stenosis. Mitral stenosis shows left atrial abnormality first.
An expected normal tracing
Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium, and the electrocardiogram reflects that as left atrial abnormality. A normal tracing is not what is expected.

D.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation is on metoprolol. A colleague suggests adding verapamil for rate control and blood pressure. What is the concern?
opts: Rebound hypertension on withdrawal
Rebound on abrupt withdrawal is a limitation of the central alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine.
Severe bradycardia and heart block
Correct. Both agents slow the sinus and atrioventricular nodes, so combining them stacks the same effect. Both are also avoided where the ejection fraction is already reduced.
Hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury
Hyperkalemia and kidney injury follow dual renin-angiotensin blockade rather than this combination.
Dependent ankle edema
Ankle edema is the commonest effect of the DIHYDROPYRIDINE calcium channel blockers rather than a hazard of this pairing.

D.io: Non-ST segment elevation
D.q: A 68-year-old woman has an hour of substernal pressure. Her electrocardiogram shows ST-segment depression of 2 mm in V5 and V6 without ST elevation, and her standard troponin I is 0.62 ng/mL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Infarction without ST elevation

Correct. ST-segment depression above 1 mm and/or T-wave inversion in two or more consecutive leads, with symptoms and an elevated troponin I (standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL), is a non-ST-elevation infarction.
Unstable angina
Unstable angina has the same kind of electrocardiogram changes but a troponin I that is not abnormal. Her troponin I of 0.62 ng/mL is elevated, which makes it an infarction.
Vasospastic angina
Vasospastic angina causes transient ST changes during an episode of rest pain that resolve, with normal coronaries at angiography. It does not explain an hour of pain with an elevated troponin I.
Infarction with ST elevation
An ST-elevation infarction needs ST elevation above 1 mm in two or more leads. Her tracing shows ST depression with no elevation, so the infarct is non-ST-elevation.

D.q: With low-density lipoprotein of 190 mg/dL or more, which step is unnecessary before starting a statin?
opts: Reviewing the full lipid profile
The labs are always reviewed carefully before a statin, since patients with the same total cholesterol can have very different profiles.
Ruling out hypothyroidism
Ruling out hypothyroidism is required whenever low-density lipoprotein is elevated, because low thyroid hormone down-regulates hepatic receptors.
Ruling out nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome raises very-low-density production and low-density lipoprotein, so it is excluded before a statin for elevated low-density lipoprotein.
Calculating 10-year risk
Correct. At 190 mg/dL or more a high-intensity statin is begun without calculating 10-year risk; the value itself defines severe primary hypercholesterolemia.

D.io: Tricuspid stenosis
D.q: A 47-year-old woman with tricuspid stenosis has right upper quadrant pain. Examination finds a tender, enlarged liver. Which explains her pain?
opts: Congestion of an enlarged liver

Correct. Obstructed inflow from the right atrium to the right ventricle backs blood into the venous system, causing portal congestion; right upper quadrant pain in severe tricuspid stenosis comes from the enlarged liver.
A dilated aortic root
A dilated aortic root causes aortic regurgitation and does not produce liver pain. Tricuspid stenosis congests the liver.
Gallstones from carcinoid
Carcinoid disease is a cause of tricuspid stenosis, not of gallstones. Her pain comes from portal congestion and an enlarged liver.
Low cardiac output to the gut
Low cardiac output in tricuspid stenosis explains the cold skin. The right upper quadrant pain is the enlarged, congested liver.

D.q: A healthy 22-year-old man establishes care. He has never had cholesterol tested and has no symptoms or family history of heart disease. What is the most appropriate step regarding lipids?
opts: Coronary calcium score first
Calcium scoring settles uncertain statin decisions at 40 to 75; it is not a screening test for a 22-year-old.
No testing until he turns 40
Age 40 opens the 10-year risk pathway, but cholesterol screening is recommended from age 20.
Test only if xanthomas appear
Most patients have no signs or symptoms, so waiting for xanthomas would miss them.
Screen for high blood cholesterol
Correct. Screening of all adults aged 20 years or older for high blood cholesterol is recommended, whatever their symptoms; most dyslipidemia is found on laboratory testing.

D.io: Mitral valve prolapse
D.q: Which auscultatory finding is typical of mitral valve prolapse?
opts: A blowing diastolic murmur to the apex
A blowing diastolic murmur radiating to the apex is aortic regurgitation. Mitral valve prolapse is a mid-systolic click at the apex.
A diastolic rumble near the xiphoid
A mid-diastolic rumble near the xiphoid is tricuspid stenosis. Mitral valve prolapse gives a mid-systolic click at the apex.
An opening snap after the second sound
An opening snap after the second heart sound introduces the diastolic rumble of mitral stenosis. Prolapse gives a mid-systolic click.
A mid-systolic click at the apex
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse gives a mid-systolic click at the apex. It is usually benign and asymptomatic, but it may develop the symptoms and signs of mitral regurgitation.

D.q: A 49-year-old man with hypertriglyceridemia has a total cholesterol of 250 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein of 40 mg/dL and triglyceride of 300 mg/dL. What is his non-high-density cholesterol?
opts: 290 mg/dL
Adding high-density cholesterol to the total gives 290, but the formula subtracts it: 250 minus 40.
50 mg/dL
Subtracting triglyceride from total cholesterol gives an unrelated number; the formula is total minus high-density cholesterol.
190 mg/dL
The formula does not involve triglyceride; subtracting the high-density value of 40 from 250 gives 210.
210 mg/dL
Correct. Non-high-density cholesterol is total cholesterol minus high-density cholesterol: 250 minus 40 is 210 mg/dL.

D.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
D.q: A 64-year-old man with a myocardial infarction three years ago has breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). Blood pressure is 104/68. There is a third heart sound (an extra sound in early diastole just after the second heart sound) and bibasilar crackles. B-type natriuretic peptide is 820. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Isolated right-sided failure from the lungs
Right-sided failure shows peripheral edema, distended neck veins and portal overload. Crackles, orthopnea and a third sound point to left-sided systolic failure.
Diastolic failure from hypertrophic disease
The diastolic chain runs with hypertension, a fourth heart sound and edema that starts peripherally. His low pressure, third sound and prior infarction point to systolic failure.
Systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy

Correct. Every link of the systolic chain is here: ischemic cardiomyopathy after infarction, a low-normal blood pressure, a third heart sound from rapid filling of a dilated ventricle, and pulmonary edema, confirmed by an elevated natriuretic peptide.
High-output failure from increased demand
High-output failure comes from anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula, with no infarction behind it. This is systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy.

D.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
D.q: A 76-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction heart failure has run low pressures for a year and asks whether his low pressure will simply go away. What is the most accurate answer?
opts: It needs a vasopressor at home
Vasopressors are for the emergency department and intensive care only, not home management of chronic hypotension.
It will end once a trigger is found
Removing a trigger fits acute or reflex hypotension; chronic cardiogenic hypotension may have an unavoidable cause.
Its cause may not be removable
Correct. Chronic hypotension waxes and wanes, and its underlying cause, here heart failure, may be unavoidable, unlike an acute trigger that can be removed.
It always resolves within weeks
Chronic hypotension persists and waxes and wanes rather than resolving within weeks.

D.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
D.q: A 44-year-old newly diagnosed hypertensive patient asks why treatment matters if she feels well. What is the strongest answer?
opts: She will begin to feel symptoms within a few months if untreated
Most patients with mild to moderate hypertension have no reliable symptoms at any point.
It causes cumulative organ damage with no reliable symptoms
Correct. The heart, brain, kidneys, aorta, arteries and retina are all injured over years, and most patients have no reliable blood pressure-related symptoms to warn them.
Treatment is optional until organ damage is demonstrated
Waiting for demonstrable damage forfeits the period in which it could have been prevented.
Feeling well means her risk is already low
How a patient feels is not a guide to the pressure or to the damage it is doing.

D.q: A 62-year-old man on chlorthalidone presents with an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. What connects this to his medication?
opts: Thiazide-induced angioedema
Angioedema is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor class effect mediated by bradykinin rather than a thiazide effect.
Thiazide-induced hyperkalemia
Thiazides cause hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia, and neither precipitates gout.
Thiazide-induced ankle edema
Dependent ankle edema is a dihydropyridine effect and would not present as an acutely inflamed single joint.
Hyperuricemia may precipitate gout
Correct, which is why uric acid is monitored alongside electrolytes and volume status in patients on a thiazide-type diuretic.

D.io: ST segment elevation
D.q: A 57-year-old woman has chest pain with ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which artery is the most likely culprit?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery is the culprit for the inferior leads II, III and aVF. Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 are lateral, pointing to the circumflex.
Left circumflex artery
Correct. Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, and lateral ST elevation points to the left circumflex artery (or a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery).
Posterior interventricular
The posterior interventricular branch supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle and the inferior wall. Lateral leads point to the left circumflex artery.
Right marginal branch
The right marginal branch arises from the right coronary artery along the right ventricle. Lateral ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 points to the circumflex.

D.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
D.q: A 74-year-old man with a prior heart attack and reduced ejection fraction collapsed abruptly while walking, with no warning except a brief racing heartbeat. He is pale, his pressure is 86/52 and his heart rate is 150 and regular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension follows standing, often with volume loss; he collapsed abruptly mid-walk after palpitations.
Cardiogenic syncope from an arrhythmia

Correct. Abrupt collapse with minimal prodrome after palpitations, in a patient with coronary disease and reduced ejection fraction, with a rapid regular rhythm, points to an arrhythmic cardiac cause.
Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope follows a bodily function such as urination, with a reflex prodrome and quick recovery.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear or heat with a warm, nauseated prodrome and a slow rather than fast heart rate.

D.io: Acute myocardial infraction
D.q: A 64-year-old man with an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction suddenly develops complete heart block on the monitor. Which artery is most likely occluded?
opts: Anterior interventricular artery
The anterior interventricular artery (the former left anterior descending) is the most common culprit overall, but it supplies the anterior wall and septum, not the atrioventricular node.
Diagonal artery
The diagonal artery is a lateral branch that helps supply the left ventricle. Complete heart block during an infarct points to the right coronary artery, which supplies the atrioventricular node.
Right coronary artery

Correct. The right coronary artery supplies the atrioventricular node, so an occlusion that produces complete heart block points to it. That is why right coronary artery infarcts are the ones most likely to cause dysrhythmias.
Left circumflex artery

The left circumflex artery can supply the sinoatrial node in a minority of people, but the atrioventricular node is supplied by the right coronary artery, so heart block implicates the right coronary artery.

D.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
D.io: ST segment elevation
D.q: A 66-year-old woman has an ST-elevation myocardial infarction at a hospital three hours from any intervention unit. She had a hemorrhagic stroke five months ago. Which therapy is absolutely contraindicated?
opts: Transfer for intervention
Transfer for percutaneous intervention is the reperfusion route when thrombolytics cannot be used. It is thrombolytic therapy that her stroke rules out.
Chewable aspirin
Chewable aspirin is the first medication in every ST-elevation infarction. The absolute contraindication after a recent hemorrhagic stroke is thrombolytic therapy.
Thrombolytic therapy

Correct. A hemorrhagic stroke in the previous year is an absolute contraindication to thrombolytics, as are active bleeding, pregnancy, major surgery or trauma within four weeks and uncontrolled hypertension above 190/100.
A beta blocker
A beta blocker is given in an ST-elevation infarction if there is no bradycardia. Her prior hemorrhagic stroke rules out thrombolytic therapy, not a beta blocker.

D.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
D.q: A 55-year-old South Asian man without diabetes has low-density lipoprotein of 150 mg/dL and a calculated 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 12%. His father had a heart attack at 50. After discussion he favors treatment. What is the most appropriate therapy?
opts: Moderate-intensity statin

Correct. At intermediate risk with risk enhancers (South Asian ancestry, premature family history) and a discussion that favors therapy, start a moderate-intensity statin to lower low-density lipoprotein by 30% or more.
A fibrate for his cholesterol
Fibrates are the triglyceride drugs; low-density lipoprotein is lowered most by statins.
High-intensity statin with ezetimibe
Combination therapy is for very high-risk disease or severe hypercholesterolemia that stays elevated; this is intermediate-risk primary prevention.
Lifestyle alone without any drug
Lifestyle continues, but risk enhancers at intermediate risk favor starting a statin.

D.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
D.q: Which setting is typical of micturition syncope?
opts: Exertion while climbing stairs
Syncope during exertion raises concern for a cardiogenic cause, which needs electrocardiography, echocardiography and cardiology input.
Voiding while standing at night
Correct. Nocturnal urination after abruptly standing from bed, voiding in the standing position, triggers an exaggerated autonomic reflex with vagal activity and reduced vascular tone.
Shock at hearing bad news
Emotional stress and fear are triggers of vasovagal syncope, the common faint, rather than the situational micturition type.
Diarrhea for several days
Several days of diarrhea cause volume depletion and non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, with a significant heart rate rise on standing.

D.q: A 32-year-old man has a white-gray ring around the edge of each cornea (corneal arcus). His low-density lipoprotein is 250 mg/dL with a normal triglyceride, and his father died of a heart attack at 52. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The homozygous form presents in childhood with xanthomas and total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000; an adult with low-density lipoprotein of 250 fits one mutant allele.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together with palmar xanthomas; his triglyceride is normal.
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia

Correct. Corneal arcus before 40 usually indicates a genetic condition, and low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 with normal triglyceride and premature family coronary disease fits the heterozygous form, in which arcus is common.
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Chylomicronemia raises triglyceride above 1000 with eruptive papules and lipemia retinalis; his triglyceride is normal.

D.q: A 46-year-old woman consistently reads 150/92 in clinic but her seven-day home average is 118/74 with a validated upper-arm device and correct technique. Which pattern does this represent?
opts: Resistant hypertension
Resistance means pressure above goal despite three complementary drugs at maximally tolerated doses, which is not the situation here.
Stage 2 hypertension
Her out-of-office readings are normal, so the office values do not establish a stage.
White coat hypertension
Correct: raised office readings with normal out-of-office readings. Recognizing it avoids treating a patient whose true pressure is normal.
Masked hypertension
Masked hypertension is the reverse pattern, with normal office readings and raised out-of-office readings, and it carries clinically important cardiovascular risk.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: A 60-year-old man is newly diagnosed with heart failure and will start a loop diuretic. Which laboratory panel should be checked before starting?
opts: Hepatic function panel
Liver tests are not what the diuretic calls for. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.
Coagulation panel
Clotting tests are not the pre-diuretic check. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.
Complete metabolic panel
Correct. The metabolic panel gives potassium and renal function (blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and filtration rate), both of which a potassium-wasting loop diuretic affects.
Thyroid function panel
Thyroid testing is not the pre-diuretic check. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.

D.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
D.q: A 60-year-old woman with two prior heart attacks, diabetes and hypertension takes a maximal statin. Her low-density lipoprotein is 95 mg/dL, and she takes no other lipid drug. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Add evolocumab
Evolocumab is considered only after ezetimibe has been added to the maximal statin, and it is less cost-effective.
Add ezetimibe
Correct. In very high-risk disease, when low-density lipoprotein stays 70 or more on a maximally tolerated statin, adding ezetimibe is reasonable, and it comes before any injectable.
Stop the statin
Stopping her statin would remove the backbone of secondary prevention; the next step adds to it.
Add niacin
Niacin raises high-density lipoprotein best, but the add-on for persistent low-density lipoprotein on a maximal statin is ezetimibe.

D.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
D.q: A 60-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve on warfarin is scheduled for a colectomy that requires stopping it. Which plan should be avoided?
opts: Stopping warfarin with no bridge

Correct. If surgery requires interrupting warfarin, it must be bridged with heparin until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic; leaving a mechanical valve uncovered is the thing to avoid.
Bridging with heparin
Heparin bridging is exactly what is required when surgery interrupts warfarin in a patient with a mechanical valve. The plan to avoid is stopping warfarin with no cover.
Resuming a vitamin K antagonist
A mechanical valve needs lifelong vitamin K antagonist therapy, so resuming warfarin after surgery is required. The error is stopping it without a heparin bridge.
Rechecking his ratio after surgery
Warfarin is bridged until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic again, so rechecking it is part of the plan. What must be avoided is an unbridged gap.

D.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
D.io: Acute myocardial infraction
D.q: A 63-year-old woman recovering from a myocardial infarction cannot take a beta blocker. Her echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular function. Which agent can reduce her mortality?
opts: Warfarin
Warfarin is recommended after a large anterior wall infarction to prevent clot. With preserved function and an intolerance to beta blockers, diltiazem is the agent that lowers mortality.
Diltiazem
Correct. Calcium channel blockers do not improve prognosis overall after infarction, but diltiazem and verapamil reduce mortality in patients with preserved left ventricular function, which she has.
Amlodipine

Amlodipine is a first-line calcium channel blocker for vasospastic angina. After infarction, only diltiazem and verapamil are credited with lowering mortality, and only with preserved left ventricular function.
Nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin is the cornerstone of angina relief but carries no survival benefit claim. With preserved left ventricular function, diltiazem or verapamil reduces mortality after infarction.

D.q: A 78-year-old woman with a prior ischemic stroke has taken a high-intensity statin for years without problems. She asks whether she should stop it now that she is over 75. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Switch to a fibrate instead
A fibrate lowers triglyceride and would not replace the statin's benefit after stroke.
Only lifestyle is advised now
Lifestyle remains important, but continuing the statin is reasonable in her secondary prevention.
Continuing it is reasonable
Correct. Above 75 with clinical atherosclerotic disease, continuing a high-intensity statin is reasonable, as is starting a moderate- or high-intensity statin.
Statins are stopped at 75
Age alone does not end therapy; continuing a well-tolerated high-intensity statin after 75 is reasonable.

D.q: How are most patients with dyslipidemia identified?
opts: From chest pain that prompts testing
Most patients are asymptomatic; premature coronary disease is a presentation of genetic dyslipidemia rather than the usual route to diagnosis.
From attacks of acute pancreatitis
Pancreatitis occurs with severe hypertriglyceridemia but is not how the majority of patients come to attention.
From abnormal lipid laboratory values
Correct. Most patients have no specific signs or symptoms, and the majority are identified after lipid abnormalities are detected in laboratory values.
From xanthomas found on the skin
Xanthomas occur, but they usually indicate an underlying genetic condition and are not how most patients are found.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: Which drug class is recommended to prevent heart failure in patients with diabetes who have no structural heart disease?
opts: Beta blocker started at diagnosis
A beta blocker is not part of stage A prevention; it is a stage B therapy once structural disease appears. Prevention in diabetes uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
This pairing is reserved for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV. Stage A prevention uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. Prevention in stage A, risk factors with a normal heart, carries one strong drug recommendation: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for patients with diabetes, ahead of any beta blocker, which is a stage B therapy.
Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
This combination belongs to symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in functional class II or III. Stage A prevention in diabetes uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

D.io: Mitral regurgitation
D.q: A 62-year-old woman has a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. She stands up quickly from squatting while the examiner listens. How does the murmur change?
opts: It becomes softer
Correct. The mitral regurgitation murmur decreases with standing or the Valsalva maneuver and increases with squatting and handgrip, which raise resistance to ventricular ejection.
It gains a click
A mid-systolic click is the sign of mitral valve prolapse, not a response to a maneuver. Standing makes the mitral regurgitation murmur softer.
It becomes louder
Louder is the response to squatting or handgrip, which raise resistance to ejection. Standing reduces the mitral regurgitation murmur.
It does not change
Standing does change it: the mitral regurgitation murmur decreases with standing or the Valsalva maneuver.

D.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
D.q: What is the commonest cause to exclude before labeling hypertension as resistant?
opts: Medication nonadherence
Correct, and it heads a list that also includes measurement error, white coat effect, high sodium or alcohol intake, interfering drugs, and undiagnosed sleep apnea or secondary hypertension.
Excess alcohol intake
High sodium or alcohol intake appears on the list, but nonadherence is the commonest single explanation.
Incorrect cuff size
Measurement error is on the list to exclude, but nonadherence is specifically named as the commonest cause.
Undiagnosed primary aldosteronism
Secondary hypertension is among the things to rule out, but nonadherence is identified as the commonest cause of apparent resistance.

D.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
D.q: A 69-year-old woman has sudden severe breathlessness, crackles and edema. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 1,150. How should this level be read?
opts: The result is indeterminate
The indeterminate range is 100 to 400. A level of 1,150 makes acute heart failure likely.
Only chronic heart failure fits
Levels above 900 point to acute heart failure, and her sudden onset fits. The result makes acute failure likely.
Acute heart failure is ruled out
Rule-out applies only below 100. A level of 1,150 is far above that and makes acute heart failure likely.
Acute heart failure is likely
Correct. Above 900 acute heart failure is likely. Above 400 heart failure is likely in general, 100 to 400 is indeterminate, and below 100 rules acute failure out.

D.io: Aortic stenosis
D.q: A 68-year-old woman with aortic stenosis on echocardiogram plays competitive tennis and often skips fluids on hot days. She asks what she should change. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Restrict fluids to keep her volume low
Restricting fluids moves her toward hypovolemia, which is exactly what aortic stenosis patients must avoid. She needs to stay hydrated because she depends on preload.
Increase training to strengthen her heart
More strenuous exercise is the opposite of the advice. Strenuous physical activity and competitive sports are to be avoided in aortic stenosis, along with dehydration.
No changes until symptoms appear
Precautions start once the stenosis is known, not when symptoms arrive. She should stop competitive sports and avoid dehydration now, because she is preload dependent.
Avoid competitive sports and dehydration

Correct. Aortic stenosis makes the patient preload dependent, so she should avoid strenuous physical activity and competitive sports and avoid dehydration and hypovolemia, both of which reduce the preload she relies on.

D.q: A 12-year-old boy with confirmed homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia has total cholesterol of 610 mg/dL on a high-intensity statin with ezetimibe. What is the treatment of choice for his disorder?
opts: Low-density lipoprotein apheresis

Correct. Apheresis is the treatment of choice, like dialysis: the elective removal of low-density particles from the circulation. Most patients also need several drugs, starting with high-intensity statins.
Add a fibrate for his triglyceride
Triglyceride is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia, so a fibrate targets the wrong lipid.
Switch to a moderate-intensity statin
Lowering statin intensity moves in the wrong direction; high-intensity statins are the usual regimen alongside apheresis.
Very low-fat diet alone for a year
A very low-fat diet is advised for triglyceride above 500 mg/dL; diet alone cannot correct a receptor defect.

D.io: Aortic regurgitation
D.q: A 47-year-old man has a Corrigan pulse (a very rapid upstroke followed by rapid collapse) and a de Musset sign (head bobbing with each heartbeat). Which valve lesion is most likely?
opts: Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis gives a delayed, weakened carotid pulse, the opposite of a rapid upstroke with collapse. The Corrigan pulse and head bobbing point to aortic regurgitation.
Aortic regurgitation

Correct. The Corrigan pulse, also called a water hammer or collapsing pulse, and the de Musset sign are findings of chronic aortic regurgitation, along with a diastolic blowing murmur and a displaced point of maximal impulse.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla. The collapsing pulse and head bobbing are signs of aortic regurgitation.
Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis causes neck vein distension and low-output symptoms, not a collapsing arterial pulse. These peripheral signs belong to aortic regurgitation.

D.q: How does hypertension prevalence change with age?
opts: It rises sharply
Correct, which is why advancing age sits among the major risk factors and why a young patient with hypertension raises more suspicion of a secondary cause than an older one does.
It falls after middle age
Prevalence continues to climb into older age rather than declining, which is why advancing age is itself a listed risk factor.
It peaks in early adulthood
Early adult hypertension is uncommon enough that it is one of the clues prompting a search for a secondary cause.
It remains flat across adult life
Prevalence rises steeply with age rather than holding constant, which is part of why age is itself a risk factor.

D.q: A 58-year-old man is found to have a raised creatinine. What is required before chronic kidney disease can be diagnosed?
opts: Albuminuria alone, regardless of duration
Albuminuria is one marker of kidney damage, but the three-month persistence requirement still applies.
Structural renal disease demonstrated on imaging
Imaging may support a cause, but the definition turns on a persisting abnormality rather than a structural finding.
A kidney abnormality persisting three months
Correct. A single raised value may reflect a reversible insult, so duration is part of the definition rather than an optional confirmation.
A single raised creatinine measurement
One measurement does not establish chronicity, which is what the three-month requirement tests.
