D.q: A 43-year-old man has a fasting triglyceride of 620 mg/dL. He drinks heavily most nights. Before any drug is started, which additional conditions should be evaluated?
opts: Diabetes, kidney disease, hypothyroidism
Correct. With triglyceride of 500 or more rule out diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, alcoholism, pregnancy and hypothyroidism; his alcohol history is important too.
Anorexia nervosa and biliary cirrhosis
Anorexia nervosa and primary biliary cirrhosis are rule-outs for elevated low-density lipoprotein, not very high triglyceride.
Lipoprotein(a) and coronary calcium
These are risk-enhancing tools for primary prevention, not the secondary causes of very high triglyceride.
Tendon xanthomas and corneal arcus
These are physical signs of high-cholesterol genetic states, not secondary causes to exclude for high triglyceride.

D.q: A 68-year-old man hospitalized with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction asks why a defibrillator is being discussed. Which cause accounts for about half of cardiac arrests in hospitalized patients like him?
opts: Acute pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is not the leading cause of these arrests. About half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.
Complete heart block
Complete heart block is not the leading cause of these arrests. About half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.
Low potassium alone
Electrolytes matter on diuretics, but about half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.
Ventricular arrhythmias

Correct. About 52% of cardiac arrests in hospitalized patients with reduced ejection fraction are due to ventricular arrhythmias, which is the reason for defibrillator protection in those who meet the criteria.

D.q: A 46-year-old woman with high-output heart failure from untreated hyperthyroidism has leg edema and breathlessness. Which treatment approach is most appropriate?
opts: Start verapamil to slow the heart rate
Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, avoided in heart failure. The approach is to treat the cause and add a diuretic.
Treat the thyroid disease and add a diuretic
Correct. High-output failure is treated by correcting the underlying cause of increased demand, here hyperthyroidism, with a diuretic for congestion.
Refer for heart transplant evaluation
Transplant does not address a problem of excess demand. The approach is to treat the thyroid disease and add a diuretic.
Start dobutamine to support contractility
Dobutamine raises output further and is an inotrope for intensive care use only. The approach is to treat the cause and add a diuretic.

D.io: Stable
D.q: A 58-year-old man has chest pressure when he climbs two flights of stairs. It fades after three minutes of rest and has followed the same pattern for months. His resting electrocardiogram is normal. Which test is most appropriate next?
opts: Ergonovine provocation test
Ergonovine or acetylcholine given during angiography is the gold standard for vasospastic angina, which occurs at rest. His pain is brought on by exertion and relieved by rest.
Exercise treadmill stress test

Correct. Stable angina is diagnosed by stress-test-induced electrocardiogram changes, usually T-wave inversion, on an exercise (treadmill), nuclear or cardiac computed tomography stress test. Coronary angiography remains the gold standard.
Posterior-lead electrocardiogram
Posterior leads V7-V9 are recorded when ST depression in V1-V3 suggests a posterior infarct. A normal resting tracing with exertional pain calls for a stress test instead.
Serial troponin I measurements
Serial troponin I draws belong to rest pain and a suspected acute coronary syndrome. His pain is exertional, brief and unchanged, which is stable angina and calls for a stress test.

D.q: A 69-year-old man had a large blood loss after surgery 2 days ago and now feels faint on standing. His pressure falls 30 mmHg with a heart rate rise from 72 to 100. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Start midodrine for neurogenic syncope
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; his brisk heart rate rise shows an intact autonomic reflex and a volume cause.
Start fludrocortisone for fluid
Fludrocortisone is best with the tachycardia syndrome and is not a substitute for correcting the blood loss itself.
Order a tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing belongs to the tachycardia syndrome and would delay treatment of an evident volume cause.
Treat the underlying blood loss
Correct. Hemorrhage is an example cause of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and the principle is to treat the underlying condition, the real diagnosis.

D.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
D.q: A 71-year-old woman with long-standing pulmonary hypertension and a dilated right ventricle develops a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Which process most likely produced her valve leak?
opts: Endocarditis of the leaflets
Infective endocarditis is the primary cause of tricuspid regurgitation in injection drug users. With pulmonary hypertension and a dilated ventricle, annular dilation is the cause.
A prior valvuloplasty
A prior valvuloplasty for outflow obstruction is the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation. Her tricuspid leak comes from annular dilation.
Dilation of the tricuspid annulus
Correct. The most common cause of tricuspid regurgitation is dilation of the tricuspid annulus from right ventricular dilation in the setting of pulmonary hypertension.
Rheumatic leaflet narrowing
Rheumatic disease narrows valves, most commonly the mitral, causing stenosis. Her leak is from annular dilation due to right ventricular dilation.

D.q: A 39-year-old woman is referred with hypertension diagnosed at 32 and an adrenal nodule found incidentally on imaging. What is the underlying abnormality if aldosteronism is confirmed?
opts: Glucocorticoid excess promoting sodium retention
That is Cushing syndrome, which carries proximal weakness, bruising, thin skin and purple striae.
Excess renin driving aldosterone production
Renin-driven aldosterone excess is secondary rather than primary aldosteronism, and occurs in renovascular disease.
Catecholamine excess from an adrenal medullary tumor
That is pheochromocytoma, which produces the paroxysmal five Ps rather than sustained aldosterone-driven sodium retention.
Autonomous aldosterone production independent of renin
Correct. The adrenal gland secretes aldosterone without the usual renin-angiotensin signal, so sodium is retained and potassium wasted regardless of volume status.

D.q: A 54-year-old arrives late for a routine visit, is taken straight to the room and has her blood pressure measured immediately while she describes her morning. The cuff is placed over her sleeve and her legs are crossed. The reading is 152/94. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat it after five minutes of quiet rest

Correct. Every departure here inflates the reading: no rest period, talking during the measurement, a sleeved arm and crossed legs. A diagnosis rests on readings taken to standard, and acting on this one would start treatment on an artifact. Correct technique matters as much as the rest period.
Diagnose stage 2 hypertension and start two agents
Two complementary agents are reasonable when pressure is substantially above goal, but not on a single reading taken outside standard conditions.
Reassure her that a single elevated reading is meaningless
It is not meaningless; it needs repeating under proper conditions. At least two readings are obtained, with any deviation from standard technique documented.
Order plasma metanephrines to exclude pheochromocytoma
Metanephrines are ordered when the history suggests episodic headache, sweating and palpitations, not because one office reading was high.

D.q: A 71-year-old man had his diuretic dose increased 10 days ago. He now has lightheadedness on standing, a 28 mmHg systolic fall and a heart rate rise from 70 to 94. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Start fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and retains salt and water; it does not address the diuretic.
Add droxidopa as an adjunct
Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is used as an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone, not to offset a diuretic side effect.
Start midodrine for the pressure
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope. Here the cause is a medication, which is reduced rather than counteracted with another drug.
Reduce the recently increased diuretic
Correct. The offending agent is removed first: iatrogenic hypotension is treated by reducing or removing the medication, with slow position changes meanwhile.

E.q: A 3-year-old boy is brought for a routine visit. His father had a heart attack at 40 and was found to have very high cholesterol. What is the most appropriate step regarding the boy's lipids?
opts: Screen only after puberty
His father's premature heart attack and high cholesterol make screening appropriate from age 2, well before puberty.
Elective lipid screening now
Correct. Elective screening is appropriate for patients as young as 2 years old with a family history of heart disease or high cholesterol.
Wait until age 9 to 11
Routine screening is at 9 to 11, but his father's premature disease and high cholesterol justify elective screening now.
Start a statin without testing
A statin follows a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia; he has not yet been tested.

E.q: A 63-year-old man describes his chest pressure while holding a clenched fist over his sternum (Levine sign). Which condition does this gesture most suggest?
opts: Myocardial ischemia
Correct. The Levine sign, a clenched fist held over the sternum while describing the discomfort, is the classic gesture of ischemic, anginal chest pain.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection classically refers pain to the left or interscapular region of the back. A clenched fist over the sternum is the Levine sign of ischemic chest pain.
Pancreatitis
Pancreatic pain goes straight through to the back. A clenched fist over the sternum is the Levine sign, which points to ischemic chest pain.
Biliary colic
Gallbladder pain refers to the right scapular region. The Levine sign, a fist held over the sternum, suggests myocardial ischemia instead.

E.q: A 57-year-old woman with a hypertensive emergency has her pressure reduced from 240/130 to 125/75 within thirty minutes. She then develops a new hemiparesis. What happened?
opts: Hyperkalemia precipitated the event
Potassium disturbance relates to renin-angiotensin blockade rather than to the rate of pressure reduction.
She developed rebound hypertension
Rebound on abrupt withdrawal is a limitation of central alpha-2 agonists and does not explain a deficit after an over-rapid reduction.
Autoregulation had adapted to the higher pressure

Correct. Her organs had reset the range over which they protect their own perfusion, so a value that would be safe in anyone else left her brain underperfused. Reducing it that fast left her brain underperfused.
The reduction was appropriate and the deficit is unrelated
Reducing to a chronic goal within the first hour is specifically capable of causing ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.

E.q: A 45-year-old woman with a family history of heart failure smokes, drinks heavily and is obese. Her heart is structurally normal. Which counseling point best lowers her heart failure risk?
opts: Family history cannot be offset at all
Family history is fixed, but her modifiable risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, obesity) can still be changed to lower her risk.
Quit tobacco, cut alcohol, lose weight
Correct. Tobacco, excessive alcohol and obesity are modifiable risk factors for heart failure. Her family history is a risk factor she cannot change, so counseling targets the ones she can.
Start a loop diuretic as prevention
Diuretics treat congestion and do not prevent heart failure. Counseling targets tobacco, alcohol and obesity.
Wait for symptoms before changing
Waiting forfeits prevention. Tobacco, excess alcohol and obesity are modifiable now.

E.q: A 75-year-old man with heart failure diagnosed three years ago has had four days of worsening orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and leg swelling. How is this episode classified?
opts: Acute new-onset heart failure
New-onset failure is a first symptomatic episode. He has had heart failure for three years, so this is acute on chronic heart failure.
Pre-heart failure, stage B
Pre-heart failure is asymptomatic structural disease. He is symptomatic with known chronic disease: acute on chronic heart failure.
Acute on chronic heart failure

Correct. Heart failure present for more than a year is chronic, and a sudden worsening on top of it is acute on chronic heart failure, the last step of the sequence from pre-heart failure through exacerbation.
High-output heart failure
Nothing suggests anemia, hyperthyroidism or a fistula. This is a sudden worsening of chronic disease, acute on chronic heart failure.

E.q: Which finding best separates non-neurogenic from neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: Whether symptoms occur on standing
Both forms produce lightheadedness and syncope on standing. The discriminating finding is how the heart rate behaves as pressure falls.
The age at the first episode
Age does not separate them. Advanced age is a non-neurogenic cause, but older patients also carry diabetes and Parkinson disease.
The heart rate response on standing
Correct. Pressure falls in both, but the heart rate rises significantly when the autonomic system is intact (non-neurogenic) and only minimally when it has failed (neurogenic).
The size of the systolic pressure fall
Both forms meet the same pressure criteria on standing, so the size of the fall does not tell them apart; the heart rate response does.

E.io: Aortic regurgitation
E.q: A 34-year-old man with Marfan syndrome has a high-pitched blowing diastolic murmur at the third intercostal space at the left upper sternal border that radiates to the apex. He has bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is blowing but holosystolic, at the apex, radiating to the axilla. This murmur is diastolic, which points to the aortic valve.
Aortic regurgitation

Correct. Blowing means regurgitation and diastolic narrows it to the aortic or pulmonic valve; the third intercostal space with radiation to the apex, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure mark aortic regurgitation. Marfan syndrome is a root-disease cause.
Pulmonic regurgitation
Pulmonic regurgitation is a brief early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space that radiates toward the right sternal border. It does not produce bounding pulses.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is diastolic too, but it is a low-pitched rumble at the apex that starts with an opening snap. Rumble means stenosis; this murmur is blowing.

E.io: Acute myocardial infraction
E.q: A 61-year-old man with an acute myocardial infarction is taken for coronary angiography. Which vessel is most often the culprit in this setting?
opts: Anterior interventricular artery

Correct. Occlusion of the anterior interventricular artery, formerly called the left anterior descending artery, is the most common cause of acute myocardial infarction (about 40–50%), followed by the right coronary artery and then the left circumflex.
Posterior interventricular branch
The posterior interventricular branch is a branch vessel, usually arising from the right coronary artery. It is not a leading culprit; the anterior interventricular artery is the most common.
Left circumflex artery
The left circumflex artery is the least common of the three main culprits, at about 15–20%. The anterior interventricular artery is the most common cause of acute myocardial infarction.
Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery is the second most common culprit, at about 30–40% of acute infarcts. The anterior interventricular artery comes first, at about 40–50%.

E.q: A 52-year-old woman has a triglyceride of 350 mg/dL. Her clinician wants the lipid measure that best reflects her heart-disease risk. Which measure should be used?
opts: Total cholesterol only
Total cholesterol includes the protective high-density fraction, so it is not the preferred measure here.
Non-high-density cholesterol
Correct. In hypertriglyceridemia, non-high-density cholesterol (all cholesterol except the high-density fraction) gives a better assessment of heart-disease risk than low-density lipoprotein alone.
High-density cholesterol only
High-density lipoprotein is one input, but on its own it misses the cholesterol carried by the atherogenic particles.
Triglyceride alone
Triglyceride is monitored, but the better heart-disease risk measure in this setting is non-high-density cholesterol.

E.q: A 50-year-old man says he can tell when his blood pressure is high because he gets a headache. How should this be addressed?
opts: Absence of headache confirms his pressure is controlled
Most patients with mild to moderate hypertension have no reliable symptoms at all.
Any headache requires emergency evaluation
It is the ABRUPT SEVERE headache that warrants immediate evaluation, not any headache.
Headache is a reliable indicator and can guide his dosing
Headache is common but nonspecific, and specifically described as an unreliable guide to the pressure.
Most patients have no reliable blood pressure-related symptoms
Correct. Headache is common but nonspecific and cannot be relied on to indicate the pressure, which is why the diagnosis and its control rest on measurement rather than on how he feels.

E.io: Aortic stenosis
E.q: An 80-year-old man has exertional syncope. Echocardiogram shows an aortic valve area of 0.7 cm2, a mean gradient of 52 mmHg, a jet velocity of 4.6 m/s and symptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement

Correct. Surgery is indicated for severe aortic stenosis (below 1, above 40, above 4) with symptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Medical treatment is not effective and is for mild and moderate disease only.
Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty
Percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty is the option for children and young adults. An 80-year-old with severe symptomatic disease is treated with valve replacement.
Nitrates and a beta blocker
Medical therapy is not effective in aortic stenosis, and nitrates and beta blockers are on its avoid list because he is preload dependent. Severe symptomatic disease needs valve replacement.
Repeat echocardiogram in one year
Watching is not appropriate once aortic stenosis is severe and symptomatic; the prognosis worsens sharply after symptoms begin. He meets the indications for valve replacement.

E.q: A 61-year-old man's blood pressure is 148/88 in the right arm and 132/80 in the left at his first visit. He has no chest pain and his pulses are symmetric and normal. Which arm should be used at follow-up visits?
opts: Compare arm and leg pressures to exclude coarctation
Coarctation is suggested by weak or delayed femoral pulses with upper limb hypertension, not by a difference between the two arms.
Average the two readings and record 140/84
The higher consistent arm is used rather than an average, since the lower arm underestimates the central pressure.
Use the right arm for all subsequent measurements

Correct. Both arms are measured at the initial visit precisely to find a difference, and the higher consistent arm becomes the one used for follow-up. Averaging the two would systematically understate his pressure.
Image immediately for aortic dissection
Asymmetric pressures raise concern for dissection when they are NEW and accompanied by abrupt severe pain. Neither is present here.

E.q: A 46-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has low-density lipoprotein of 130 mg/dL. She has no atherosclerotic disease and no other risk factors. What is the most appropriate lipid therapy?
opts: Fibrate monotherapy
Fibrates are the triglyceride drugs; her target is low-density lipoprotein, which a statin lowers most.
Moderate-intensity statin
Correct. Adults 40 to 75 with diabetes and low-density lipoprotein of 70 or more start a moderate-intensity statin without calculating 10-year risk.
Ezetimibe as monotherapy
Ezetimibe is an adjunct added to a statin; it is not the initial therapy for the diabetes statin-benefit group.
Lifestyle changes alone
Lifestyle is the foundation, but diabetes at this age with low-density lipoprotein of 70 or more is itself a statin indication.

E.q: A 62-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 28%). She is breathless with ordinary exertion but comfortable at rest, and takes no renin-angiotensin drug. Which agent fits her symptom class?
opts: Metolazone alone
Metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic used as needed for congestion, not renin-angiotensin therapy. Her class fits sacubitril-valsartan.
Sacubitril-valsartan
Correct. Symptoms with exertion are New York Heart Association class II, and the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is recommended for class II to III in reduced ejection fraction.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, which is avoided in heart failure. Her class II reduced ejection fraction fits sacubitril-valsartan.
Dobutamine
Dobutamine is an inotrope for intensive care use only. Her class II reduced ejection fraction fits sacubitril-valsartan.

E.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
E.q: For a patient at risk for heart failure who has diabetes, which drug class is recommended first?
opts: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. In stage A, at risk for heart failure, the one strongly recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes. A beta blocker enters only at stage B, once structural disease exists.
Loop diuretic such as furosemide
Diuretics treat congestion, which a stage A patient does not have. The recommended drug for an at-risk patient with diabetes is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Beta blocker as the first agent
A beta blocker is not recommended in stage A. It enters at stage B. The first drug for an at-risk patient with diabetes is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
These belong to symptomatic heart failure, strongly for reduced ejection fraction. In stage A with diabetes the drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

E.q: Which two lipoproteins are the main transporters of triglycerides?
opts: Low-density lipoprotein and lipoprotein(a)
Both are cholesterol-rich particles built on apolipoprotein B-100; neither is a main triglyceride carrier.
High-density lipoprotein and chylomicrons
Chylomicrons do carry triglyceride, but high-density lipoprotein carries cholesterol back to the liver, so the pair is half wrong.
Chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoprotein
Correct. Triglyceride transport belongs to chylomicrons (dietary fat) and very-low-density lipoprotein (made by the liver); cholesterol transport belongs to the low- and high-density classes.
Low- and high-density lipoprotein
These two are the cholesterol transporters, the 'bad' and 'good' cholesterol respectively, rather than the carriers of triglyceride.

E.io: Acute myocardial infraction
E.q: A 72-year-old woman with no current symptoms has a routine electrocardiogram showing pathologic Q waves in leads II, III and aVF. What do these Q waves indicate?
opts: A completed prior infarct
Correct. Pathologic Q waves appear hours to a day after an infarction and persist for months: they mean the infarct has already happened. They mark completed damage rather than ischemia in progress.
Subendocardial ischemia
Subendocardial ischemia shows ST depression over the ischemic region. Pathologic Q waves are the persistent sign of an infarct that has already occurred.
Coronary vasospasm
Vasospasm causes transient ST changes during an episode of rest pain that resolve. Pathologic Q waves are a lasting mark of a completed infarct.
Hyperacute ischemia now
Hyperacute T waves with ST elevation appear in the first minutes to hours of an ST-elevation infarction. Persistent Q waves without symptoms mark an old, completed infarct.

E.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
E.q: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has leg edema, crackles and breathlessness climbing stairs. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 62% and B-type natriuretic peptide is 640. Which therapy carries the strongest recommendation now?
opts: A diuretic as needed for congestion

Correct. With preserved ejection fraction and congestion, diuretics as needed carry the strong recommendation. A sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is next at moderate strength; the neprilysin combination, antagonist and receptor blocker are weak.
A beta blocker titrated to heart rate
A beta blocker is core therapy in reduced ejection fraction, not the strongest recommendation with a preserved fraction. Her congestion is treated with a diuretic as needed.
An inotrope such as dobutamine
Inotropes are for intensive care use only. With preserved fraction and congestion, the strong recommendation is a diuretic as needed.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
That pairing is for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV. With preserved fraction and congestion, the strong recommendation is a diuretic.

E.q: A 47-year-old man has blood pressure of 162/98 on three agents. His potassium is 3.1 mmol/L without diuretic use. Which screening test is appropriate?
opts: Plasma free metanephrines
Metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma, suggested by episodic headache, sweating and palpitations rather than by hypokalemia.
A low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
That screens for Cushing syndrome, suggested by proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, thin skin and broad purple striae.
Renal duplex ultrasound
Renal duplex investigates renovascular disease, suggested by an abdominal bruit and asymmetric kidneys.
A morning aldosterone to renin ratio
Correct. Resistant hypertension with unexplained hypokalemia is a classic trigger to screen, and the ratio is positive above roughly 20:1 provided the aldosterone concentration itself is adequate.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
E.q: A 52-year-old woman and her 52-year-old husband ask at a wellness visit whether their age already counts as a coronary risk factor. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Only for her
The thresholds run the other way. Women reach the age risk factor at 55 or older, men at 45 or older, so at 52 only the husband qualifies.
For neither of them
Her husband already qualifies: age is a coronary risk factor at 45 or older in men. She will reach the female threshold at 55.
Only for her husband
Correct. Age becomes a nonmodifiable coronary risk factor at 45 or older for men and 55 or older for women. At 52 he has crossed his threshold and she has not.
For both of them
They share an age but not a threshold. Men count from 45 and women from 55, so the 52-year-old woman does not yet have age as a risk factor.

E.q: Why should fundoscopy be part of the examination in every newly diagnosed hypertensive patient?
opts: The retina allows direct visualization of the microvasculature

Correct, and the findings carry prognostic weight independent of the pressure reading: retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk, and retinal arterial narrowing predicts the future development of hypertension.
It determines which antihypertensive class to start
Agent selection follows comorbidities and patient factors rather than retinal findings.
It establishes whether the hypertension is primary or secondary
Fundoscopy assesses damage rather than cause. The distinction between primary and secondary rests on the clues in the history, examination and laboratory work.
It replaces the need for renal and cardiac assessment
A normal fundoscopy does not exclude injury elsewhere, so it supplements rather than replaces assessment of the other target organs.

E.io: Acute coronary syndrome
E.q: A 46-year-old man with six hours of atypical chest discomfort has a normal electrocardiogram and two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L. Which disposition is most appropriate?
opts: Discharge with follow-up
Correct. Troponin is a tool that says who can safely go home. Two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L, far below the men's 20 ng/L, with a normal electrocardiogram rule out an infarct.
Start thrombolytic therapy
Thrombolytics treat ST-elevation infarction when catheterization is far away. His normal electrocardiogram and high-sensitivity troponin I of 4 ng/L show no infarct.
Urgent cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is for a patient with an infarct or high risk. Two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L and a normal electrocardiogram rule out a heart attack.
Admit to intensive care

Intensive care is for high-risk acute coronary syndrome, such as a TIMI (Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction) score of 3 or higher. Two not-abnormal high-sensitivity troponin I values allow safe discharge.

E.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
E.q: A 74-year-old man had a faint while urinating at night after an evening of drinking alcohol and little water. He takes an alpha-1 blocker and lisinopril. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Stand quickly to void at night
Abruptly standing from bed is part of what provokes micturition syncope; slow position changes are advised.
Drink less water in the evening
Relative dehydration is one of his predisposing factors, so restricting fluid would add to the risk.
Limit alcohol and keep hydrated
Correct. Alcohol and relative dehydration predispose him to micturition syncope, and reflex hypotension is managed by reducing or removing the trigger.
Start midodrine at bedtime
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is not listed for situational reflex syncope.

E.q: A 60-year-old hypertensive man has an electrocardiogram that does not meet voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, but he is breathless on exertion and has a significant murmur. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Conclude that hypertensive heart disease is excluded
A normal electrocardiogram specifically does not exclude hypertensive heart disease, which is the practical consequence of poor sensitivity.
Order a chest radiograph to measure the cardiac size
Radiography is appropriate when pulmonary edema or cardiomegaly is suspected, but it does not assess ventricular mass, geometry or function.
Repeat the electrocardiogram in six months
Repeating an insensitive test does not answer the question that echocardiography would.
Proceed to echocardiography

Correct. The voltage criteria are specific but NOT sensitive, so false negatives are common. Unexplained dyspnea and a significant murmur are both indications for echocardiography in their own right. A normal tracing does not exclude hypertrophy.

E.io: Non-ST segment elevation
E.q: A 64-year-old man is diagnosed with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His oxygen saturation (SpO2) is 97% on room air and his heart rate is 88. Which is part of his initial treatment?
opts: A thrombolytic agent
Thrombolytics are reserved for an ST-elevation infarction when percutaneous intervention is two or more hours away. A non-ST-elevation infarction is treated like unstable angina.
A calcium channel blocker
A beta blocker, not a calcium channel blocker, is used to reduce myocardial oxygen demand in the initial treatment. Calcium channel blockers do not improve prognosis after infarction overall.
Supplemental oxygen
Oxygen is given only if the oxygen saturation is below 91%. At 97% on room air, supplemental oxygen is withheld because it causes peripheral vasoconstriction.
Chewable aspirin

Correct. Unstable angina and non-ST-elevation infarction are a medical emergency treated alike: chewable aspirin, a beta blocker and intravenous nitrates if appropriate, and dual antiplatelet therapy with or without anticoagulation.

E.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
E.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after taking a large quantity of a relative's blood pressure pills. His pressure dropped suddenly over the past hour and he is dizzy. How is his hypotension best classified?
opts: Long-lasting acute infectious hypotension
Infection causes long-lasting acute hypotension, and nothing here suggests bacteremia or sepsis.
Chronic hypotension from a cardiac cause
Chronic hypotension comes from cardiogenic causes such as cardiomyopathy and waxes and wanes over time.
Acute hypotension from a toxic cause
Correct. Medication-mediated overdose is a toxic cause of acute hypotension, which is of sudden onset, usually symptomatic and tied to a specific trigger.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a postural fall from autonomic failure, not a sudden drop after an overdose.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
E.q: A 60-year-old woman has vomited for 2 days, has dry mucous membranes, and fainted on standing; her heart rate rises from 70 to 98 as her pressure falls 30 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Start midodrine for autonomic failure
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; a brisk heart rate rise shows her autonomic reflex is intact.
Treat the underlying volume loss
Correct. Her intact heart rate response and dryness point to volume depletion, and orthostasis is managed by treating the underlying condition.
Refer her for an echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope, which nothing in her history suggests.
Order a tilt-table test first
Tilt-table testing belongs to the tachycardia syndrome; her diagnosis is already clear from orthostatic readings.

E.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
E.q: A 57-year-old woman presents with an average blood pressure of 168/104 and no comorbidities. How should treatment begin?
opts: One first-line agent, titrated upward as needed
A single agent is reasonable in stage 1; at this level two complementary agents are considered.
Two complementary first-line agents

Correct. Pressure substantially above goal is the reason to start with two rather than one, and a single pill is preferred because adherence is itself a major determinant of control. A single-pill combination is preferred.
Four agents from the outset
Two complementary first-line agents are considered when pressure is substantially above goal, not four.
Lifestyle measures alone for six months
Lifestyle applies to every category, but it does not replace medication at this level.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
E.q: A 45-year-old man has a fasting triglyceride of 780 mg/dL and low-density lipoprotein of 110 mg/dL. Diabetes, kidney disease, alcoholism and hypothyroidism have been excluded. Which management plan is most appropriate?
opts: Observation with a recheck in a year
Triglyceride above 500 carries a risk of acute pancreatitis, so it is treated now rather than watched.
Bile acid sequestrant with no diet change
Sequestrants lower low-density lipoprotein as adjuncts; they do not address triglyceride above 500.
Ezetimibe with a high-carbohydrate diet
Ezetimibe lowers triglyceride only 5% to 10%, and excess carbohydrate raises hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion.
Very low-fat diet plus a fibrate
Correct. Above 500 mg/dL the plan is a very low-fat diet (under 15% of calories from fat), weight management, physical activity and a fibrate, niacin or both.

E.q: In a patient aged 0 to 19 years, what does a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia call for?
opts: Apheresis in every case
Apheresis is the treatment of choice for the homozygous form specifically, not for every young patient with the diagnosis.
Lifestyle alone until age 40
Waiting until 40 ignores an inherited receptor defect; a familial hypercholesterolemia diagnosis in youth leads to a statin.
A statin
Correct. In the 0-to-19 age group, lifestyle prevents or reduces risk, and a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia leads to a statin.
A fibrate
Triglyceride is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia; in the 0-to-19 group the diagnosis leads to a statin.

E.io: Pulmonic stenosis
E.q: A 21-year-old woman has pulmonic stenosis seen incidentally on an echocardiogram. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Refer to a cardiologist
Correct. Whether congenital or related to heart failure, pulmonic stenosis present on echocardiogram should be referred to a cardiologist.
Balloon valvuloplasty now
Balloon valvuloplasty is for severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms. An incidental finding is first referred to a cardiologist.
No further evaluation
Pulmonic stenosis on an echocardiogram is referred to a cardiologist, congenital or not, even though mild disease needs no treatment.
Start lifelong warfarin
Warfarin is for mechanical heart valves, not a native stenotic valve. The step for pulmonic stenosis on echocardiogram is cardiology referral.

Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
E.q: A 47-year-old man with borderline-high low-density lipoprotein asks which foods can help lower his cholesterol. Which dietary advice is most appropriate?
opts: Add more saturated and trans fat
Saturated and trans fat down-regulate hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptors and raise low-density lipoprotein, the opposite of the goal.
Eat more refined carbohydrate
Excess carbohydrate increases hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion, worsening the lipid profile.
Add soluble fiber and plant sterols

Correct. Therapeutic lifestyle changes include less saturated fat, more soluble fiber and plant stanols or sterols, cholesterol-lowering substances found in grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds.
Cut out all vegetables
Vegetables are among the natural sources of plant stanols and sterols, which lower cholesterol.

E.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
E.q: A 44-year-old man describes episodes of pounding headache, drenching sweats, palpitations and pallor, each lasting about twenty minutes. Between episodes he feels well. His blood pressure is 176/104 during an episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pheochromocytoma
Correct. The five Ps are pressure, perspiration, palpitations, pallor and tremor, and the paroxysmal pattern with well intervals is what distinguishes it from sustained hypertension.
Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea drives sustained sympathetic activation through nocturnal hypoxemia, presenting with snoring and daytime sleepiness rather than daytime paroxysms.
Hyperthyroidism
Thyroid excess raises cardiac output with predominantly systolic elevation and persistent symptoms rather than episodic pallor and sweating.
Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism raises pressure steadily with hypokalemia rather than producing discrete symptomatic paroxysms.

E.io: Mitral stenosis
E.q: Which electrocardiogram finding is expected in mitral stenosis?
opts: A short PR (P wave to QRS) interval
A short interval between atrial and ventricular activation is not a mitral stenosis finding. The expected change is left atrial abnormality, often with atrial fibrillation.
Right atrial enlargement alone
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy is the tricuspid stenosis pattern. Mitral stenosis shows left atrial abnormality.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is the electrocardiogram finding of severe aortic stenosis and chronic aortic regurgitation. Mitral stenosis spares the left ventricle and shows left atrial abnormality.
Left atrial abnormality

Correct. Mitral stenosis shows left atrial abnormality on the electrocardiogram, atrial fibrillation is common in severe disease, and right ventricular hypertrophy appears once pulmonary hypertension develops.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
E.q: A 64-year-old woman with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy has an ejection fraction of 30% after six months of optimized guideline-directed therapy. She is breathless with exertion but not at rest and is otherwise healthy. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator
Correct. She meets every criterion: non-ischemic cardiomyopathy with ejection fraction 35% or less, class II, optimal guideline-directed therapy and life expectancy of at least one year.
A calcium channel blocker for rate
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. She meets the criteria for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.
Inotropes in the intensive care unit
She is stable and class II; inotropes are for critical illness. She meets the criteria for an implantable defibrillator.
Heart transplant listing right away
Transplant is for failure beyond control; she is class II. She meets the criteria for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
E.q: Which electrocardiogram findings indicate left ventricular hypertrophy?
opts: Tall R waves in V5 and V6, deep S in V1 and V2
Correct. Tall R waves in V5 and V6 with deep S waves in V1 and V2 indicate left ventricular hypertrophy, the structural change that underlies the diastolic chain.
Low voltage across every limb and chest lead
Low voltage is the opposite of the hypertrophy pattern, which shows tall R waves in V5 and V6 and deep S waves in V1 and V2.
T-wave inversions confined to leads V1 to V3
Those inversions belong to right heart strain. Left ventricular hypertrophy shows tall R in V5 and V6 and deep S in V1 and V2.
Right axis deviation and right bundle branch block
Those belong to right heart strain, with T-wave inversions in V1 to V3. Hypertrophy shows tall R in V5 and V6 and deep S in V1 and V2.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
E.q: A 72-year-old man with diabetic autonomic neuropathy takes midodrine but still has lightheadedness on standing. He has no supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat). Which addition is most appropriate?
opts: Vasopressin in clinic
Vasopressin, like the other pressors, is reserved for the emergency department and intensive care.
Phenylephrine at home
Phenylephrine is a pressor used only in the emergency department and intensive care, never as a home medication.
Droxidopa as an adjunct
Correct. Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is usually used as an adjunct with midodrine or fludrocortisone rather than on its own.
Strict fluid restriction
Restricting fluid lowers volume and worsens orthostatic symptoms; it is not an add-on treatment.

E.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
E.q: A 58-year-old woman has a week of fatigue and mild breathlessness. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 250. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Acute heart failure is ruled out
Rule-out applies only below 100. At 250 the level sits in the indeterminate range of 100 to 400.
Acute heart failure is likely
Acute heart failure becomes likely only above 900. At 250 the result sits in the indeterminate range.
Heart failure is likely
Heart failure becomes likely only above 400. At 250 the result sits in the indeterminate range.
Indeterminate for heart failure
Correct. Between 100 and 400 the peptide has no useful sensitivity or specificity for heart failure, so the clinical picture and imaging have to settle the question.

E.io: Mitral regurgitation
E.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic mitral regurgitation also has atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension. He is not yet a surgical candidate. Which is part of his medical management?
opts: Ignoring the rhythm for now
Atrial fibrillation is one of the comorbidities that medical management of mitral regurgitation specifically treats, along with pulmonary hypertension.
A nitrate to lower his preload
Avoiding nitrates is the preload rule for aortic stenosis. The named medical steps in mitral regurgitation are raising forward output and treating atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.
Balloon valvotomy of the valve
Balloon valvotomy treats severe mitral stenosis, not a leaking valve. Medical care for mitral regurgitation treats the comorbid atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.
Treating his atrial fibrillation

Correct. Medical treatment of mitral regurgitation aims to increase forward cardiac output while reducing regurgitant volume, and to treat comorbidities such as atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.

E.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
E.q: A 66-year-old woman in a clinic has hypotension from a suspected overwhelming infection and is awaiting transfer. Which therapy should not be started in the clinic?
opts: Reviewing her medications
Reviewing medications is appropriate, since medication-mediated hypotension is treated by reducing the offending drug.
Arranging urgent transfer
Arranging transfer is appropriate, because the drugs her hypotension may need are used only in the emergency department and intensive care.
Repeating her vital signs
Repeated readings are appropriate, since each reading is only a snapshot in time.
A norepinephrine infusion
Correct. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
E.q: An 84-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure has progressive symptoms despite treatment of its cause and is not a transplant candidate. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Inotropes started for home use
Inotropes are for intensive care use only. Without a transplant option, palliative care focused on symptoms is the route.
Calcium channel blocker for comfort
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. Without a transplant option, palliative care focused on symptoms is the route.
Discharge without follow-up care
Withdrawing care is not the plan. Without a transplant option, palliative care focused on symptoms is the route.
Palliative care focused on symptoms

Correct. Right-sided failure is treated like left-sided failure, with symptom management, treatment of the cause, heart transplant or palliative care. When transplant is not an option, palliative care is the route.

E.io: Mitral valve prolapse
E.q: A 24-year-old woman has a mid-systolic click at the apex. An echocardiogram is ordered. Which finding confirms the suspected valve problem?
opts: A calcified, narrowed aortic valve
Thickened, calcified aortic leaflets with reduced opening are the echo finding of aortic stenosis. Prolapse shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.
A dilated tricuspid annulus
A dilated tricuspid annulus causes tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension. The echo finding of prolapse is thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.
A dilated aortic root
A dilated aortic root is a cause of aortic regurgitation found on echo. Prolapse is confirmed by thickened, redundant mitral leaflets over 5 mm.
Thick, redundant mitral leaflets

Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed by echocardiogram showing thickened, redundant mitral leaflets greater than 5 mm, flaring into the left atrium during systole, from myxomatous degeneration.

E.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
E.io: Acute myocardial infraction
E.q: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a large myocardial infarction and develops hypotension, cool extremities and falling urine output from cardiogenic shock. Which infarct feature makes this complication more common?
opts: Reperfusion inside 90 minutes
A door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes is the goal because time is muscle; prompt reperfusion limits damage. Shock is more common with a left-sided infarct, not with timely care.
A right-sided infarct
Right ventricular infarction can tip into shock if nitroglycerin drops the preload it depends on, but as an infarct complication, cardiogenic shock is more common after left-sided infarcts.
A small subendocardial infarct
A subendocardial infarct involves only the inner wall and shows ST depression. Cardiogenic shock follows loss of pump function and is more common with left-sided infarcts.
A left-sided infarct

Correct. Cardiogenic shock is more common in left-sided myocardial infarctions, and left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality. The left ventricle supplies the systemic output that shock takes away.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for atherosclerosis and lipid disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 6. infant 7. child 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
E.q: An 8-year-old boy has firm yellow nodules over the backs of his hands, elbows and heels. His total cholesterol is 780 mg/dL with a normal triglyceride, and both parents have markedly elevated cholesterol. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The heterozygous form runs low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 mg/dL and is usually found incidentally on screening, not with childhood xanthomas and cholesterol near 800.
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Chylomicronemia raises triglyceride above 1000 mg/dL and causes eruptive papules and pancreatitis; this child has a normal triglyceride.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia

Correct. Presentation in childhood with cutaneous xanthomas on the hands, elbows and heels, total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 mg/dL, normal triglyceride and two affected parents fits two mutant alleles.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 mg/dL with palmar xanthomas, not isolated cholesterol near 800.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
E.q: A 23-year-old woman has palpitations and dizziness on standing that improve when lying down, and her standing heart rate climbs well above baseline without a fall in pressure. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
opts: A tilt-table test
Correct. The tilt-table test is the listed diagnostic test for the syndrome, with a sensitivity of about 40% and specificity above 80%.
An episode log
An episode log supports the history-based diagnosis of reflex syncope rather than confirming the tachycardia syndrome.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope such as cardiomyopathy or valve disease, not this syndrome.
A stress test
A stress test is part of the arrhythmia work-up for cardiogenic syncope rather than the confirmatory test here.

E.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
E.q: A 75-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction heart failure faints abruptly while walking after a brief racing heartbeat. After his electrocardiogram, which further test helps capture an intermittent arrhythmia?
opts: Orthostatic vitals
Orthostatic readings test for a postural fall; an abrupt faint after palpitations needs rhythm monitoring.
Cardiac monitoring
Correct. The arrhythmia work-up is an electrocardiogram, cardiac monitoring and a stress test, together with cardiology consultation.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is listed for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not for capturing an arrhythmia.
A patient log alone
A log supports reflex syncope; an intermittent arrhythmia is captured by monitoring the rhythm.

E.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
E.q: How do hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism differ in their effect on blood pressure?
opts: Hyperthyroidism raises vascular resistance and hypothyroidism raises output
The mechanisms are the other way round: raised output belongs to hyperthyroidism and raised resistance to hypothyroidism.
Both raise systolic pressure with tachycardia
Only hyperthyroidism produces that pattern. Hypothyroidism raises vascular resistance with diastolic elevation and bradycardia.
Neither affects blood pressure
Both are described as contributors, which is why thyroid-stimulating hormone is among the baseline screening tests.
Hyperthyroidism raises systolic; hypothyroidism raises diastolic

Correct, and the heart rate separates them further: tachycardia accompanies the systolic pattern and bradycardia the diastolic one, so the pulse points to which is operating. Hyperthyroidism does it by raising cardiac output, hypothyroidism by raising vascular resistance.

E.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
E.q: A 71-year-old woman with 20 years of poorly controlled hypertension has ankle swelling that has recently spread to crackles at both lung bases. Blood pressure is 176/98. A fourth heart sound (a sound in late diastole just before the first heart sound) is heard. Echocardiogram shows thick left ventricular walls with an ejection fraction of 62%. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy
Ischemic cardiomyopathy leads the systolic chain with a reduced ejection fraction and low-normal pressure. Her hypertension, fourth sound and preserved fraction are diastolic.
Diastolic failure from hypertrophic disease

Correct. The diastolic chain is complete: hypertension driving hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a fourth heart sound from atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle, peripheral then pulmonary edema, and a preserved ejection fraction.
Systolic failure from dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy gives a weak squeeze, a reduced ejection fraction, a normal or low pressure and a third sound. Her findings are the diastolic chain.
High-output failure from thyroid excess
Hyperthyroid high-output failure brings tachycardia and palpitations from increased demand. Her long hypertension and fourth sound point to diastolic failure.

E.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
E.q: A 49-year-old man who drinks heavily is admitted for an unrelated procedure. On the second day his blood pressure rises sharply. What explains this?
opts: Only chronic excess raises pressure; withdrawal has no effect
Withdrawal is specifically capable of producing acute severe hypertension, which is what is happening here.
Alcohol withdrawal can produce acute severe hypertension
Correct, and the relationship runs both ways: excess alcohol raises blood pressure chronically, and withdrawal from it can raise it acutely.
Moderate alcohol should be resumed for cardiovascular benefit
Starting or resuming alcohol for cardiovascular benefit is specifically not recommended; intake is limited to low-risk thresholds.
Alcohol lowers pressure, so stopping returns him to baseline
Excess alcohol raises rather than lowers blood pressure, so this reverses the relationship.

E.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
E.q: A 58-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve asks whether she could take daily aspirin instead of her current anticoagulant. Which long-term therapy is recommended for her?
opts: A vitamin K antagonist
Correct. With a mechanical heart valve, vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over no vitamin K antagonist and over antiplatelet agents. Warfarin is the one most commonly used.
No drug after one year
A mechanical valve requires lifelong anticoagulation; it is biological valves that stop after the postoperative period. She stays on a vitamin K antagonist.
Aspirin in place of it
Antiplatelet agents are specifically ranked below vitamin K antagonist therapy for a mechanical valve. Aspirin cannot replace her anticoagulant.
Heparin every day
Heparin bridges gaps in warfarin around surgery; it is not the long-term therapy. The recommendation is a vitamin K antagonist.

E.io: Stable
E.q: Which platelet-inhibiting approach is more effective for preventing future anginal attacks?
opts: Aspirin alone
Aspirin alone is a platelet inhibitor for chronic stable angina, but the two agents are more effective together. The stronger approach is aspirin with clopidogrel.
Aspirin with clopidogrel

Correct. Aspirin and clopidogrel are both platelet-inhibiting agents for preventing future attacks, and they are more effective used together. Aspirin is used in chronic stable angina and survivors of acute coronary syndrome.
Warfarin with heparin
Warfarin and heparin are anticoagulants, not platelet inhibitors. For preventing future anginal attacks, aspirin with clopidogrel is more effective than either agent alone.
Clopidogrel alone
Clopidogrel alone is a P2Y12 receptor antagonist, but it is more effective when paired with aspirin. The stronger approach is aspirin with clopidogrel.

E.io: Tricuspid stenosis
E.q: A 44-year-old woman has a mid-diastolic rumble at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Which electrocardiogram finding is most expected?
opts: Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy is pulmonic stenosis, where the right ventricle is pressure loaded. Tricuspid stenosis enlarges the right atrium.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. Tricuspid stenosis obstructs inflow from the right atrium to the right ventricle, so the electrocardiogram shows right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy.
Left atrial abnormality
Left atrial abnormality is the mitral stenosis electrocardiogram. Tricuspid stenosis dilates the right atrium instead.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy belongs to aortic stenosis and chronic aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid stenosis shows right atrial enlargement.

Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
E.q: What is the most important part of diagnosing the source of orthostatic syncope?
opts: A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is the listed test for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and its low sensitivity makes it weak as a primary tool.
Serum electrolytes
Laboratory tests help exclude metabolic or infectious contributors, but the history is what identifies the source of orthostatic syncope.
The history
Correct. History is the most important portion of accurately diagnosing the source of orthostatic syncope, or of referring to the right specialty for confirmation.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope. The source of orthostatic syncope is found mainly through the history.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. E.q: A 38-year-old man with untreated heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia asks why treatment matters when he feels well. Which complication is he at risk of?
opts: Loss of vision
Corneal arcus is a common marker of the disorder rather than its danger; the threat is premature coronary disease.
Sudden death in childhood
Sudden childhood death is the devastating complication of the homozygous form; he is an adult with one mutant allele.
A premature heart attack
Correct. Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia accounts for up to 5% of premature heart attacks in men under 55 and women under 65, and it causes premature atherosclerotic disease.
Acute pancreatitis
Pancreatitis is the risk of triglyceride above 500; triglyceride is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia.

E.io: Angina pectoris
E.q: A 49-year-old woman has anginal chest pain with ST changes, and her physician suspects microvascular angina. Which test is required before that diagnosis can be made?
opts: Coronary angiography
Correct. Microvascular angina is a diagnosis of exclusion, and it requires angiography to rule out coronary artery disease; the arteries must be shown to be normal before the label applies.
Coronary calcium score
A calcium score is risk stratification for future disease, not a test that excludes coronary artery disease. Microvascular angina needs angiography showing normal arteries.
Exercise treadmill test
An exercise treadmill test can show ischemic changes but cannot show whether the coronary arteries are normal. Microvascular angina requires angiography to rule out coronary artery disease.
Transthoracic echocardiogram
An echocardiogram shows wall motion, such as hypokinesia or akinesia, but not the coronary lumen. Excluding coronary artery disease for microvascular angina requires angiography.

E.q: A 17-year-old girl began isotretinoin for severe acne three months ago. Her triglyceride has risen from 120 to 410 mg/dL, with normal thyroid and kidney function. Which is the most likely cause of the rise?
opts: Familial chylomicronemia
Chylomicronemia usually raises triglyceride above 1000 with pancreatitis; a rise that tracks a new drug points to the drug.
Isotretinoin
Correct. Isotretinoin, used for acne, can elevate triglyceride, as can estrogen, glucocorticoids, beta blockers and bexarotene.
Anabolic steroids
Anabolic steroids decrease high-density lipoprotein; they are not the triglyceride-raising acne therapy.
Hypercholesterolemia
Hypercholesterolemia is a raised low-density lipoprotein state, not a cause of a new triglyceride rise.

E.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
E.io: ST segment elevation
E.q: Which drug is avoided in a right ventricular infarct?
opts: Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is a P2Y12 antagonist given once catheterization is confirmed. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.
Heparin
A heparin drip is given once catheterization is confirmed, whatever the territory. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.
Aspirin
Chewable aspirin is given in every ST-elevation infarction, right ventricular or not. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.
Nitroglycerin

Correct. In a right ventricular infarct nitroglycerin is not given: lowering preload removes the Frank-Starling support the failing right ventricle depends on, dropping output and precipitating shock.

E.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
E.q: Primary tricuspid regurgitation from infective endocarditis is typical of whom?
opts: Children with tetralogy of Fallot
Tetralogy of Fallot commonly includes pulmonic stenosis. Tricuspid endocarditis is typical of intravenous drug users.
Intravenous drug users
Correct. Primary tricuspid regurgitation comes from infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users. Endocarditis from other sources more often involves the mitral valve.
Healthy women aged 15 to 30
Healthy women 15 to 30 are the typical patients with mitral valve prolapse. Tricuspid endocarditis is typical of intravenous drug users.
Adults older than 70
Over 70 the leading valve problem is degenerative aortic stenosis. Primary tricuspid regurgitation from endocarditis is typical of intravenous drug users.

E.q: A 65-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and numb feet has a 30 mmHg standing pressure fall with a heart rate rise of only 3 beats and no sign of dehydration. What is the most likely mechanism of her syncope?
opts: Reduced volume from fluid loss
Fluid loss is the non-neurogenic mechanism, and it is usually accompanied by dehydration and a brisk heart rate rise.
A fast rhythm reducing output
A fast arrhythmia reducing output is cardiogenic syncope, often with abrupt collapse and palpitations rather than a flat heart rate.
A vagal surge with vasodilation
A vagal surge with sympathetic inhibition is the vasovagal reflex chain, which is transient and triggered rather than postural.
Inadequate norepinephrine release
Correct. Autonomic dysfunction leaves too little norepinephrine released from sympathetic postganglionic neurons, so vessels fail to constrict and the heart rate rises less than expected.

E.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
E.q: A 45-year-old man with known pulmonic regurgitation now has fatigue, ankle edema, distended neck veins and ascites. Which process explains these findings?
opts: Left-sided heart failure
Left-sided failure causes orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and rales. Edema, distended neck veins and ascites from a pulmonic lesion are right-sided failure.
Low-output hypotension
His findings are congestive, not low-output. Right ventricular overload from pulmonic regurgitation produces right-sided heart failure with edema and ascites.
Right-sided heart failure

Correct. Retrograde flow from the pulmonary artery overloads the right ventricle, and the symptoms of pulmonic regurgitation are those of right-sided heart failure: fatigue, peripheral edema, jugular venous distension and ascites.
Pulmonary edema only
Pulmonary edema is the congestion of left-sided failure. Peripheral edema, neck vein distension and ascites mean right-sided heart failure.
